title: Are You Okay... Really?
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: We ask it out of habit every single day, but we rarely listen for the truth. "How are you? Are you okay?" "Yeah, I'm fine." It's the ultimate American defense mechanism. We live in a culture that glorifies the grind, praises independence, and tells us to "fake it till we make it." So when things get heavy, our language shrinks. We reduce an entire ocean of burnout, anxiety, and quiet exhaustion into a single automatic wall. "Have you been crying?" "No, just tired." "Just tired." It's the perfect cover-up. Because nobody questions it. In a world where everyone is exhausted, it's easy to hide. But there's a massive difference between needing sleep and being tired of waking up feeling empty. Depression doesn't always look like tears or dramatic breakdowns. In reality, it looks like complete isolation. It's sitting in a crowded room in New York or a quiet suburb in Ohio, surrounded by people, yet feeling entirely invisible. It's building walls so high that even the people who love you can't reach you. "Do you want to talk about it? You can tell me anything." "No, there's nothing to talk about." When someone pushes you away, it's rarely a rejection. Most of the time, they literally just don't have the words. How do you explain a profound sadness that has no specific cause? How do you tell your family or your friends that your life looks great on paper, but feels completely hollow inside? So they say "No," hoping you'll leave them alone, but secretly praying that you won't. They don't need a lecture, they don't need a motivational speech, toxic positivity, or a 10-step plan on how to fix their life. "Do you want a hug?" "Yeah." Sometimes saving a life doesn't take a hero, it doesn't take the perfect words. It just takes the willingness to sit in the dark with someone. The most powerful thing you can say to someone who is drowning isn't "I understand." It's simply, "I'm here, and you don't have to carry this alone." Right now, millions of people are fighting battles they don't talk about. And ironically, the people who spend all their energy checking on everyone else are often the ones drowning the fastest. Do me a favor today. Don't just send a casual text asking "How's it going?" Call someone, look them in the eyes, break through the automatic answers. Because you never truly know how heavy a burden is until you offer to help hold it. Check on your people today.
caption: A male speaker delivers a poignant and reflective monologue about mental health, isolation, and the superficiality of daily social interactions. His voice is calm, warm, and deeply expressive, spoken with a slow, deliberate pace that allows each word to resonate. A soft, melancholic piano melody plays continuously in the background, enhancing the emotional depth and sincere tone of the narration. The speaker discusses how common phrases like "I'm fine" and "just tired" are often used as defense mechanisms to hide deep-seated anxiety, depression, and exhaustion. He encourages listeners to move beyond casual check-ins, call their loved ones, and offer genuine presence and support, noting that sometimes saving a life simply requires sitting with someone in their darkness. The audio is clean and intimate, with well-balanced sound design.

transcription: I won't be weak. You gave me a voice, and yet I was weak. You taught me to stand, and taught me to speak. Though I was depressed, and though I was sad, you pushed me and loved me enough to be glad. With you by my side, the heavens would stand. My pain and my anger, my feelings command. You've been there for me and taught me enough, though there would be days I went through some stuff. The things that I saw and things that I've seen, I've struggled in silence, and that's what I mean. You stood by my side and gave me a voice, though I'm writing these words, you know it's my choice. So deeply depressed and deeply in pain, I wrote you these words with feelings I gained. You pushed me enough to fight through the shame. I took back my power and gained back my name. I won't be weak.

transcription: Crazy. You thought I was crazy for loving you much. For so many years, I would dream of your touch. My body would ooze with feelings of love. Though my feelings for you, they say is enough. But then you would lie and slander my name. They laughed and they laughed and put me to shame. You gave me a voice when I didn't feel heard. I'm deeply depressed that I wrote you these words. The things that you said that caused me to break. So misunderstood that my body would shake. You thought I was crazy for loving you well. I heard what you said, that's a story you tell. My heart and my soul were destroyed on that day. Yet my feelings for you would never go away. You slandered my name and made me look weak. So I wrote you these words with things that would speak. Crazy.

title: Inside the Mind of Someone Who Feels Alone | Deep Narration About Loneliness
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Sometimes the loneliest feeling isn't when you're alone, it's when you're surrounded by people and still feel like you don't belong. The room is full of voices, laughter, conversations, noise, but somehow, none of it reaches you. You smile when they look at you, you nod like you're listening, you say you're fine, because it's easier than explaining what's going on inside your head. Sometimes you hold your phone, staring at the screen, wanting to text someone, but not knowing who would understand. You start typing, then delete everything, because how do you explain a feeling you don't even understand yourself? Outside, the world keeps moving. People walk with purpose, cars pass by. Everyone seems to be going somewhere. And you wonder why you feel stuck in the same place, every single day. Loneliness isn't always silence. Sometimes it's noise that doesn't include you. Sometimes it's laughing with people, but feeling nothing inside. Sometimes it's going home and realizing, no one really knows how you feel. You sit in your room, the lights are off. The only sound is your own thoughts, and they don't stop. You ask yourself questions: Why do I feel like this? Why can't I connect? Why does everything feel so far away? But even on days like this, when the silence feels too loud, a small part of you is still there. Still breathing, still trying, still hoping. And sometimes, that's enough. Sometimes, making it through the day while feeling alone is already a victory. And maybe tomorrow feels lighter. Maybe not easier, but a little less heavy. And that small difference can keep you going. You can follow for more simple psychology explained.

title: The Foundry Pitch Competition Informational Video
transcription: Before starting Amplab, I definitely was the type of person to not go outside the box and kind of just do what was asked of me. But then coming to Amplab and having my brother be here before, I kind of saw how important it is to step outside the box to get something out of Amplab. You have access to so many connections and like a huge network here, it's crazy. So using that network to really help set your business apart was a big thing for me. So here at Amplab, they focus on problem-solving a lot. You need to have a problem to be able to come up with solutions. So I looked into my own life and kind of took my love for animals a part of that and saw my dog was having issues with nutrition and saw how big of a role nutrition actually plays in pets' lives. So I saw his food allergies and his skin issues and how they were connected, so I wanted to create a pet food business that focused on the customization of nutrition and showed how high-quality ingredients can really help with that. So preparing for the Foundry was a lot, but it was very empowering. We spent a couple weeks working on our pitch, which was five minutes long, and then we also prepared for the Q&A that the judges did. And with that, we just asked each other questions and prepared that way. My business, Tailored Bites, that me and my business partner worked on, we also competed in Innovate WithIn, so we used a lot of our Foundry prize money towards that competition. So a lot of it went to ingredients so we created a bunch of food to sell at the Fort Wayne Farmers Market that is right here by Amplab. So a lot of it was ingredients to make the meals. We had a human-grade chicken dog food. We also prepped the judges' food for the Innovate WithIn contest and created custom lunch boxes with our food in it. So anyways, without further ado, the winner of the first-ever Foundry pitch competition, Tailored Bites. I would say really put your best effort. It is really rewarding to see it all come together at the competition like seeing the months of preparation come out and to be able to show it to your family and friends and also community members is really impactful.

It's the first time undergraduate students get an opportunity to pitch to the UNSW Investment Committee for a real investment. title: The Perfect 60-Second Startup Pitch (Investors Will Remember)
transcription: The perfect 60-second startup pitch. Imagine you step into an elevator with your dream investor. You have exactly 60 seconds before the doors open. Would you know what to say? Most founders make one big mistake. They try to explain everything about their business. The truth is, your goal isn't to close the investment in 60 seconds. It's to make the investor want another conversation. Here's a simple framework that works. First, start with the problem. What pain are you solving? Keep it simple and relatable. If the investor doesn't understand the problem, they won't care about the solution. Next, explain your solution. In one sentence, describe what your company does. Avoid technical jargon or long explanations. If someone outside your industry can't understand it, it's probably too complicated. Then, explain why now. Why is this the right time for your business? Maybe a new technology has made your solution possible. Maybe customer behavior has changed. Maybe the market is growing rapidly. Investors want to know why this opportunity exists today, not 5 years ago. After that, share your traction. You don't need millions in revenue, but you do need evidence that you're making progress. That could be paying customers, user growth, partnerships, pilot programs, or even a growing waitlist. Traction reduces uncertainty and builds confidence. Finally, finish with the opportunity. Don't end by asking for money. Instead, leave the investor wanting to learn more. Give them a reason to schedule a second meeting. Remember, a great pitch doesn't answer every question. It answers just enough to create curiosity. If an investor walks away wanting to know more, you've done your job. The best founders don't overwhelm investors with information. They tell a clear story, communicate confidence, and make their business easy to understand. Because at the end of the day, investors don't invest in the longest pitch, they invest in the clearest one. title: The 5 Things Angel Investors Look for Before They Invest
transcription: How angel investors actually decide to invest. Imagine you've spent months, maybe even years, building your startup. You finally get a meeting with an angel investor. You walk in, deliver what you think is the perfect pitch, and they pass. So what happened? The truth is, angel investors aren't just investing in ideas. They're investing in founders. They're investing in execution. And most importantly, they're investing in the probability that your business can succeed. Here are the five things they're really looking for. First, the founder. This is by far the most important factor. Investors know that startups rarely go exactly according to plan. Markets change, products evolve, and unexpected problems come up all the time. They're asking themselves one simple question: Can this founder figure it out? A great founder is resilient, adaptable, and able to execute even when things don't go as planned. Second, the problem. Is it a real problem that people genuinely want solved? Or is it just a nice idea? The bigger and more painful the problem, the more valuable the solution becomes. Great businesses solve expensive problems, not minor inconveniences. Third, the market. Even an incredible product has limited potential if it's built for a tiny audience. Investors look for large growing markets because they want companies that can scale. If the opportunity isn't big enough, neither is the return. Fourth, traction. One of the biggest myths is that you need massive revenue before investors will take you seriously. That's simply not true. What investors really want is evidence that people care. That could be growing users, paying customers, partnerships, a waiting list, or strong engagement. Any sign that the market is responding positively reduces the risk of investing. And finally, why you? What's stopping another company from copying your idea tomorrow? Maybe it's your experience, maybe it's your technology, your network, your community, or simply your ability to execute faster than everyone else. The strongest startups don't just have a great idea. They have a compelling reason why they're the best team to bring that idea to life. At the end of the day, angel investing is all about reducing risk. Every customer you gain, every milestone you hit, and every problem you solve gives investors one more reason to believe. Because investors don't invest in certainty, they invest in confidence. title: Choosing the Wrong Person to Pitch Your Startup | Chinese Competition Reality
transcription: A lot of international entrepreneurs, they underestimate how important the applicant actually is for Chinese startup competitions. The applicant can make or break the deal. You can either succeed through this or you just fail. We had startups that applied twice to one competition, one year one applicant, the other year another applicant, and we figured out that it is extremely important who applies and the background of the applicant. Some startups, they choose to let an intern or a manager apply to the competition, but the problem here is that they do not have the relevant background to get through the entire process. What Chinese startup competitions usually want to see is the CEO or at least C-level applicants that have a substantial amount of equity in the startup. There are certain startup competitions, usually most of the competitions, they require at least 30% of equity in the startup. Not at this time, but usually in the process of the establishment of the startup, you should have had at one point 30% of equity. There are some competitions that do not require this. We usually highlight this in the process of supporting you to get through the startup competition, but these competitions are usually rare. And sometimes it's not really important that the CEO applies, because if your education background is not top-notch, so you don't have a master degree or a PhD, then maybe another person of your business should apply to the competition. Because usually the higher the the degree, the better the chances of getting through. So, if you have someone in your team that you can trust with the establishment of the entity in China, then you could choose a PhD manager in your company to apply to this competition. Also, please be aware that the applicant has to usually pitch through the entire process of the competition, which is usually the preliminary round, the semi-finals, the final, and usually you also have to come to China to receive the prize. So education background is extremely important, the amount of equity in the startup is extremely important, and also the relevant background is important. So if you're in biotech, but you do not have a biotech background, so you don't have a university degree in this, then it's very hard for you to get through. One plus that you can do is, if you have a Chinese team member, you can let them apply to the competition, because then usually the trust of the judges of you succeeding in the Chinese market is also higher. But if you don't have that, that's not a problem. Usually choose the one with the highest university degree and with the highest amount of shares, and make sure that this person can be and will be in China if you win a good amount, and if you can come to China. If you want to increase your chances of winning at a Chinese startup competition, reach out to us. We have helped thousands of startups to land substantial winning prizes from all different regions of the world. Subscribe to the channel to get more updates, give us a like if you also liked the content of the video, and if you want to get support in your next application, just write in the comments and we will reach out to you. Thank you for watching, and see you in the next video.

transcription: Hi, my name is Carl Gunther. I'm the founder of Seven Castle Cider. We are a beverage company from Western New York producing non-alcoholic sparkling apple cider made from our locally sourced upcycled apples that would otherwise be thrown out. Our flagship product is a modern 12 oz can made with just fresh apple juice and carbonation. No artificial additives, no added sugars, no preservatives, none of that nonsense. The non-alcoholic beverage industry is growing rapidly, but sparkling cider is being left out. Most options are seasonal, sold in large bottles, or made from concentrate. Seven Castle Cider reimagines cider as a year-round, everyday social beverage, something that belongs at dinners, weddings, celebrations, gatherings, parties, anything without alcohol being a barrier. Our mission is to create inclusive social spaces while also helping the environment and our local economy. Whether someone doesn't drink for health, faith, or personal reasons, they still deserve a drink to feel celebratory. We validated this demand through in-person tastings, parties, and over 200,000 organic social media views before launch. Operationally, we are ready to launch. We have our scheduled processes all complete. We have one last inspection for our 20-C commercial production license, and we have our sales tax authority for New York State. We are also in the talks with local co-packers so we can get our beverage produced at large scales through them. We have MSRP at 2.99 can, which gives us room for profits and growth. We are bootstrapped, we are value-driven, and we are built for sustainable growth, and we are not just a beverage. We are selling a more inclusive way for people to gather. title: Inside the VC Mindset: What Makes a Pitch Win
transcription: Hi everyone, this is Jaden Chow. Welcome to the Shark Tank PHS virtual club space. Today we're answering an important question. What is crucial if you want a VC to fund your business idea? First, what is a VC? VC stands for Venture Capitalist. A VC is someone who gives money to new businesses they believe can grow big. Instead of getting paid back like a loan, they receive part ownership of the business. If the business succeeds, they succeed, too. Because of that, VCs don't invest in just any idea. They invest in ideas that are clear, realistic, and ready to grow. That's where the winning pitch formula comes in. First is the problem. You must clearly explain a real pain point people actually have. Second, the solution. What is your product or service, and how does it work? Third, the value proposition. Why is your solution better or different from others? Fourth, the market. Who is this for, and how many people need it? Fifth, the business model. How does your idea make money? Next is traction. This is proof that people want your idea, like users, sales, or strong interest. Then comes competition. Other solutions exist. Explain who they are, and why your idea can win. Next are financials. You don't need perfect numbers, but you need to show you understand costs and revenue. Then there's the ask. How much money are you asking for, and what are you offering in return? Finally, vision and scale. Show how your idea can grow bigger in the future. If you can clearly explain all 10 of these, a VC is much more likely to listen. Thanks for watching. See you in the next lesson.

The average cost of construction projects on, on average in 2024, and I'll be happy to show you more of that in the, in detail on the side, but in 2024, the average cost of every construction project is up by 14% based on this issue, and that is slow pay, that is cost of carry, that is legal issues from mechanics liens, and such. There is an increasing amount of work happening, and less and less people to do the work, and good help is hard to find. So, if you are the contractor who pays on time, good help is not going to be nearly as hard to find. What's your, uh, market validation or traction today? We are testing our MVP as we speak. But we have a long list of people ready to go once we're ready to go. title: Why Didn't Robinhood Blame AI for Layoffs?
transcription: Why didn't Robinhood blame AI for layoffs? Robinhood is still cutting about 290 jobs, even as the company reports growth, and CEO Vlad Tenev left AI out of the memo entirely. That omission is the story, because plenty of tech companies now use AI as the reason for shrinking teams. The layoff note came from CEO Vlad Tenev, and he did something unusual for a tech chief right now. He made no mention of AI. That matters because Robinhood is not hiding behind a productivity story. The company is still shrinking its workforce while saying the business is growing, so the message is blunt. The cuts are about the company's structure, not a public AI excuse. That silence stands out because many tech companies have started using AI language in layoff announcements. Amazon, Block, Coinbase, GitLab, and Intuit have all used similar logic around leaner teams, less bureaucracy, and fewer silos. Robinhood chose not to join that script. Instead, the note pointed away from AI and toward a broader internal reset. That analyst view reinforces the point. According to Citizens JMP Securities analyst Devin Ryan, AI-driven efficiency was not the main driver of the reduction, because Robinhood has long been aggressively leveraging artificial intelligence across the organization. In other words, if AI was already part of the machine, it could not be the easy excuse for the cuts. The company's internal message had to point somewhere else. This is why the Robinhood memo is getting attention beyond one company. Tech firms are under pressure to justify layoffs at the same time AI tools are being sold as efficiency machines. Robinhood's choice suggests that the AI blame game may be losing credibility fast. If a company already uses AI broadly, saying AI caused the cuts starts to sound like a cover story, not an explanation. Robinhood cut 10% of its staff, about 290 jobs, but skipped the AI script that many peers now lean on. The real takeaway is simple. Companies are being pushed to explain restructuring more directly, especially when AI is already part of their operations.

transcription:
Tonight, new political turmoil. Alabama and Tennessee are the latest states rushing to redraw congressional districts after a Supreme Court ruling that further weakened voting rights. CBS News Congressional Correspondent Nicole Killion has the latest. Nicole.

Six months out from the midterms and the redistricting wars are intensifying for control of Congress after a recent Supreme Court ruling rolled back a key part of the Voting Rights Act. The Supreme Court's 6-to-3 decision to strike down Louisiana's congressional map hits right in the heart of Cleo Fields' seat. The district was created, first of all, Louisiana's minority population, black population, is over a third of the state. The Democrat represents the sixth congressional district, which slinks from Shreveport to Baton Rouge. But the high court ruled the newly drawn majority-minority district was an unconstitutional gerrymander since it was based on race. Congressman Troy Carter represents the other majority-minority district in New Orleans. It can wipe out both of our seats. We can, realistically, end up having six congressional districts with no African-American or Democratic representation. Ahead of early voting this weekend, Louisiana officials suspended House primary elections slated for November until the state can redraw its map. I don't think that it's going to result in a loss of minority representation, and I think that we have to give the—the people a chance to draw their districts the way the people want to see them drawn. Before the Supreme Court ruling, at least seven states had already passed new congressional maps as part of mid-decade redistricting. Now, several Southern states are using the High Court's decision to justify changes before the midterms, including Florida, Alabama, and Tennessee. It was really not about, you know, that little seat in Louisiana. It's about redistricting all over the nation. It's about the voting rights of people all over the nation. title: Supreme Court appears skeptical of mail-in ballots that arrive after Election Day
transcription: The Supreme Court just finished hearing arguments in a major case that raises questions about the legality of mail-in voting. And the conservative justices appeared skeptical about allowing states to count ballots that are mailed on time, but arrive after Election Day. The court's ruling could upend the voting process in more than a dozen states just months before this November's midterm elections. NBC News legal affairs reporter Gary Grumbach joins us now. So, Gary, this case stems from an election law in Mississippi, so walk us through it and what we've heard so far from the justices. Yeah, the oral arguments were supposed to be about whether postmarked ballots by Election Day could be accepted after Election Day, but it really turned into a debate on a variety of different election-related topics, from who is actually delivering that ballot to the state, topics about like ballot harvesting, to conversations about potentially people being able to recall their votes. For example, if you were to send something in via FedEx, could you tell FedEx, "Oh no, I actually want that back"? And then there was conversations about the length of time the state allows a voter to be able to get their ballot in and have it count. So, for example, some states do a week, some states do 21 days. Conservative Justice Samuel Alito, predictably, was pretty upset about all of this. He said, "We used to have Election Day, now it's election month or election months," guys. Gary, if the Supreme Court does rule in favor of the RNC and Mississippi's GOP, what does that essentially mean more broadly for the rest of the country when it comes to these midterms? So, Mississippi was the state that was arguing this and defending their own law, but there's 13 other states that have similar laws, so this would be a very significant thing for almost half the country here in terms of whether or not ballots would be allowed to be counted after Election Day. You have a map there that shows states, both red and blue states, that we're looking at there. And it also specifically relates to some of these military ballots, right? Folks that are serving overseas in our military, especially right now, uh may not be able to get their ballots in on time even though they are postmarked by Election Day. We will have to see exactly how the justices write this opinion, which we should be getting it by the end of June. We thank you for watching, and remember, stay updated on breaking news and top stories on the NBC News app or watch live on our YouTube channel.

title: Supreme Court weakens the Voting Rights Act after 61 years
transcription: The US Supreme Court dealt a blow to the landmark Voting Rights Act on Wednesday after knocking out a major pillar of the law that had protected against racial discrimination in voting and representation. In the six decades since it was signed, the Voting Rights Act became one of the most consequential laws in the nation's history, preventing discrimination against minorities at the ballot box. It also helped elect Black and Hispanic representatives at all levels of government. But on Wednesday, the Supreme Court hollowed out the landmark civil rights era law by striking down a majority Black congressional district in Louisiana. That ruling could provide an open door for political mapmakers to undermine minority representation. The Voting Rights Act was signed into law by President Lyndon B. Johnson on August 6, 1965, five months after the Bloody Sunday attack on civil rights marchers in Selma, Alabama, gave momentum to the bill. Wherever there is discrimination, this law will strike down all restrictions used to deny the people the right to vote. In recent years, AP reporter Gary Fields sat down with some of the people who were pivotal to the birth of the Act. After having talked to these individuals and to a number of other people about why voting rights was so important, the reason for why they were so important then hasn't changed now. In a democracy or a republic such as ourselves, the vote is the thing that you have that is the coin of the realm that allows you to say I'm a full participant in this society, in this endeavor that we call the United States of America. The question now is what comes next for minority representatives and the communities they represent.

title: Supreme Court Steps In After Judge Orders Trump Arrested Live—Emergency Appeal Changes Everything.
transcription:
The sealed 94-page leak: What nobody is connecting yet.

A sealed 94-page federal grand jury transcript leaked Tuesday night, and the legal fallout is already escalating. Federal grand jury testimony is classified as secret under Rule 6 of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, meaning this document was never supposed to exist in the public domain. Yet, at 11:47 p.m. on Tuesday, the full unredacted transcript hit ProPublica's servers. Someone on the inside broke protocol to leak it, which is a federal felony in itself. However, the true significance lies within the contents of the testimony, specifically, brand new sworn statements provided by former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson during an undisclosed session in January 2026. Unlike her previous public appearances, this fourth session under oath involved different prosecutors, different targets, and crucial documentary evidence. On page 12 of the transcript, when asked if she maintained personal knowledge of White House communications, Hutchinson revealed that she kept a personal record comprising text message screenshots, calendar entries, and three handwritten journals. Because these were maintained as personal records, rather than official government property, they fall outside standard executive privilege claims and cannot be shielded as easily. Hutchinson essentially created her own paper trail, which has now become central to the prosecution's case. The transcript lays out a detailed timeline of post-election strategy. Page 18 introduces Exhibit 47, a November 9, 2024, text message from Mark Meadows instructing Hutchinson to establish a direct line with former DOJ official Jeffrey Clark and then Michigan Senate Majority Leader Mike Shirkey. Page 23 details a November 11th conference call arranged by Hutchinson featuring Donald Trump, Mark Meadows, Jeffrey Clark, Mike Shirkey, Rudy Giuliani, an Arizona State Senator, and Hutchinson herself. According to her testimony, the explicit topic of the call was developing strategies to delay election certification in Michigan and Arizona, focusing directly on disrupting the certification process, rather than pursuing standard court challenges.

What did that phrase mean to you in, in musical terms? Well, uh, just as a quick aside, the thing is this, the, the DEVOs love R&B. They grew up listening to R&B. So when I came on board, I made really sure that the bottom end of their records was really R&B. There was, the band was a small band. It was not meant to have lots of overdubs. It was, should be, it was a simple band. Everyone played their part, one part each, right? When they played together, it was an ensemble. But it was more like a string quartet. It was tight and it was together, but it had an R&B bottom end. And I made very sure that that stuck, that the bottom end, the kick in the bass, were the R&B, had the R&B feel. And then they put the, the monster on the top. But it was an R&B body with a, with an alien head. That's what DEVO is. Yeah. When you first heard it, do-do-do-do-do, ping, dow, were you thinking? Five up, two down. Da-da-da-da-da, five notes. Bam-bam, two notes down. Very simple, very easy to remember, very impulsive feel. Those guys are marvelous. Mark is a marvelous songwriter. Jerry knows how to really write the lyrics. Jerry is a real politician. And you know, he just had a baby last year or the year before. And he's, He's pushing 70. But they also had that genius in the idea of the, uh, image, you know, the look. Yeah. When you look at their live show, you can, when you look at their live show, you really realize how really tight and highly organized they are. They are absolute geniuses at this stuff. All we had to do is just not drip stuff all over them, sugar coating and syrup and bullshit, and just let them play their instruments and play out, and maintain their impulsive energy. title: How Indie Creators Are Building Shows With Shorts
transcription: Vertical short-form animation used to feel to me like this weird side quest. Like something you did for the algorithm, but not for your actual career. But lately, I've been seeing indie animators use shorts to quietly build entire worlds. Characters, shows, fan bases, momentum. So today, I want to break down the storytelling formats that are actually working and how you can use them for your own projects. Because here's the truth: most of us don't get to make a full series right away. We don't get handed a season order and a budget and a team. We build things slowly. And shorts are how a lot of creators are doing that right now. They help you test ideas, grow an audience, prove there's really something there. They're not throwaway content. They're like micro-pilots, proof of concepts. I've been doing this storytelling thing for a while now, in studios and independently. And the creators who are really winning in short form aren't just posting random clips. They're actually telling tiny, strategic stories. Hi, I'm Emily Brundige, and I create cartoons for a living. Over the past decade, I've pitched and sold eight original animated shows. Most recently, I created my own original animated show, Goldie, for Apple TV. It's been nominated for two Emmys, including Best Writing. When I look at the shorts that turn into long-term fandoms, I see the same three storytelling models that really work. They seem simple, but structurally, they're doing something very smart. Let's start with the most classic storytelling format. Self-contained stories. Mummy Joe is a great example of this. Every short is its own tiny episode: beginning, middle, and end. Nothing carries over, so you can click on any one, and you're not lost, you're just in. Why does this work? You don't need context, you don't need lore. You just click and you're watching a whole story. You feel satisfied.

title: Who Is LB~Sickning? | The Story Behind SicKKo Entertainment
transcription: So, who is LB Sykning? He's more than a rapper, more than a creator, more than a personality online. LB is a storyteller, someone who uses music, visuals, and conversation to shine a light on the real emotions most people try to hide. The name Sykning carries attitude, edge, impact. It represents the side of life that isn't polished—the late nights, the struggle, the scars, the lessons learned the hard way, and the strength it takes to survive all of it. Because behind the music is a human being who's lived through real things: pain, chaos, growth, redemption, reflection, and instead of burying that, LB turned it into art. Okay, enter Syk Kaco Entertainment. Not just a name, not just a label, but a movement. Syk Kaco Entertainment became the platform where music, video content, collaborations, conversations, and creativity all come together under one vision: keep it real, keep it raw, keep it authentic. There's no big corporate machine here, no glossy PR filter, just independent grind, built brick by brick. Syk Kaco Entertainment grew as a space where outsiders felt seen, where people who've been through something could recognize the emotion in the music and say, "Yeah, I feel that." So what makes pound Sykning's music different? It's the truth inside it. The delivery is raw, emotional, and unapologetic. There's no pretending to be something else, no fake image, no plastic persona. LB talks about real-world issues: pain, struggle, love, loss, frustration, survival, street-level reality, mental battles, and the journey toward becoming stronger than the past. Every bar carries weight, every verse comes from a place of experience, not imagination, and that's why the audience connects, because the music doesn't talk at you, it talks to you. It speaks a language that resonates with anyone who's ever had to fight to find their way. But here's the thing...

title: Audio Files: Lessons NOT YET Learned
transcription: The Tech on Demand podcast brought to you by GrowerTalks. Audio Files Episode 76. Lessons Not Yet Learned. From the February 2026 issue of Green Profit magazine, written by Bill McCurry, narrated by Bill Calkins. Lessons Not Yet Learned. Philip quadrupled his dad's operations during his 23-year term as CEO. He invested in new operations, dramatically improving results. At 46, Philip died unexpectedly. Alex, his 20-year-old son, assumed control of the organization. Not everyone felt this was the right choice. Alex dismissed those who wouldn't get on board. He wisely continued the investments in new technology, results in even greater success than his father had achieved. By the time of Alex's unforeseen death at 33, the organization was 10 times the size it had been at his father's death. 5 years later, that organization had deteriorated to substantially smaller than when Philip ran it. Alex was toasted and written about as one of the greatest leaders in history. He was probably the first PR-based autocratic personality with no true leadership beyond misleading publicity and fear. Beginning in 343 BC, Aristotle tutored Alex for 3 years. Today we call him Alexander the Great. Based on the outcomes for his organization, team, and citizens, he should be called Alexander the Goof. At his deathbed, generals asked Alexander, "Who shall lead us?" Alexander replied, "Whoever is the strongest." The reality is Alexander would leave behind only fighters and no trained leaders. None of the generals were taught anything but rampaging, knocking heads, and killing. They had no understanding of negotiation, compromise, or leadership. The generals fought each other for elevation to Alexander's position. As a result, that era's Greek empire withered away in civil wars, rebellions, disintegration, and loss of power and influence. Alexander didn't expect to die young and didn't plan or train for succession. His leadership style was complete control. He neither trained his possible successors nor shared any information with them. His iron-handed rule gave no thought for the future.

title: Scientists studied doomscrolling. Here’s what they found.
transcription:
What does the science actually say about whether social media is ruining our attention spans? Personally, I'm finding it a lot harder these days to sit down and read a book or watch a movie without scrolling on my phone, and it's those short vertical videos that feel particularly addicting. So, how much of that is my ability to focus actually getting worse versus me just worrying about losing my attention span? All of these fears are fairly new, so there's not a ton of high-quality studies that have been done, but there are a few. And recently, the science YouTuber, Joss Fong, posted a really great explanation on her channel, How To, where she dove into what the existing science can tell us about whether that brain rot is real, or if it's all just in our fearful heads.

In this conversation about attention spans, there's a phrase that I keep hearing, which is "brain rot". What do we actually mean by that phrase "brain rot"? What are we actually thinking is happening to ourselves and what is happening to ourselves?

I think what people mostly mean when they talk about brain rot is a kind of low-quality internet content on mostly algorithmic social media feeds, probably primarily these short-form video feeds, but also things like on Reddit or Twitter. I think people imply a low quality, but also they're implying a certain effect that they have on, that this is having on our minds.

So it's the content and the impact of the content.

I think so, yeah. And, and for me the question has been, if I'm spending more and more of my life consuming this kind, this kind of media, is that having an impact on my brain? And I think what we hear from a lot of people is, "I used to be able to read books and now I can't. I used to be able to watch movies, um, and now I can't." And so the implication with brain rot is that it's not just our environment changing and the fact that we have this device that's constantly distracting us, but there's actually a change happening in our brains. And that was the question that I really wanted to chase down, is whether that's actually true.

So, you went digging into an enormous amount of research, and I love what you found, because there are actually people who have done scientific studies, rather than just us thinking this is our perception, they've actually gone through and they've kind of measured what is happening. Um

transcription: Oh, are you enjoying the race, little kitty? Absolutely, it's amazing. Salute to the person who invented the first car. Well, not exactly. The car wasn't invented by just one person. It was actually the result of a long, competitive race between inventors, all trying to build the future. Let's travel back in time and explore the story behind one big question: who invented the car? Zoom in! The story starts in 1769 with a French engineer named Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot, who built what is widely considered the first self-propelled vehicle. It was a steam-powered machine designed to haul cannons for the French army. It worked... sort of. It was slow, heavy, and even crashed into a wall during a demonstration. Still, it proved something revolutionary: vehicles didn't need horses to move. This idea sparked a technological race, as inventors across Europe experimented with steam, electricity, and eventually, gasoline. The real breakthrough came later in the 19th century with the development of the internal combustion engine, an engine that burns fuel like gasoline to create motion. This changed everything. Instead of bulky steam engines, vehicles could now be smaller, faster, and more efficient. That's when Carl Benz, a German engineer, entered the race. In 1885...

The incident occurred shortly before midnight adjacent to Hill Air Force Base, KHIF, according to reports from KUTV and KSL. Emergency responders from the Layton Fire Department said the aircraft, identified as a Cessna 172, lost altitude rapidly before the engine cut out, then landed on the highway and flipped inverted. Both the pilot and passenger self-extricated from the wreckage before being transported to a local hospital. Crews contained a fuel spill at the scene, and no post-crash fire occurred. Layton police said the aircraft likely departed from Ogden and may have been attempting to land at Hill Air Force Base when the accident happened. Authorities told Univision that wind may have been a contributing factor, though the precise cause remains undetermined. The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board, NTSB, have been notified and are leading the investigation. This incident follows a series of recent general aviation accidents in Utah, including a fatal Cessna 172S crash in Box Elder County and an emergency landing near Smithfield. The NTSB typically releases preliminary findings within two weeks. Final reports can take significantly longer. A passenger medical emergency forced Southwest Flight 512 to return to Honolulu on Tuesday night after departing for San Diego. The aircraft had left Hawaii around 9:00 p.m. when crew declared an emergency following an undisclosed medical issue aboard.

title: History Buffs: The Odyssey Impressions
transcription: Hey, history buffs, it's Nick Hodges here. Now, I know my niche is reviewing historical movies and TV shows, but today, I'm going to make an exception. I just got back from Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, arguably the most talked about movie of 2026. People were already divided on it before they'd even seen it. Well, now I have, and I'm going to answer the question everyone's asking: Is this a movie you're going to like? Well, that depends. How much do you care about Greek mythology, or more specifically, how much do you care about Homer's Odyssey? Do you expect this movie to follow that story beat for beat, and if it doesn't, how much is that going to bother you? Because if all you care about are the monsters, I can tell you right now you're getting the Cyclops, the Laestrygonians, the witch Circe, the Sirens, Scylla, and Charybdis. They're all there. Strangely, though, there are almost no gods. Okay, we're probably entering spoiler territory here, but if you don't mind minor spoilers, Odysseus never speaks to Hermes, Aeolus, or Poseidon. The only god he ever interacts with is Athena, and even she is presented more like a hallucination than an actual goddess. Which doesn't really make much sense to me because there's definitely magic in this movie. Circe genuinely turns Odysseus's men into pigs. Calypso's in the movie too, but she isn't a goddess. She's just a mortal woman who rescues Odysseus and feeds him lotus leaves. There's no temptation of immortality like there is in the original story. If you're wondering how Christopher Nolan handles the gods, the answer is he mostly doesn't. Poseidon never appears. The closest the film gets is, after the Cyclops is blinded, he cries out to Poseidon, and Odysseus's crew conclude that the Cyclops must be his son. That's about as explicit as it gets. And yet, a little later, Odysseus literally travels to Hades and speaks to the dead. Tiresias is there, his fallen comrades from Troy are there, so the afterlife is definitely real. But the Olympian gods? Apparently, that's where Christopher Nolan draws the line. Now, what are the monsters like in the movie? Well, to be honest, the Cyclops is really disappointing. He never talks to Odysseus and his men, he just walks into the cave, seals the entrance, eats a few of Odysseus's men, and then goes straight to sleep, not considering these tiny humans a threat at all. In the original story, it's much more interesting. Odysseus actually talks to the Cyclops, he gets him drunk on wine, and then blinds him while he's asleep. By cutting all of that out, Nolan's Cyclops just comes across as an idiot. I
caption: In this audio clip, a male speaker with a clear, expressive British accent, identifying himself as Nick Hodges from the channel "History Buffs," delivers an enthusiastic and critical review of Christopher Nolan's film "The Odyssey." The speaker discusses how the movie adapts Homer's classic epic, specifically highlighting the differences in the portrayal of mythological elements. He notes that while various monsters like the Cyclops, Circe, and Scylla are included, the film largely excludes the active participation of the Olympian gods, presenting Athena more as a hallucination. He contrasts the film's portrayal of Calypso as a mortal and points out the simplified, less interactive depiction of the Cyclops, which he finds disappointing compared to the original text. The review is set against an upbeat electronic background music track with occasional sound effects that complement his narration.

transcription: ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിലേക്ക് വരുന്നതിൽ ബാഴ്സലോണ പേടിക്കണം എന്ന് പറയുന്നവരുണ്ടല്ലോ. ശരിക്കും ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോ വരുന്ന ഈ വർഷം, അതായത് 2023 മുതൽ നോക്കുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ ഒരു ചരിത്രത്തിനെയൊക്കെ അടിസ്ഥാനപ്പെടുത്തിയാണ് നമ്മൾ സംസാരിക്കാൻ പോകുന്നത്. ആദ്യമേ പേടിക്കണോ എന്ന് ചോദിച്ചു കഴിഞ്ഞാൽ നമ്മൾ ഹിസ്റ്ററിയെ ബേസ് ചെയ്തിട്ടുള്ള ഒരു കാര്യമാണ് പറയാനായിട്ട് പോകുന്നത്. ഇതിങ്ങനെയൊക്കെ തന്നെ സംഭവിക്കണം എന്ന് നിർബന്ധമൊന്നുമില്ലെങ്കിലും പലപ്പോഴും ഫുട്ബോളിൽ ഈ ചരിത്രമാവർത്തിക്കുകയാണല്ലോ എന്ന് പറയുന്ന പോലെ ഒരു സംഭവത്തെക്കുറിച്ചാണ് നമ്മൾ പറയാൻ പോകുന്നത്. ബാഴ്സലോണ ശരിക്കും ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയെ പേടിക്കണോ? ഇതാണ് ടോപ്പിക്. അപ്പൊ എന്തായാലും നമ്മൾ വിഷയം വിഷയമായിട്ട് സംസാരിക്കുന്നതിനു മുൻപായിട്ട്, നിങ്ങൾക്ക് നമ്മുടെ കാര്യപരിപാടികൾ യൂട്യൂബിൽ ഇഷ്ടപ്പെടുന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ എന്തായാലും യൂട്യൂബിൽ ഒന്ന് സബ്സ്ക്രൈബ് ചെയ്തു കൂടെ കൂടുക. നമ്മളങ്ങനെ 9000 സബ്സ്ക്രൈബേഴ്സ് ആയിരിക്കുകയാണ്. ഇനി 10 കെ യിലേക്ക് അടുത്തോണ്ടിരിക്കുകയാണ്. സോ നിങ്ങൾ ഫോളോ ചെയ്യുകയാണ്, സബ്സ്ക്രൈബ് ചെയ്യുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ അത് പെട്ടെന്നാവും എന്ന് ഓർമ്മിപ്പിച്ചുകൊണ്ട്, വെൽക്കം ടു 80 പോഡ്കാസ്റ്റ് ഫുട്ബോൾ ക്ലബ്ബ് ആൻഡ് ദിസ് ഈസ് ആർ ജെ ആറ്റപ്പൻ. ആദ്യം തന്നെ പറയാനുള്ള ഒരു കാര്യം എന്ന് പറയുന്നത് 2010 ൽ സ്പെയിൻ വേൾഡ് കപ്പ് അടിക്കുന്ന ഒരു സമയമുണ്ട്. അതുകഴിഞ്ഞു കഴിഞ്ഞാൽ നേരെ അടുത്ത സീസൺ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിലേക്ക്, അതായത് ആ അടിച്ച വർഷത്തെ സീസൺ തുടങ്ങുന്നത് ഈ പറയുന്ന പോലെ തന്നെ ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയോടൊപ്പമാണ്. അതായത് 2010 മുതൽ 2013 വരെക്കുമാണ് ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോ ദി സ്പെഷ്യൽ വൺ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിൻ്റെ ഹെഡ് കോച്ച് ആയിട്ട് വന്നിട്ടുള്ളത്. ആൻഡ് ഇതിൻ്റെ ഇടയിൽ തന്നെ നമ്മൾ ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയെ കുറിച്ച് എപ്പോഴും പറയുമ്പോഴും ഈ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിൻ്റെ ഈയൊരു ചെറിയ സമയം എന്ന് വേണമെങ്കിൽ പറയാം, അല്ലെ? ഒരു മൂന്ന് വർഷം. അല്ലെങ്കിൽ നാല് വർഷം എന്ന്, നാല് വർഷം കൺസിഡർ ചെയ്യാൻ പറ്റില്ല പക്ഷേ എന്നാലും അങ്ങനെ. മൂന്ന് സീസൺസ്. ഈ മൂന്ന് സീസൺ കൊണ്ട് എങ്ങനെയാണ് റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിനെ ഈ പറയുന്ന പോലെ തന്നെ ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോ മാറ്റിയതെന്ന് വച്ച് കഴിഞ്ഞു കഴിഞ്ഞാൽ അത് ട്രോഫികളുടെ നമ്പർ വെച്ചിട്ടോ, വിന്നിങ് പെർസെൻ്റേജ് വെച്ചിട്ടോ, എൽ ക്ലാസിക്കോയിൽ അടിച്ചിട്ടുള്ള ജയങ്ങൾ വെച്ചിട്ടോ ഒന്നുമല്ല. പകരം ഹി വാസ് ബിൽഡിങ്. നമ്മുടെ ടോണി സ്റ്റാർക്ക് അയൺമാനിലൊക്കെ പറയുന്ന ഒരു സാധനമില്ലേ, ഐ ആം ദി മെക്കാനിക് എന്ന് പറയുന്ന പോലെ തന്നെ ഹി വാസ് ദി മാൻ ഹു ഡിസൈൻഡ് റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡ് എന്ന് വേണമെങ്കിൽ പറയാം. അതായത് രമണാ, എങ്ങനെയാ പറയാന്ന് വച്ചുകഴിഞ്ഞാൽ ആ ഒരു മൂന്ന് സീസൺ കൊണ്ട് റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിനെ ശരിയായ റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡ് ആയിട്ട് മാറ്റാൻ ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയ്ക്ക് സാധിച്ചു എന്നുള്ളതാണ് ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയെ സംബന്ധിച്ചിടത്തോളവും റയൽ മാഡ്രിഡിനെ സംബന്ധിച്ചിടത്തോളവും ജോസെ മൌറീന്യോയുടെ സമയം പുള്ളിയുടെ പേര് വെച്ചുതന്നെ നമ്മൾ പറയുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ ഒരു സ്പെഷ്യൽ വൺ അല്ലെങ്കിൽ ഒരു സ്പെഷ്യൽ സീസൺ ആയി മാറുന്നത് എന്നുള്ളതാണ്. അത് എന്തുകൊണ്ടാണ് എന്ന് ചോദിക്കുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ, ഞാൻ ആ പറഞ്ഞ സമയം കൊണ്ട് തന്നെ പറഞ്ഞു വരികയാണ്. സ്പെയിൻ വേൾഡ് കപ്പ് അടിച്ചു കഴിഞ്ഞു കഴിഞ്ഞിട്ട് ബാഴ്സലോണയുടെ കാര്യമെടുത്ത് നോക്കുകയാണെന്നുണ്ടെങ്കിൽ പിന്നെ അങ്ങോട്ട് ബാഴ്സലോണ യൂറോപ്പ് ഭരിച്ചിരുന്ന സമയമാണ്. എന്ന്

title: Trump v3.0 | The Most Viral Content Creator | StandUp Comedy by Rahul Dua | 2026
transcription: उसका थोड़ा विटामिन कम है। या उसका पोटैशियम ज़्यादा आया है, क्या चक्कर क्या है उसका? रोज़ सुबह कोई अजीब बात कर दे। है ना? ऐसे ही लगता है ना? है ना? यही तो आप रह गए। आप उसका विज़न ही शेयर कर पा रहे। आप लोगों को पर्सपेक्टिव बदलने की बहुत... देखो, I know the general sentiment is कि बहुत इरैटिक आदमी है, रोज़ सुबह उठ के नई फुद्दू बात करता है। मैं कह रहा हूँ कंसिस्टेंट देखो कितना है। रोज़ सुबह उठ के एक नए सिरे से एक नॉवेल, स्टेट ऑफ़ द आर्ट, फुद्दू बात सोचना। और फिर उसको करने का जिगरा रखना। आर्ट है, कला है ये। पूरी दुनिया का फ़न लगा के रखा है, उसके चक्कर में बिग बॉस की रेटिंग नहीं आ रही है। हाँ, हाँ! सही? आंटियां इंडिया में टाइम पे सो जा रही हैं। कि नींद पूरी कर लेते हैं, कल सुबह मज़ा आएगा। It is not easy being the President of United States, it becomes very lonely at the top. Poor guy is lonely. He is out there to make friends, दोस्त बनाने निकला है वो। अब... अगर रास्ते में कहीं थोड़ा बहुत तेल मिल रहा है... उसमें प्रॉब्लम क्या है? पर दोस्ती में कोई कॉम्प्रोमाइज नहीं देखो, बिल्कुल कोई, कोई फॉर्मेलिटी नहीं करता दोस्ती में। वेनेजुएला का प्रेसिडेंट बताओ निकर-ट्रैकसूट में उठा लाया है। ये रहे यार यहाँ आके। दिल का कितना साफ़ है। कितना जो दिल में है, ज़ुबां पे है। बीच में माइंड का कोई रोल ही नहीं है। आप देखो, अरे! यार नहीं, हेलो, एक सेकंड। माइंड का क्यूँ हो रोल भी, दिल... माइंड तो बाहर है। उसकी पीआर टीम... मर गई कह-कह के। कि नहीं-नहीं, वेनेजुएला वॉज़ इन अ स्टेट ऑफ़ अनरेस्ट, उनकी गवर्नमेंट उनके लिए काम नहीं कर रही थी, डिस्टर्ब स्टेट थी, इसलिए हमको इंटरवीन करना पड़ा। कह रहा है चुप हो जाओ बिल्कुल, झूठ नहीं बोलो अब तुम। भैया, मैं बताता हूँ, इनको नहीं पता। हम उनको वेनेजुएला तेल के लिए जाना था। हमारे हेयर फ़ॉल हो रहा है, रिसीड हो रही। सीधी बात करना है, बिल्कुल कुछ छल-कपट, छलावा कुछ है ही नहीं उस आदमी के पास। आधी बात बताता है। पूरी नहीं बताता। कि, "You have to figure the fuck out."

transcription: धुरंधर देखी है आप लोगों ने? हाँ लगभग सभी ने, हाँ ठीक करा देख ली। मैंने भी देखी थी, इतना झूठ दिखा रखा ना उस पिक्चर में भाई। सही में शुरू में तो मुझे पता ही नहीं चला था। मैंने देख ली थी ऐसी ही, कि चार-पांच एक्टर हैं तो बढ़िया ही होगी पिक्चर और बढ़िया लगी मुझे। पर फिर एक दिन ऐसा हुआ, मेरा एक दोस्त है, नदीम उसने मुझे ध्रुव राठी की वीडियो भेजी और मुझे फ़ोन करके कह रहा, अबे वीडियो देख जो मैंने भेजी तुझे है। वो तो एक प्रोपेगैंडा फिल्म है, कुछ भी सच नहीं दिखा रखा उसमें। मैंने कहा सच नहीं दिखा रखा? तो भाई मैंने देखी वो जर्मन सिटीजन की वीडियो। वो खुद झूठ बोल रहा है उसमें। कह रहा बर्फ में कत्लेआम दिखा रखा बर्फ में, भाई पूरी पिक्चर में एक भी सीन बर्फ में लड़ाई का नहीं है। बर्फ वो सिर्फ गिलास में डाल रहे, और कहीं बर्फ नहीं और ये मुझे फ़ोन करके कह रहा तुम्हारा तो कोई भी काट देता है अंधभक्तों। मैंने कहा भाई इसमें काटने वाली क्या बात है, हमें तो बढ़िया लगी पिक्चर और रही बात काटने की तो सुन भाई नदीम। देख हमारा तो बचपन में नहीं कटा अब तो क्या ही कटेगा। नहीं कुछ बच्चों के साथ होता है स्कैम ये। देख वो रही चिड़िया, वो रही, वो रही, वो रही, ए उड़ गई, उड़ गई, नीचे साँप। अरे! भाई तुम समझ नहीं रहे। देखो दो साल का बच्चा है छोटा सा, उसके हाथ में डेढ़ लाख का मोबाइल है महंगा मोबाइल है ३०-३५ हज़ार की सिर्फ डिस्प्ले है। अब उसके हाथ से लेना हो गिरा ना दे तो क्या करना पड़ेगा? तब चिड़िया ही काम आती है। हाँ, तुम कहीं और पहुँच गए थे। पर फिर भी मुझे बुरा लगा यार कि मैं कैसे नहीं पकड़ पाया वो झूठ। तो मैंने दुबारा पिक्चर देखी वो। कितना झूठ दिखा रखा भाई आदित्य धर ने उसमें। पाकिस्तान में गलत दिखा दिया बताओ डांस। पाकिस्तान में! हैं? और वहाँ पे वो गार्ड रणवीर सिंह को रोक के बोलता है अन्दर सिर्फ कपल की एंट्री है।

title: How Jumping Rope Changes the Human Body.
transcription: The 5-minute jump rope will help you burn fat, create strong and powerful legs, and have you feeling younger than you actually are. This jump rope right here cost me about $5 on Amazon. Cheap, simple tools can have the greatest effect on your body. There's a study that shows jump rope is just as good at improving cardiovascular fitness as running. I am not here to argue that jump rope is any better than running, but there are some unique benefits to jump rope. Number one, you can plainly see on the screen right now. I can't go jogging down the street leaving my boys here to fend for themselves, but I can get 5 to 10 minutes of jump rope in while they play on their scooters around me. It can be the non-runner or parents' weapon to getting into incredible shape in the comfort of your backyard. Now, I assume that jumping rope originated with boxing, but that was only when it was popularized in America. Jump rope started as a fun game for kids way back in ancient Egypt, China, and Greece and Rome. It was brought to America by the Dutch, and eventually turned into an exercise that athletes, especially boxers, still utilize today. Why? Well, it comes down to one quality: rhythm. Boxers have found that the rhythmic, quick feet required to jump rope translates great to their sport. This is a lost quality in modern-day fitness. Many people sit on machines, lay on benches, losing that rhythmic quality that most of us had when we were younger. Here's a few things you probably didn't know about rhythm. Number one is that our brains crave it. It's why we love music. It's why dancers are the most embodied athletes. Rhythmic movement increases coordination, triggers the parasympathetic nervous system, and even increases heart rate variability. Rhythm, combined with bouncing on your feet, strengthens the vestibular system. This improves balance, coordination, and spatial awareness, all things that we slowly lose as we age. And a benefit that you won't find listed on Google is that all these qualities combined result in somewhat of a natural high. And the more competent you become with the rope, the more you experience these elevated feelings. But we also lose muscle and bone density as we age, and the less that we physically train, the easier it is to deteriorate. Most people know to do some resistance training and some cardio, but 90-something percent of the population are missing out on the benefits of plyometrics. Plyometrics are quick, explosive movements that involve lengthening the muscle and then quickly shortening it. And every time you land and rebound, it's three times your body weight in that moment. This has incredible effects on strengthening muscles, connective tissue, and bones. It's a quality that can literally keep you younger, and I think jump rope is the easiest way to safely maintain it. These small doses of impact result in a very strong frame. Skipping rope strengthens your whole lower body structure, and specifically your quads, glutes, and calves. title: Give me 5 minutes. I'll Fix your Hips. (5 simple steps)
transcription: The ground will rewild your body back to its natural form. It's simple, free, and a better teacher than any mobility coach or influencer's flexibility plan. People have been using it for thousands of years. Here's how you can free your body for no cost and just a little effort. Katie Bowman is a renowned biomechanist who's literally wrote the book on natural movement. She's a proponent of using the connection to our natural environment to bring back our mobility. She uses this cool analogy of orca whales in captivity. Their dorsal fin starts to collapse because it lacks the natural forces of the ocean. Wild orcas do not collapse. Aren't humans the same? We need the natural forces of gravity and the ground. Soft chairs and couches give us less feedback and we become stiff. Ironically, the hard ground keeps our body softer and more pliable. Sitting cross-legged on the ground, just like when we were kids, can start to restore natural levels of hip and spine mobility. I mean, look no further than yogis, the most flexible people in the world, who spend hours sitting cross-legged in meditation. Back in 2015, I was stiff as a board. I read Katie's Move Your DNA and I started to do some computer work sitting on the ground. It didn't happen overnight, but my hips were gradually restored from all of the heavy lifting and hours of chair sitting I put them through. You can do the same. Start with using a pillow under your hips to make it more comfortable, especially if you're stiff. Just a few minutes at first, and then gradually up the time and work it into your life like I did. Kneeling on the ground with the feet flat against the floor is an ancient Japanese position used by samurai warriors. It's been used for meditation, tea ceremonies, and simply having a meal. This position starts to loosen the ankles, knees, and hips, and fully bending the knees becomes lost to many older folks. This position ensures you keep it. The feet and ankles become rigid as we age because of soft shoes and repetitive movements. This position keeps them soft and pliable, but to heels was too much for my 2015 body. I started with a prop to raise my hips slightly. Start with 30 seconds here, then reach 1 minute. Then turn it into a habit throughout your day. Changing the foot position takes this position even further. When the toes extend, we strengthen the first ray and this is our connection to the ground. This influences the way that we walk and move and working on this often restores the plantar fascia on the bottom of the foot. It also improves dorsiflexion, the ankle's ability to bend forward. Toes extended is way more intense. Start with a few sets of 10 seconds and you can also explore reps like I'm doing here. You'll be surprised at how restoring the hips, feet, and ankles with those first three positions naturally leads you to a more relaxed deep squat. We've talked so much about deep resting squats here. I'll just hit the main benefits. Restore hip and ankle mobility, improve diaphragmatic breathing and digestion, decompress spine after sitting or standing for a while. The squat is much more than an exercise, it's a natural human position used for rest, play, and function. Spending time here daily is almost a non-negotiable. title: Gemini Spark | I/O 2026 Keynote
transcription: Let me show you how Spark works with some examples from my personal life. So here we are, we have the new Gemini app. It's been completely redesigned. We'll talk about that later in the show, and I want to take you into Spark here. And what you can see immediately is a dashboard with all the different tasks that I have going on in the background. It allows you to check in on these things, and I'll paste in a task right off the bat. This is a pretty straightforward example, but it's so useful. "Help me draft an email to the team, compile everything about our recent Gemini Live launches, and wins from the last week, use /ghostwriter." So there's a few things happening here. Compile everything. This goes across Docs, email, your chat, and grabs the most important information that you need for this update. It also is going to use all of the stuff you've seen in the time period of the last week with the /ghostwriter. That's a personal skill that I've written so the email sounds like me. And what's great is that with Spark, you can upload your favorite skills you find online. So we're going to let this run in the background. You can see it's already started doing various tool calls. And I'm going to switch over to another one from our personal life. We're planning a big block party. And you can see here, this is a pretty complex prompt. We want help grabbing all the RSVPs, keep a list of who's bringing what, remember to email those neighbors who haven't signed up yet. And what's amazing here is Spark will go through step-by-step. Look at all these steps, all the time it saves you going through, and again, work across the various skills and apps that you have. And what's really amazing is it'll break it down and also be able to generate files for you. So the first one here, this is a live RSVP tracker right in Google Sheets. You can see that it shows who's confirmed and who hasn't. What's amazing about this is it'll actually update because it's connected to Gmail. So when L. Thompson, row eight, RSVPs, it'll update, which is pretty amazing. The other thing is it keeps track of all the different guests, as well as sending follow-up reminders to who hasn't signed up yet. So again, this will happen, it'll create the drafts, and under my control, I can send them. And then finally, what the prompt did is it created a hype deck for the block party. And you can see, creates right in Google Slides, perfectly integrated. And you can see it even pulls in things like our giant bounce house that's going to be in the cul-de-sac. Now, all of this is happening in the background and under my control.

title: 11th Annual HBCU Climate Change Conference | March 2026, New Orleans, LA
transcription: This here is a movement of the people, the earthworking ones dedicated to soil and soul. This is what a community built on rhythm looks like, built on drum beat, built on heartbeat, built on the backs of the indigenous ones. Here is the pulse of the people. We find it through the touch of the architect, the one who reminds us that environmental racism is real and the toxic stink still lingers. But the culture bearer reminds us that we can't let nobody turn us around. Here is where the workers' champion tells us that the people are the legacy, leads us to the believer, the one who jumpstarts us with dedication, who guides us to the thinker, because in all of this work, we can't lose our heads, even when we lose our signals. When toxic waste and race loom over our heads, here we are saying that no matter the circumstance, small groups make a big difference. I am Dr. Beverly Wright, the founding director of the Deep South Center for Environmental Justice. And along with Dr. Robert Bullard, who runs the Bullard Center for Environmental and Climate Justice, we are so excited and happy to co-sponsor this event every year. Attending conferences like these, where you can be surrounded by people of all different disciplines and all different races, we all have a very common, shared, lived experience. And hearing people from all across the country talk about the same things that I've experienced is very powerful. And you cannot get that anywhere else. Our HBCU Climate Change Conference is unique. It provides a space for our students, faculty, and our community partners to come together and explore the kinds of strategies that will get us to solutions. We are really interested in presenting the facts, and the science, and the data, but also in coming up with actions that can make a difference. These last three days have really been exciting. We've done this for 11 times and it seems that it's getting better and better. We're here to try to find solutions to the harm that climate change is doing to all of our communities. We're also very excited to honor the founders of the Environmental Justice Movement. I think this is the first time that we have had all of them in one space at one time in many years, so we are happy to put on this event. We are also so excited to host a group of young people that we identify as Generation Next. We're excited that they can be a part of this conversation and interact with college kids while they try to figure out what it is they want to do in life. We are here to make a difference. We are here

This extensive coastline supports rich biodiversity, fisheries, and coastal livelihoods, but it also places the country at the forefront of climate change impact, such as sea-level rise, erosion, and marine pollution. These coastlines and marine and coastal ecosystems are not only of immense value for heritage conservation, but also play a vital role in fisheries, tourism, and a wide range of socioeconomic activities that sustain communities and contribute significantly to national development. Sri Lanka also holds at least 88 square kilometers of mangrove ecosystems, which are among the most important blue carbon habitats in the region. These mangroves play a vital role in storing carbon, protecting shorelines from erosion, and serving as nurseries for marine biodiversity. Sri Lanka's marine and coastal ecosystems are among its most valuable natural assets. They sustain livelihoods, protect biodiversity, and support national resilience. Yet, these ecosystems, like in most other places in the world, are undergoing pressure from climate change, pollution, and the ongoing degradation of critical habitats. Meeting these challenges demands more than awareness, and it requires coordinated, science-based action at every level.

title: Ryan Short | Keynote Speaker on Place Branding | CivicBrand
transcription: There's this Latin phrase, probably won't say it right, but I think it's "esse quam videri." It means "to be rather than to seem." Said by Cicero a long time ago. In 1893, North Carolina made it part of their seal and their motto. And I think the spirit of it is hopefully pretty obvious, but it's like, it's not something you say. It's something that you do, right? If you say you're about something, it should show up in your, your policies and your budgets and your actions, not just your marketing campaigns and the words that you say. I was talking to director of Arts and Culture Department for a city, and they, he, they had done a council workshop. It's kind of day-long thing where they're going to, you know, like councils do. The whole first half of the day, budget cuts. What are we cutting? Public art, zero. His department just got gutted, ripped apart, everything. "Where can we cut? Where can we cut? Where can we cut?" to where he's like, "I don't even have anything left to cut." Because there's, there's important stuff: fire, safety, public safety, like real things that like, we can't cut those things, so we're going to cut the art and the culture and some of these things first, right? These are the nice-to-have things, and times are tough, nobody wants to do it, but we got to be adults. We got to, you know, make the hard choices. And people get that. I think smart people get that. But then at the close of the council workshop, "Let's end on a positive note. Budget talk wasn't fun. Let's have a new mission statement, vision statement for the city." They kind of brainstormed ideas. What are we all about? Art and culture was front and center. "This is what we're about: art and culture." And he stood up, he's like, "Are you kidding me? We just spent the whole day gutting arts and culture, our reality, to then just go put it on a little poster and say, 'We're about arts and culture.' That is the opposite of "to be rather than to seem." That is, we want to seem like we're about arts and culture, but we're not really about arts and culture.

title: Minimizing Tech Turnover in Conferences & Festivals | Cut E-Waste, Reuse Gear & Recycle Responsibly
transcription: Welcome. Today we're exploring how conferences and festivals can minimize technology turnover, reducing costs, extending equipment life, and supporting sustainability across every stage of event design and production. Today's events rely heavily on technology, from digital signage to mobile apps to interactive displays, all designed to elevate audience engagement. But rapid upgrading cycles push many devices out of service long before the end of their usable life. This constant replacement adds financial pressure, creating higher purchasing, storage, and transport costs. With smarter planning, events can maintain quality while utilizing existing equipment more efficiently and sustainably. Tech turnover often stems from a desire to impress with the newest gear, even when older equipment is still functional. This perception-driven cycle leads to high volumes of discarded tablets, displays, LED panels, and networking devices. Replacing equipment too frequently strains event budgets and contributes to growing e-waste streams. Each discarded device contains materials that require proper disposal through licensed recyclers to avoid environmental harm. Strong inventory management helps reduce unnecessary replacements. By keeping accurate records of equipment age, usage, and condition, event teams can clearly determine when upgrades are truly needed. Asset management systems allow devices to be rotated across multiple events, extending their lifespan. These tools also reveal when a piece of equipment can be repaired or refurbished instead of being replaced outright. With better visibility, purchasing decisions become smarter, more cost-effective, and more sustainable. Modular equipment is one of the most valuable strategies for reducing turnover. Interchangeable components allow lighting, audio boards, and AV systems to be repaired easily without replacing entire devices. Firmware upgrades can also extend the useful life of older equipment. Interoperability ensures older and newer devices function together, preventing unnecessary full system upgrades. Planning for modularity reduces both long-term costs and the environmental footprint of constant tech replacement. Not every event requires brand-new technology. Many attendees care far more about meaningful content and clear audiovisual output than the generation of the device being used.

title: Shettima Urges Governors on Economic Growth | Senate Approves E-Transmission | 2026
transcription: This is Megastar Magazine TV. Hello and welcome to Megastar Magazine TV. My name is Monique Agbey. In the news, Vice President Kashim Shettima urged governors of the 36 states, ministers, and other public officials to pursue an inclusive economic growth model that filters down to the everyday lives of Nigerians. Shettima spoke in Abuja while delivering the keynote address at the opening of the National Economic Council, NEC, conference, a two-day retreat of governors and key stakeholders aimed at strengthening national economic coordination and accelerating inclusive growth. The Vice President warned that the government's mission would remain incomplete if progress does not translate into dignity, opportunity, and hope for citizens across the country. The Senate has approved the electronic transmission of election results to the Independent National Electoral Commission's results viewing portal, while permitting manual collation to serve as a backup where technology fails. The decision followed a reconsideration of a disputed clause in the Electoral Act Amendment Bill during an emergency plenary on Tuesday. The upper chamber stopped short of making electronic transmission compulsory and also rejected the provision for real-time upload of results. Under the reviewed section, presiding officers at polling units are to electronically transmit results to the IReV portal after voting and documentations are completed. The amendment, however, provides that where electronic transmission cannot be carried out due to communication or network challenges, the manual results sheet, form EC8A, will become the primary basis for collation and declaration. The Court of Appeal sitting in Abuja held that the Senate acted within its powers when it suspended the lawmaker representing Kogi Central, Senator Natasha Akpoti-Uduaghan, for misconduct. The court held that the suspension did not violate the senator's parliamentary privileges or her constitutional rights. The court set aside the contempt proceedings and the 5 million Naira fine earlier imposed on the lawmaker over an unprofessional apology she directed at Senate President, Godswill Akpabio.

title: Archaea are Highly Prevalent in the Small Intestine

My name is Maria Jesus Villanueva Millan and I am project scientist at MAST program, and I am presenting a poster at DDW 2022, which is entitled "Archaea are highly prevalent in the human small intestine and the absolute abundance of Methanobrevibacter is associated with older age and greater microbial diversity."

Archaea are part of the microbiomes, but once they were underestimated. But now we know that they have beneficial and detrimental properties. For example, Methanobrevibacter smithii is associated with constipation and obesity, but also appears in more abundance in centenarians. Most of the studies are focus on stool, but we want to do this study to know what happens in the small intestine. And also, we wanted to use absolute abundance to have a real idea of the potential biological impact of these microorganisms.

To achieve this, we collected duodenal aspirates from human subjects that were in the REIMAGINE study. And these subjects underwent EGD without colon prep. 343 subjects were analyzed in this study, and one of the main results were that the most prevalent and abundant archaeal phyla were the phyla Methanobacteriota and Thermoproteota. title: Multi-Objective Evolutionary Design of Molecules with Enhanced Nonlinear Optical Properties
transcription: Hi, my name is Gamrich, and I'm here to talk about our GECCO project called the Multi-objective Evolutionary Design of Molecules with Enhanced Non-linear Optical Properties. So, NLO materials are essential for mainly telecommunications infrastructure, and we look at specifically the device called an electro-optic modulator, which modulates a beam of light. So, we're looking at NSGA-II, MAP-Elites, MoAM, mu-lambda, and then simulated annealing. So, a mix of QD and multi-objective optimization algorithms, and then some single-objective ones. How we encode molecules is using SMILES. We limit our molecular search space to organic atoms, and we employ these seven mutation operators, and we do not use crossover in our evolution. And you can see how symbols are used to encode molecules. We evaluate the properties which we're optimizing using quantum chemistry, and specifically the Hartree-Fock level of theory with the PySCF library. So, our multi-objective algorithms maximize the beta over gamma ratio, which is important for frequency conversion. We target a range of 100 to 500 atomic units for linear polarizability. Our HOMO-LUMO gap, we target a range of 2 to 4 electron volts. And then our energy per atom, we try to minimize, and this promotes stability in the molecule. And then our single-objective algorithms simply optimize the beta-gamma ratio. So, each algorithm evaluates approximately 2,000 molecules across 20 independent seeds. Our main metric for performance here is the global hypervolume. As you can see, we have two variations of each of the QD algorithms. We have an F and a C. That simply means fine and coarse-grained binning. So, the F is fine, C is coarse. And that's because we have a 10-by-10 and a 20-by-20 archive based on the atom count and the bond count, which the atoms range from 5 to 30 and the bonds from 4 to 32. So, the MoAM with the fine-grain binning, so MoAM F, does the best in our global hypervolume, and you can also see in the final Pareto fronts here.
