title: How to Start Journaling as a Beginner | Daily Journaling for Self Growth & Mental Clarity
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You open your journal, you pick up your pen, and then, nothing. You stare at the blank page, and you do not know where to begin. Sound familiar? Welcome to ReadUp Daily. Today, we are solving the number one problem every beginner journaler faces: not knowing what to write. And by the end of this video, you will have a simple technique, three powerful words, and a full page ready to write. Let us begin. The technique is called stream of consciousness writing. It sounds complicated, but it is actually the simplest and most freeing way to journal. Here is how it works. You write whatever comes to your mind, no rules, no grammar checks, no perfect sentences, you just write whatever you are feeling, whatever you are thinking, whatever is sitting heavy on your heart right now, you put it on the page, and you do not stop until the page is full. That is it. That is stream of consciousness writing. Now, let us learn three words that will make your journaling more powerful and more expressive. Word one: overwhelmed. Overwhelmed means feeling like you have too much on your mind or too much to handle all at once. Example sentence: Today, I feel overwhelmed, but I know that writing it down will help me breathe again. Write that in your journal. Word two: clarity. Clarity means the feeling of being clear and certain in your mind. When the confusion clears, and you finally understand what you are feeling or what you need to do. Example: Every time I journal, I find a little more clarity about who I am and what I truly want. Write that in your journal. Word three: release. Release means to let something go, to free yourself from a feeling or a thought that has been holding you back. Example sentence: Journaling gives me a safe place to release everything I have been carrying inside me. Write that in your journal, too. Now, let us use stream of consciousness writing together. Do not think, do not edit, just write what you feel as you read along. Ready? Right now, in this moment, my mind feels...

title: Why Paper Journaling Is More Powerful then Digital Journaling
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: In a world where we do almost everything on screens, you might wonder: Does it really matter whether we journal digitally or on paper? Surprisingly, it does. Writing in a paper journal can actually be far more powerful for healing, self-awareness, and changing behavior than typing on a screen. In this video, I'm going to explain why writing by hand can create deeper emotional clarity and lasting personal change. Writing by hand engages the brain more deeply. When you write on paper, your brain works differently than when you type. Handwriting activates multiple parts of the brain related to memory, emotion, and learning. Typing tends to be fast and automatic. But writing by hand slows your thinking down. That slower pace allows you to process your thoughts more carefully, which helps you understand your emotions and experiences more clearly. In other words, handwriting helps your brain move from reacting to reflecting. Slowing down creates emotional awareness. Healing starts with awareness. When you journal on paper, the natural rhythm of writing encourages you to slow down and become more aware of what you are feeling. Instead of quickly typing and moving on, you begin to notice your emotions, your thoughts, your reactions, and the patterns in your behavior. This moment of pause is incredibly powerful because you cannot change what you are not aware of. Paper feels more private and honest. A physical journal often feels safer than digital writing. It isn't connected to the internet. There are no notifications, no audience, no distractions. Because of that, many people feel more comfortable writing honestly about things like fears, regrets, anger, sadness, or uncertainty. And that honesty is essential for healing. Your journal becomes a place where you can tell the truth without being judged. The physical act of writing releases emotion. There's also something deeply therapeutic about the physical act of writing itself. The movement of pen on paper can feel grounding and calming. When emotions feel overwhelming, writing them out physically can help release that tension. Many people notice that after writing honestly about something difficult, they feel lighter, calmer, clearer. Sometimes, the page holds emotions that were too heavy to carry alone. Your journal becomes a record of growth. One of the most powerful aspects of paper journaling is that you can see your journey over time.

title: The 5-minute Journal trick that calms panic
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Have you ever been lying awake at 2:00 a.m. feeling a physical weight in your chest while your mind races through a tornado of unfinished tasks, looming deadlines and vague anxieties? That sensation signals a specific biological chain reaction taking place in your nervous system. When you perceive a threat, even something as small as a tense email, your brain's threat detection center, the amygdala, fires an alarm and floods your system with cortisol. If this stress stays chronic, neuroimaging shows that your amygdala actually grows larger and more reactive, while your prefrontal cortex, the area responsible for rational executive planning, shrinks and effectively goes offline. To break this cycle, you need a mechanism called cognitive diffusion. By taking those chaotic, swirling thoughts out of your head and translating them into physical words on a page, you force your rational prefrontal cortex to re-engage, which physically turns down the amygdala's alarm system. The worry dump is a structured, analog practice designed to create this distance. It requires putting pen to paper to begin the process of externalization. Grab a physical pen, a piece of paper, and a timer. We are going to walk through this exact process together right now. Moving thoughts onto paper provides a physiological intervention to stall cortisol and reclaim your cognitive control. Step one is to find a quiet, private space where you will not be interrupted. You need an environment where your analytical left brain can focus on the physical act of writing, giving your creative right brain the safety to wander and release everything it's holding onto. Set your timer for exactly five minutes. When it starts, your only job is to write down every single worry, task, and anxious thought currently occupying your mind. Here is the single most critical rule for this phase: you must write continuously. Do not pause to organize your thoughts. Do not prioritize the list. And do not stop to analyze why you are stressed about a certain item. Ignore your inner critic. If you stop to correct your spelling or fix your grammar, you will pull yourself out of the flow and stall the exercise. Keep your pen moving. If your mind suddenly goes blank and you run out of things to say, simply rewrite your last sentence over and over again until a new thought emerges, or until the timer officially sounds. Your output does not need to make sense to anyone else. A single word, a fragmented phrase, or a complete sentence are all equally valid forms of output. Just get it on the page.

title: Why Your Journal Sounds Fake (and how to fix it)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription:
Have you ever written something in your journal, re-read it, and thought, "that sounds absolutely nothing like me"?
Here's a thing that doesn't get talked about enough: most people's journal entries sound like they're being written for an audience. Not a real audience—an imaginary one. Some future version of themselves who's going to judge the quality of the writing. Or worse, some hypothetical person who might one day read it. And so, instead of writing, "I'm absolutely furious, and I don't even fully understand why," you write, "today was challenging, and I'm processing some complex emotions." And then you close the journal feeling like you just filed a report rather than said anything true. This is the invisible reader problem, and it's the actual reason most people find journaling uncomfortable. Not because they're bad at it, but because they're performing instead of writing. So why does this happen? Because we've been trained our whole lives to write for a reader: school essays, work emails, texts to people we want to impress. Everything we write has an audience in mind, and we've calibrated our language to manage how that audience sees us. A journal asks you to do the opposite: write for no one. And that turns out to be genuinely hard, especially at first, because your brain keeps switching into "how does this sound?" mode rather than "what is actually true?" mode. The result is entries that are technically accurate but emotionally hollow. The words are right, but the voice isn't yours, and you can feel it when you re-read it—that slight uncanny valley feeling where you recognize the handwriting, but not the person. Honest journaling sounds a lot like how you'd tell a story to your best friend at midnight: short sentences, incomplete thoughts, words you'd never use in formal writing, repetition, contradiction, starting a sentence and stopping halfway through because you realized something while you were writing it. It doesn't have to be coherent. It doesn't have to conclude anything. It doesn't have to read well. The only job it has to do is be true.

title: The Journaling Practice That Will Change How You See Your Past
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You've probably started a journal at some point and quietly given up on it. A few pages of raw feeling, then silence. You decided writing just wasn't for you. Most people assume that putting pain into words works because it lets something out, but release was never really the point. What actually changes you on the page looks more like construction than release, and it explains why some people write for years and feel exactly the same, while others rewire their relationship to a single memory in four short sessions. In the 1980s, the psychologist James Pennebaker ran an experiment that seemed almost too simple to matter. He asked people to write about their most upsetting, unresolved experiences for 15 to 20 minutes, four days in a row. No structure, no therapist, no feedback, just a blank page and permission to be honest. Some of the people in that study wrote about things they had never told another living person. Health visits dropped in the months that followed. Immune markers improved. People slept better and reported less physical pain, and none of it involved anyone hearing their story out loud. Here is where it gets stranger. Pennebaker and later researchers went back through the writing itself, word by word, looking for what separated the people who improved from the people who didn't. It wasn't how much emotion they expressed. It wasn't how many painful details they included. It was whether their language changed. The people who benefited most were the ones whose sentences shifted across those four days from chaos toward explanation. They started using more words like because, realize, and understand. Their writing stopped being a wound repeated on the page and became something closer to a story with a cause and an effect. That shift has a name in psychology: insight. And it turns out insight, not catharsis, is what your mind is actually rewarded for.

title: Top 5 Journaling Practices That Feel Like Therapy for Your Mind (2026)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Have you ever wished you could talk to someone about your deepest thoughts, but didn't know where to start? What if you could do that without saying a word? Journaling offers you a safe space to express your emotions, organize your thoughts, and process everything you're feeling. Whether you're feeling overwhelmed, stressed, or just in need of clarity, journaling can help guide you through it. In this video, we'll dive into the top five journaling practices that can feel like therapy. These powerful methods can help you work through emotional challenges, boost your self-awareness, and even improve your mental health. Let's get started. One, stream of consciousness, brain dumping. One of the simplest, yet most effective journaling practices is stream of consciousness writing, often referred to as brain dumping. The concept is easy to grasp. Take a few minutes and write whatever comes to mind without worrying about structure, grammar, or punctuation. It's all about letting your thoughts pour out onto the page freely. Set a timer for about three to five minutes and just write without stopping. Let your mind flow naturally. The therapeutic benefits of brain dumping are vast. This practice provides a powerful outlet for releasing pent-up emotions and mental clutter. Often, our minds are filled with a whirlwind of thoughts, worries, and stresses that can weigh us down. By putting these thoughts on paper, we get the opportunity to unload all the noise and clear our mental space. It's this huge massive disconnect between the amazing world we've built around us and the, well, often chaotic world that exists inside our own heads. I mean, just look at our external world. We've achieved this incredible level of mastery, right? We've engineered our environment for total control, for maximum comfort. But then, you look internally, and what's going on in there? For most of us, it feels like a total storm of thoughts and emotions. It's accidental. It's reactive. It's completely out of our control. It's like we've perfected everything outside of us, but left our inner world, our inner landscape, totally up to chance. And this points to a really fundamental mistake in how we chase happiness, doesn't it? We're kind of taught that if we just get the right job, the right house, the right partner, you know, fix our external world, then our inner world will magically fall into place. But Sadhguru says, nope. You've got it completely backwards. The quality of your life is not determined by what's happening around you. It's all about what's happening within you. In this article, I want to draw attention to a method that dates back to the Roman and Hittite states and has helped shape the formation of states that still exist today. Although these organizations were created by states that owed their existence to the labor and effort of their individuals, they actually presented a structure that encompasses the individual's own life cycle. Individuals who found themselves within a ready and continuously developing order integrated into the system very easily, and growth continued uninterrupted. In short, if we want to capture the stability of the ancients while searching for direct sources for our own personal development today, we must learn how they lived and integrate ourselves within an organization suited to that lifestyle. Come, let's look at an example and see how we can adapt our personal growth as apprenticeship, journeyman, and mastery. Our goal is to maintain stability in our lives by making decisions with professional foresight and tracking them through mastery. Historical foundation. Apprenticeship as a liminal stage in medieval English guilds. This structure is most clearly seen in the guild system of medieval England. As Rhiannon Sandy states in her 2022 PhD thesis, Apprenticeship indentures and apprentices in medieval England, 1250 to 1500, apprenticeship was an important liminal stage between childhood and adulthood, during which young men and women were molded into respectable adults. Guild contracts, indentures, clarified everything. The master was obligated to teach the apprentice the secrets of the craft. In return, the apprentice promised to serve bene et fideliter, honestly and faithfully, committing to rules of honesty, confidentiality, avoiding taverns, gambling, and sexual misconduct. The master acted in loco parentis, in place of a parent, and was responsible for the apprentice's moral well-being. This system transformed the individual from a passive learner into a responsible, respected adult, exactly the model of stable growth we seek today. Martin Prak and Patrick Wallis emphasize in Apprenticeship in Early Modern Europe, Cambridge, 2019, that this framework organized both technical and ethical development across Europe. Well, the great news is there is a way to start closing some of those tabs. There's a way to find that clear signal in all the static. And that way? Well, it's journaling. But before we get into the solution, I think it's really important we understand the problem. Why do so many of us feel this way? It really all starts with the state of our modern, and often, very overwhelmed minds. And you know, there's actually some science to back up that feeling of being overwhelmed. Our minds are always, always on. But what's wild is that a huge chunk of that mental energy gets spent on thoughts that are repetitive, unproductive, and sometimes even negative. They just kind of spiral around, causing stress, but never really solving anything. So, how do we get that energy back? How do we point it in a better direction? Well, that brings us to a really simple path forward. And the best part, it doesn't cost anything, and you don't need any special gear. At its heart, this is all journaling really is. It's just this simple act of taking all that chaos swirling around in your head, and giving it some shape on a page. Think of it like having a conversation with the one person who knows you best: yourself. So, what makes it such an amazing tool? Well, for starters, there's literally no barrier to entry. It's free. Plus, it's completely, 100% private. It's a space just for you, where you can be totally honest without ever worrying about being judged. title: Why You've Become Hard to Read
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: People used to know what you were thinking. You were a open book. Easy to read. Easy to reach. Somewhere along the way, you changed. Now, people say you're hard to read, quiet, contained, difficult to get to. And part of you wonders if something closed off, if the openness you used to have was better than what you are now. It wasn't. You didn't close, you you learned, and there's a difference. If that feels familiar, stay with me. Becoming hard to read is usually the result of being misread too many times, not one big betrayal, just a a slow accumulation. Moments where you said the real thing and it landed wrong, you were opened up and the other person wasn't careful with it. I did this for years, said whatever I was thinking, assumed everyone operated the same way I did. They didn't. And somewhere in that pattern, I got quieter, not colder, just careful. That's not damage, that's data. Quiet isn't the same thing as as closed. They see someone who doesn't broadcast everything and read it as withholding, as coldness, as something being off. But there's a version of quiet that isn't absence, it's presence that's become more deliberate. You're still there, you're still thinking, feeling, noticing. You've just stopped narrating all of it out loud for people who weren't really listening anyway. There's a kind of openness that isn't actually brave, it's just untested. Early openness is easy, you haven't been burned yet. You don't know what happens when you hand someone something real and they don't handle it well. I overshared constantly in my 20s, thought that that was authenticity.

And I'm here to tell you that I know that one of the tools that is best to help with your mental health and strengthening you and how you think and how you feel is the power of a journal. Let's talk about it. Okay. So maybe this isn't a brand new idea for you, the idea of using a journal on your mental health journey. But what do you write and how can that be helpful for you? Well, if you want to use journaling as a tool for your mental health journey, I want to give you some simple things that you can write down and use and spend time with in your journal that are going to have big dividends and impacts on your mental health. Let me start with the first one. So, first is just to start with, write awareness. What are you seeing? What are you experiencing? What are you feeling? One of the best things that journaling can help us do is to slow down and to notice. It can be tied to or even part of kind of a mindfulness or meditation practice. But when we write it down, then we capture it in a more solid way and it helps us notice things. So, it's very helpful to just notice our feelings. What experiences did we have that day? How did that impact us? How are our relationships right now? What are we noticing that we're feeling off kilter or even really strong and capable and powerful? Just noticing as much as we can and recording that can be very helpful with and using journaling for that. Number two, gratitude. I've talked about this a lot and I'll keep talking about it. Gratitude is one of the most powerful forces that we can have to help us feel better. There's so much research around this and journaling is one of the best ways to do that because you get to write it down, you get to record what you're grateful for and even if you want to go a step further

title: THIS IS ADDICTION
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: This is addiction. It's a 3:00 a.m. phone call, the one you knew was coming but prayed never would. It's a doctor standing in a hallway saying there's nothing left to do. It's a mother falling to her knees like her heart just got ripped in two. It's a waiting room full of people blaming themselves for the pain, replaying every moment wondering what they could have changed. Questions you can't outrun, answers you'll never find. This is addiction. It don't just take one life. It leaves empty chairs at the table, every single night. It don't care who you are or how hard you fight. This is addiction. It steals in plain sight. It's a son and a daughter growing up trying to understand why. It's waking up to a world that don't make sense anymore inside.

title: SEMPER FI THROUGH THE STORM
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: They teach you two words the day you earn the title: Semper Fi. Always faithful. Faithful to your brothers, faithful to your country. But nobody tells you sometimes the hardest battle is the one that follows you home. Yellow footprints in Carolina sand, drill instructor shaping a man, sweating grit in the rising sun, turning boys into the chosen ones. Brothers forged through fire and rain, learning courage through the pain. Every Marine knows what that means, standing tall with the Marines. You can leave the battlefield, but the battlefield won't leave you. Semper Fi through the storm, when the night feels long, God held the line when my strength was gone. War in my mind, but my heart held on. Semper Fi, Semper Fi through the storm. The world sees a Marine and they see strength, they see discipline, they see courage. But what the world doesn't see are the battles that happen in the quiet, memories that don't fade, storms that don't stop just because the war is over. title: If I Fade First - After Everything [Official Lyric Video]
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription:
Some things don't leave
when the door closes.
They just find quieter places
to sit.
I surveyed the room before I spoke a word.
Measure every step like the floor could give way.
The kitchen lights stayed on until morning came.
Nobody slept but nobody said a thing.
Like I could keep the peace that I didn't break.
Good at carrying blame that wasn't mine to take.
My name got tangled up in every argument
like I was born knowing something I never spent.
I spent years
trying to become smaller,
thinking less of me
would make more room for everyone else.
So why do I still flinch when somebody raises their voice?
Why does my chest lock up every time I have a choice?
I built my life around surviving,
forgot that there was another way.
I've been living like a storm was coming,
even on the calmest days.

title: What I Survived [Official Lyric Video]
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: You call it confusion. I call it what I survived. You call it confusion, 'cause you can't stand what's alive. You hate pain and try to rename it, like that makes you right. You call it confusion, but the wound and the name don't match. You never came to hear me. You came ready to speak. You don't need someone to talk to, you need someone to talk at. That's the difference, that's the bruise. Every wound turns into your sermon. Every silence into proof. You call me lost when I don't fit the neat version in your head. You call it help, but it lands like blame, with that same old voice instead. You hear fracture, you say confused, like saying it twice makes it true. You see something you can't control, so you drag it down till you... You call it confusion, I call it what I survived. You call it confusion, 'cause you can't stand what's alive. You hear pain, then try to rename it, like that makes you right. You call it confusion, but the wound and the name don't match. You use your hurt to talk down, like nobody else has bled, like pain belongs to the loudest mouth, or the one who talks best. That's the poison, that's the trick. You make other people smaller, just to make your version stick. You don't want another opinion.

title: The Space Between My Lines | Official Lyric Video (Full Song)Written by © Kush_Lar 2026 ART-101

transcription: Hum... I don't intend to hide the truth, I only draw what I can see. The pencil seems to know much more than the frightened parts of me. Sometimes I stop before the end, not because I've run out of time. The picture simply asks for things I haven't found inside. If every page could whisper, if every pencil mark could speak, the space between my lines holds the pieces I can't find. Sometimes the picture isn't finished, it's only waiting for its time. Read the words I've never spoken, follow every pencil sign. Sometimes all that's left of me is the space between my lines. Hum... Some people see a simple sketch, a tree, a bird, a little sun. They never see the hidden roads the pencil's walking on. A broken branch, an empty chair, a window open just a crack, tiny clues left quietly for anyone looking back. Every color tells a story, even when it's left behind. The space between my lines holds the pieces I can't find, sometimes...

Search is now an AI agent, Gmail is an AI agent, Android is an AI agent, your glasses are an AI agent, and as I watched the keynote, I realized something. Google is no longer trying to organize the world's information with blue hyperlinks, because search engines are now an archaic technology. Instead, Google is trying to become the interface to reality itself before Anthropic and OpenAI create better realities. But luckily, Google I/O wasn't all about AI. I didn't see any updates about Angular, but I did come across a new awesome web API that every web developer should know about. In today's video, we'll break down everything you missed at Google I/O. Not only is it serving its core products to billions of daily active users, but in the last two years, they've gone from serving 9.7 trillion tokens per month to a staggering 3.2 quadrillion tokens per month, and that number is going to continue accelerating. In addition, Alphabet's capital expenditures have exploded, building new infrastructure to support all these stupid AI images you guys create with nano banana. Demis Hassabis, who might be the smartest guy at Google, appears to be fully world-modeled pilled, because models like this don't just generate pixels anymore. title: Macbook Neo Impressions: Reincarnated!
transcription: Alright, so Apple is doing a week of new release stuff and it's all headlined by what I saw today, which is the newest, cheapest entry to the MacBook lineup: the MacBook Neo. First of all, interesting name. We've never heard that word from Apple before. I thought when it was leaked it was maybe just a code name. I would have bet it's just called "the MacBook" but no, it's actually MacBook Neo. And the basics are this: it is a 13-inch laptop, powered by the A18 Pro chip, 8GB of RAM, 256GB of starting storage, and it is a super thin and decently light all-aluminum laptop. Two USB Type-C ports on the left-hand side, not Thunderbolt. There's a headphone jack on the left as well, and then there's some side-firing stereo speakers. And it comes in four colors: Indigo, Blush, Citrus, and Silver. They all have this sort of a whitish keyboard that is kind of tinted to match the color of the laptop. In person, maybe the lighting is terrible in here, but it was kind of hard to tell when looking at a single laptop. But you can, when they're some next to each other, see that the keyboards are tinted. And there's a 1080p webcam up at the top hidden in that bezel, no notch. And most importantly, the starting price: $599. And this is really interesting. They actually hit the price. This is now, you know, the cheapest entry-level Mac laptop. It's the same price as a Mac Mini, which has actually been one of the best deals in tech for a little bit now, and I think this one's also shaping up to be pretty good value. Now, the X factor is how will the A18 Pro chip perform inside a computer? Now, in case you don't remember, the A18 Pro is the same chip that was in the iPhone 16 Pros last year, but actually, this is a binned version. This is a 5-core GPU version instead of 6-core. But I think in general, there's a lot of tasks that regular people do on regular computers that clearly don't require a ton of power. Web browsing, emailing, shopping, spreadsheet-type of stuff, right? And before I've done any testing, just messing around on this thing for a few minutes, it seems like it would be totally fine for that. I would not expect to edit videos or do anything really intensive on this thing, that would be kind of crazy. But I also wouldn't be surprised if it could handle some light photo editing, some multitasking, and just, you know, generally be a solid computer. Think of it like a Chromebook, but

title: Leading Change Webinar Clip
transcription: Hi, and welcome. This is Leading Change from Where You Are, Empowered Strategies for Navigating Transitions. My name is Cassie Blossey. I'm the co-founder of Sageburg Consulting, I'm a nonprofit executive leader, education policy is the core of my background and experience and I love working in the community, specifically around change management in nonprofits and small businesses. One of the things that is really important about nonprofits is that they're so core to our community and, whether they like it or not, they also experience change pretty regularly, and in fact change is the only constant, right? So what I have seen in my experience is that nonprofits that set up systems to help them go through change, uh, experience much more um, long-term success and they see fewer disruptions in their actual services, and so they can meet their impact and mission. So today, we're going to talk about a couple of key areas of change. These three are the top types of change that I see in nonprofits and small businesses every day. Uh, the first one is one that we have a little bit more control over and we'll talk about the next two because they tend to give us a little bit more anxiety, so let's start with planned. Planned change has to do with change that you can anticipate, something that you know for sure is coming up. That can be a retirement, the end of a temporary role, maybe it's the end of a grant, maybe it's something that you knew you were going to start and then had a very clear end date. So when you're talking about planned, uh, change, one of the things that's really important is making sure you have really good communication systems and thinking about, "Okay, we know that this transition's going to happen in March, so we should start setting us, ourselves up for success by thinking about that transition, maybe in January, how are we making sure that everything will be successful once that change happens?" So, you have a lot more control in this area of change. The next two, as I mentioned, not our favorite, but you can still be successful. Emergent change is the unfortunate change that happens when there's something sudden, it's unexpected, sometimes it comes with additional risk, for example, sudden illness or a natural disaster.

She categorizes change into three main types, focusing on "planned" and "emergent" change. title: top marketing strategies to grow your business fast in 2026
transcription: If you're still pasting a single headline and one block of primary text into Facebook and calling it a day, we seriously need to have a conversation. You can and absolutely should be serving up multiple diverse variations for every single ad you run. Facebook actually allows you to upload up to five different headlines and five primary text options for every single ad set. Sticking with just one option is honestly the biggest mistake you can make right now. The entire reason we run ads is to learn things fast about what actually resonates with people. You want to know which creative hooks land, which copy flavors make people stop scrolling, and which lines actually drive the clicks. Setting yourself up for variation means you learn more quality information in a fraction of the time. Here is a super practical workflow that I personally rely on to scale my ad copy effortlessly. Start by writing just one solid headline and one primary text option that you feel good about. Then immediately take that original content and plug it directly into your favorite AI tool for variations. Ask the AI for five alternate headlines, specifically requesting different tones like punchy or benefit-focused. You'll do the exact same thing for your primary text options, asking for variety in length and style. Don't forget, you can also use Meta's built-in copy suggestions right inside the ad creation interface. Be warned, though, those auto-suggested lines are truly a mixed bag of quality. Some of those suggestions are absolute gold, but many others are honestly not very good at all. That means you absolutely have to act as the final human filter for everything that comes out. Always pick the best ones, quickly tweak the rest, and be ruthless about discarding anything that feels totally off brand. If you are smart and promoting video content, the next step is pairing your copy variations with multiple creative cuts. This is exactly where a tool that automates video editing becomes a total game changer for your workflow. Forget manually trimming a long webinar or podcast episode down into just one hopeful clip. Instead, an AI finds those truly viral-worthy moments and spits out multiple short clips that work on their own. Your new workflow can look like this: auto-edit several clips from one long video source. Then, auto-schedule those clips to post at different times across your channels. Finally, pair every single clip with a range of different headline and text combinations. This process allows you to generate dozens of unique ad permutations without getting buried under the editing work. The reason this variety matters so much is because Facebook's internal learning phase heavily favors testing different combinations. The other kicker is that uh that budget that we have that we've been spending on tech rivals that of our CIOs. title: This One Mindset Will Change Your Life || Keep Your Blinders On | Raj Shamani Motivation
transcription: So first is aap koi bhi field me chale jao log tumhe compare hi karenge. Hamare paas na billions of dollars hain to reach people, na government connections hain, na first mover advantage tha. Kuch nahi tha hamare paas. Kuch hai hi nahi kuch bhi nahi tha. Hum toh bas hustle kar-kar ke hi yahan tak aa gaye aur hum aage bhi chale jayenge. But I don't look at competition at all. Our competition, if you truly ask, is people wasting time on entertainment. That's my competition. I don't care about individuals. That's how I think. Tumhe lion philosophy pata hai? Huh? You know there's... So lion philosophy hoti hai ki, lion dekha hai? Wo din bhar sota rehta hai. Wo sirf usi time uthta hai jab wo bhooka hota hai aur fir wo uthta hai aur wo aise hunt karta hai aur jab tak hunt nahi karta hai kaat ke leke nahi aata tab tak wo wapas rest nahi karta hai. So I like that philosophy and mentality. Ki you rest the whole day, chill, sote raho, aalsi raho, let the world think that you are like this, but then the moment you see something that you can kill it then you go for hunt and then tum khatam karke aao. Fir bhale hazar hyenas ho ya sau deers ho ya koi bhi ho beech me you will go and like get your hunt and you won't come back home until you have that. So I believe in that philosophy and I operate like that. Ek cheez hai jo hum karte hain aur sabko karni chahiye is, tum kahin bhi ho kisi bhi field me kuch bhi kar rahe ho whether job, business, podcast, content creation, anything at all. Just khudse obsessed ho jao aur khudpe hi kaam karo. Let the world say that you are obsessed, tum delusional ho, tum arrogant ho, tumhe duniya ka farq nahi padta. Let it be. Become that person. Ki tumhe genuinely farq hi na pade ki paas me agar koi office aa jaye aur uska bahut bada podcast ho toh tumhe pata hi na ho uska naam kya hai. Tum us level ke bas itne blinders lagake apne hi kaam karo. That is the best mindset shift and habit that people can have.
caption:
In this audio clip, a young man speaks with a passionate and determined tone, sharing his perspective on competition, focus, and self-improvement. Speaking in a mix of Hindi and English, his voice is clear and resonant, carry a strong sense of conviction. 

He begins by dismissing traditional ideas of competition, stating that he doesn't worry about other individuals or businesses because they lack the massive resources others might have. Instead, he defines his real competition as the time people waste on entertainment. 

He then introduces what he calls "lion philosophy," describing how a lion rests and appears lazy until it is hungry, at which point it hunts relentlessly and successfully, regardless of any obstacles. He relates this to his own work ethic of resting but then executing with extreme focus.

Finally, he urges listeners, whether in jobs, business, or creative fields, to become completely "obsessed" with their own growth. বেশি করবেন তত আপনার স্কিল ডেভেলপমেন্ট হবে। তার সঙ্গে আর একটা গুরুত্বপূর্ণ যে খুব সম্ভবত ৯০% আমি যা দেখছি সারা ভারতবর্ষের সিচুয়েশন, টেট আমাদের দিতে হবে। তো যেহেতু টেট আমাদের দিতে হবে, এমন কোর্সগুলো সিপিডি কোর্সগুলো বেছে নেব যেগুলো আমাদের টেট দিতে সুবিধা হবে বা টেটের কিছু নলেজও গ্যাদার হবে, সেই বিষয়টাও আজকে আলোচনা করবো। যেমন ৫০ ঘণ্টা যেটা আছে সেটা হচ্ছে ম্যান্ডেটরি করা হয়েছে সিপিডি কোর্সের এবং title: 🎓 How to Become a Company Secretary (CS) in 2026 | Complete Step-by-Step Guide | Neha Patel
transcription: अगर आप 2026 में सीएस बनना चाहते हो या फिर सीएस स्टार्ट कर रहे हो तो इस वीडियो को एंड तक देखना। सो यस गाइस आज के वीडियो में मैं आपको बताने वाली हूं कि सीएस आप कैसे बन सकते हो, सीएस के स्टेजेस के बारे में डिस्कस करेंगे, सीएस क्या होता है यह समझेंगे, ट्रेनिंग्स क्या होती है, सीएस आप कहां से कर सकते हो, कौन से रिसोर्सेज रिफर करने हैं, एवरीथिंग। यह 15 मिनट का जो वीडियो है वह आपका आगे आने वाला 50 साल पूरा डिस्कस कर लेगा, एक पूरी क्लैरिटी मैप आपको मिलने वाली है। सो यस फ्रेंड्स वेलकम बैक टू माय चैनल, दिस इज नेहा पटेल। मैं खुद एक कंपनी सेक्रेटरी और लॉयर हूं, मैंने सीएस क्लियर किया था इन द ईयर 2020 विद एन ऑल इंडिया रैंक इन ऑल द थ्री स्टेजेस एंड ट्रस्ट मी गाइस 2020 के बाद से सीएस काफी ज्यादा चेंज हुआ है एंड 2026 में तो काफी ही ज्यादा चेंज हो गया है सीएस, क्या चेंज हुआ है वह भी हम इस वीडियो में डिस्कस करेंगे तो चलो शुरू करते हैं। सो गाइस सबसे पहले मैं कुछ डाउट्स क्लियर करना चाहती हूं। बच्चों को यह डाउट आता है कि मैं साइंस बैकग्राउंड से हूं तो क्या मैं सीएस कर सकता हूं, कर सकती हूं? तो डेफिनेटली सीएस में कोई एंट्री बैरियर नहीं है, आप साइंस से हो, आर्ट्स से हो, कॉमर्स से हो, हर कोई सीएस कर सकता है। सेकंड, एलिजिबिलिटी जो है सीएस करने की वह होती है ट्वेल्थ, ठीक है? तो यहां पर दो तरीके से आप सीएस में आ सकते हो, नंबर वन इज की आप अपना ट्वेल्थ क्लियर करके सीएस में आ जाओ, सेकंड इस की आप ग्रेजुएशन करके सीएस में आओ। तो ट्वेल्थ की बात करें तो ट्वेल्थ के बाद आपको तीन स्टेजेस करने पड़ेंगे, पहला होता है सीएसइइटी जो कि आपका एंट्रेंस है, उसके बाद सीएस एग्जीक्यूटिव एंड देन सीएस प्रोफेशनल। अगर आप ग्रेजुएशन के बाद आना चाहते हो तो एंट्रेंस आपका एक्जेंप्ट हो जाता है, आप सीधा आपको डायरेक्ट एंट्री मिलती है एग्जीक्यूटिव में एंड देन प्रोफेशनल। मेरी पर्सनल रिकमेंडेशन यही होगी कि आप ट्वेल्थ के बाद से ही सीएस स्टार्ट कर लो अगर आप एकदम श्योर शॉर्ट क्लियर हो बिकॉज जब तक आप ग्रेजुएट होगे तब तक तो आप सीएस बन भी जाओगे, तीन ही साल का कोर्स होता है, दैट्स व्हाई। तो अभी हम बात करते हैं इसके पहले स्टेज की जो की है सीएसइइटी - सीएस एग्जीक्यूटिव एंट्रेंस एग्जाम टेस्ट। नाउ गाइस इसमें काफी ज्यादा चेंज आया है, अगर आप 2026 के पहले सीएस करने की सोच रहे थे ना, तो सीएसइइटी आप घर बैठे-बैठे एमसीक्यू में अपने कंप्यूटर में पास हो जाते, बट अभी आपको एक्चुअल में सेंटर्स में जाना पड़ेगा और आंसर लिखना पड़ेगा। एक्चुअल में तीन घंटे पेपर आपको देने हैं, चार सब्जेक्ट होता है एंड सेंटर में जाकर आपको पेपर देना होगा, बस एक ही पेपर है सीएसइइटी का जो कि अभी एमसीक्यू बेस्ड होगा वह है लॉ का पेपर, बाकी तीनों सब्जेक्ट्स आपको लिखने हैं तो यह सबसे बड़ा चेंज आपके एंट्रेंस लेवल पर ही आया है। जो सीएसइइटी है वो साल में तीन बार होने वाला है फेब में, जून में एंड अक्टूबर में।

transcription: [Applause] I'm going to say three words which you're all going to know immediately and associate with the Admiral. Make your bed. [Laughter] Nine years ago, you made the commencement address here at the University of Texas, and that commencement address went viral. It's become iconic. Everybody can summon those words as an admonition, almost. How did that speech come to you, Bill? Yeah. So Bill Powers, when he was the president here, had invited me to be the commencement speaker, I don't know, three or four months before May. And obviously, you know, anytime you're invited to be a commencement speaker, it's quite an honor. Uh but I had a day job. So I was still I was running the university, I'm sorry, I was running the Special Operations Command. So I started writing the speech about, uh, yeah, maybe two weeks before uh I was supposed to give it, and I'd kind of been mulling some ideas over in my head. So I started writing it on the weekends, a little bit here, a little bit there. And I had this great theme and I thought I was going to pull it all together, and then the Wednesday before the Saturday that I was supposed to give the speech, I realized the speech didn't work. I mean, it wasn't wasn't a good speech. And I I went downstairs. I'd been writing upstairs. I went downstairs, I see Georgeann and I go, "Oh, my God. It, it doesn't work." [Laughter] "It's, it's not a good speech." I said, "I don't know what I'm going to do. I mean, I'm giving the speech in a couple of days." And she says to me, she said, "Well, why don't you write about something you know?" And I thought, "Well, there's an interesting concept." Um. And I told her, I said, "Yeah, but the only thing I know is how to be a Navy SEAL." And she said, "Well, write about that." But at the time, you know, you may recall there had been a number of kind of administration officials that had been, you know, scheduled to give commencement addresses and then the student population kind of voted them down and they didn't end up doing it. And I thought, "You know, if I talk about being a Navy SEAL to uh university students here and, you know, 8,000 students were graduating, I think, that year and 25,000 uh family members," I thought, "I I I'm going to be in uniform. I don't know how this is going to go."

title: Panel Discussion: Putting YOU into your Business Brand (life after "Corporate")
transcription:
Now, Susie, you mentioned that you've, you know, you've come from a different background. You worked in the corporate space, you worked in technology. Um, and you've had to shift from kind of that corporate mindset to a small business owner, someone who is now looking at corporate marketing to marketing your own brand, marketing yourself, marketing your small business. I'd love to know, like, what is one shift that you personally had to navigate making that transition? And what can you offer to other women in this room that are making that shift as well?

It was so hard. I don't know how many other folks left corporate and suddenly had to come out and start talking about themselves. So, I spent a lot of time on that messaging at my at my company. And it was the company's voice, it was the company's style, and it was the company's message. And it was great. I was good at it, right? It was awesome.

And then suddenly, the company wasn't there anymore. Social media was new when I was working in corporate. I never posted my own thoughts and feelings about the world because everything I said was going to reflect back on my company. How was how were they going to look at this, right? I was working for somebody else, it was their brand. I came out and suddenly said, "I am my brand. I can talk about anything I want to talk about because I am my brand." It was scarier than heck, I hated it, I didn't want to talk about myself, I didn't want to sell myself, I didn't want to market myself. It was really intimidating. And so, that was my biggest kind of hurdle as I came into this, right? I had to worry about my skills, I had those. I had to worry about my pricing, I figured that out. But talking about me and putting myself out there was a huge mental shift for me. And I wrote a blog post for the Sunnyvale Chamber of Commerce all about going my own experience going to get photos taken of myself and how terrifying it was and how important it was to get those photos to tell my story. And I was talking about it, I was using my voice, and it was great, and it felt good. And then I got to my about me, and I switched into, "Susie McFaddin is an internationally published award-winning photographer who blah blah blah." And the folks who reviewed it for me said, "That's great, but it didn't sound like you as soon as you started talking about yourself."

title: This Week in Review | Fed Meeting, US GDP, Eurozone GDP (July 31, 2026)
transcription: Hello and welcome to This Week in Review. This is our weekly segment that's designed to highlight a few important developments that you might have missed this week, and we'll talk about what they mean for markets, and, most importantly, the potential impact for investors. To stay up to date with our latest market insights, subscribe to our YouTube channel or visit fisherinvestments.com. Now, let's review what happened this week. First, the Fed meeting. On Wednesday, the Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, voted to hold the interest rate steady at 3.5 to 3.75%. This was the fifth straight meeting without an interest rate change. It was also a split decision, and three members voted to hike rates by 25 basis points. Headlines quickly seized on the story of a divided Fed, but we wouldn't really read too much into that. Differing opinions among Fed officials tells us very little about what the committee will do next, and dissenting votes don't make a rate hike more or less likely in the meetings ahead. Some investors may also worry that Chairman Kevin Warsh's decision to step back from so-called forward guidance may make monetary policy harder to predict or less transparent. We see that differently. Central banks can, and often do, change their minds without notice based on changing economic data or fundamentals. So rather than trying to guess their next move, we think investors are better served by keeping their focus on the broader fundamentals driving markets. Central bank decisions are just one of many forces shaping the global economy and capital markets, and while we believe a rate hike would be a mistake, the talk today is of small hikes. And, really importantly, even a hike or two from here would leave policy rates within a range that this bull market has already successfully navigated. Additionally, when we look around the developed world, yield curves remain steep and healthy. For long-term investors, that's perspective worth holding on to.

title: Clorox (CLX) Stock Analysis 2026 – Graphs, Risks, Opportunities & Valuation ✅
transcription: Clorox is a good example of a defensive consumer staples business that the market once priced for certainty, then sharply repriced when that certainty broke down. In the pandemic era, investors were willing to pay a premium for bleach, disinfecting and household staples because demand looked unusually strong and durable. In hindsight, that was one of the market's big mistakes. It capitalized peak demand as if it were normal demand. Then the opposite happened. The August 2023 cyberattack followed by ERP-related shipment disruption in fiscal 2024 reminded investors that even a boring staples company can suffer real operational volatility. But Clorox also had real successes. Fiscal 2024 gross margin rose to 43.8%, adjusted EPS reached $6.10, and operating cash flow climbed to $1.04 billion as cost savings and recovery actions took hold. Today the stock looks much less loved. Clorox is trading around $132.85 with a trailing PE of about 21.8x. Against management's fiscal 2025 adjusted EPS outlook of $6.55 to $6.80, the stock is trading at roughly 19 to 20x forward earnings. The quarterly dividend is $1.22 or $4.88 annualized, which puts the yield near 3.7% at the current price. For a company that historically often attracted a much richer multiple because of brand strength, resilience and dividend dependability, that is a meaningful derating. The market is no longer paying up for Clorox as a premium safe haven. It is pricing it more like a mature business that has to prove earnings quality again. The reason the multiple is compressed is not that the brands stopped mattering. It is that fiscal 2025 is messy. In Q1 FY25, net sales fell 15% to $1.39 billion, organic sales were down 15%, and gross margin slipped to 38.8% from 42.1%. Management kept full-year guidance, but said results were likely to land toward the lower end because earlier order fulfillment problems caused consumption and market share losses.

title: Navitas Semiconductor (NVTS) Q2 2026 Earnings Explained | Why the Market Misread the $0.95 EPS Loss
transcription: Navitas Semiconductor's second quarter 2026 earnings triggered a sharp market reaction, but the headline tells only part of the story. Investors focused on a reported GAAP loss of 95 cents per share, a result that appeared to miss expectations by roughly 22 times. At first glance, that looked alarming. However, a closer examination of the financial statements reveals a very different picture. The reported loss was driven almost entirely by a one-time non-cash accounting adjustment rather than a deterioration in the underlying business. Once that accounting impact is removed, the operational performance appears considerably stronger. The key comparison begins with two earnings figures. While GAAP earnings showed a loss of 95 cents per share, the non-GAAP loss was only 4 cents per share. At the same time, revenue exceeded expectations by approximately 7%. The difference between those two earnings figures was a $203 million, one-time, non-cash SPACC earn-out accounting charge tied to the company's 2021 SPACC transaction. This adjustment had no impact on cash flow or ongoing operations, and has now been fully recognized, meaning it will no longer affect future financial statements. Operationally, the quarter showed meaningful progress. Revenue reached $10.53 million, representing 22% sequential growth and finishing at the high end of management's guidance. Looking ahead, management projected another 28% increase in revenue during the third quarter. The operational loss also improved modestly, declining from $11.7 million in the previous quarter to $11.4 million. Viewed through that lens, the underlying business improved rather than weakened. Much of the market reaction reflected a comparison between a GAAP result and non-GAAP expectations, effectively comparing two different accounting measures. Once those figures are separated, the operating trend becomes much clearer. Understanding Navitas also requires understanding its position within AI infrastructure. While AI discussions often focus on GPUs and computing power, every AI data center ultimately depends on efficient power conversion.

title: Tesla Reports Huge Miss on Earnings for Second Quarter
transcription:
You think about what we heard from Tesla, adjusted EPS coming in at 33 cents, that is well below the analyst expectation of about 51 cents on average. It's not often that you see a miss of that magnitude for a company as mature and as large as Tesla. So, back this out for me and sort of make the math work.

Okay, Katie, I think it's, uh, it's compounded in that they beat the top line revenue by close to $3 billion. So, you have a massive top-line beat, and then you have this bottom-line, uh, huge miss. And in the car business, that's pretty straightforward math. Uh, they are falling to the temptation of feeding the top line, uh, which is a beast to continue to keep growing, with discounts. And when you discount, uh, in the form of price and in the form of the APR that people are paying, and they've done both, you see what happens to margins. They can, they can have a huge top-line beat because of course, people are going to buy a, uh, less expensive product or a below market price product, but then the profitability falls dramatically. And in this case, they missed EPS by more than a third. And I think that's the story here. This is not an AI investment story, this is a story in the base business. And the base business, I think, is giving hints that the, the product lineup is older, it's dated, and in order to move that product, you've got to discount it. And that hits, that hits the bottom line, and that's exactly, I think, what we're seeing here in these earnings.

Yeah, absolutely, a big tension there. And you think about, uh, the issues that they are having when it comes to their base business, the car business. How much of a setback is that for some of the ambitions that we know that the stock has been valued on when you think about, uh, AI, autonomous vehicles, robotics? The list goes on.

Well, I think they, the original plan was you've got a cash-flowing auto business that's going to fund you to the, then, future of autonomous cars, robotaxis, and robots. But you've got to have that cash flow, uh, and that cash flow has to be healthy, uh, and to the extent that your base business isn't funding the future, now you've got to go out and either fund it through equity or debt, uh, on top of this. And so, I think that's the question for investors, is to look forward and, and to really try to determine how much capital it's going to take to get to that future and then, uh, where that capital is going to come from. I think we see this across industries, it's one of the reasons we formed Vistashares is because the, the market tends to focus on end producers like Tesla. And the, the money's actually made in the supply chain. The supply chain has double the profit margins that Tesla has in the end. Uh, and so, although Tesla's getting squeezed by the end market, their supply chain is likely much healthier, and that's probably where investors want exposure versus betting on Tesla as an end producer here.

title: The Highest-Paid Podcasters Of 2026
transcription:
Today on Forbes, the highest paid podcasters of 2026.

When Jay Shetty started his podcast, On Purpose, in 2019, he remembers people telling him he was too late. The medium was already saturated, they said, with little room for growth. And wasn't he really just a content creator?

Seven years later, the 38-year-old self-help guru hosts one of the most popular podcasts in the world, competing not only with the biggest TV, radio, and internet-native talk shows, but blurring the lines between them entirely. Just as many people watch his lengthy interviews with celebrities, including Michelle Obama and Matt Damon, on YouTube, as listen on the iHeartMedia Network. Distribution deals that Forbes estimates paid Shetty $21 million over the past 12 months.

And when those deals expired this year, Shetty landed a new kind of contract, in which the audio and video of his show will not only be distributed by Spotify, it will also stream on Netflix, with the two companies combining to pay him an estimated $100 million over the next 3 years. Shetty tells Forbes, quote, "When I started, video wasn't normal for a podcast. Now we have the four largest streamers bidding for the show. To see that kind of interest and enthusiasm was pretty amazing, for me and for the industry overall."

The impressive thing about mega-deals like Shetty's is that, unlike the makers of movies, TV, or other forms of entertainment, podcasters retain ownership of their shows' underlying IP, meaning networks and platforms are paying millions just to license it as a distributor and ad sales partner for a set number of years. That's one reason why premium streaming giants like Netflix, Hulu, and Tubi had largely ignored the industry's rise over the past decade, allowing YouTube to grow into the largest podcasting platform in the world.

But beginning in 2025, hoping to cut into YouTube's dominance over engagement time, the streamers have made a splashy entrance. Industry dealmakers say that after Netflix's initial $1 million to $2 million bids for top podcasts were roundly rejected, the streamer adopted a strategy similar to the one it used previously to capture market share in scripted television: overpaying to lure talent away from incumbent platforms. Offers of $10 million or more per year, on a one- or two-year trial term, eventually convinced marquee shows from Spotify, iHeart, and Barstool Sports to sign on. Goalhanger, a UK-based podcast network, reportedly landed $19 million from Netflix to stream just 40 episodes of its daily talk show, The Rest Is Football, during the World Cup. Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said during the company's earnings call earlier this year, quote,

title: Heather Cox Richardson Video Summary: Supreme Court Expands Presidential Power (June 29, 2026)
transcription: For over a century, unassuming buildings like this have served as the quiet engine rooms of the American government. Inside, thousands of civil servants do the unglamorous work of regulating markets and keeping the country running. Starting in the late 19th century, Congress began building a specific feature into these independent agencies. They were intentionally designed as bipartisan bodies, deliberately insulated from the direct control of the President. The logic was simple. Keeping the air clean, ensuring consumer products are safe, and stopping monopolies requires technical expertise that doesn't change with every election. By keeping the executive branch at arm's length, Congress created a buffer. It guaranteed that decisions affecting public safety and financial security were driven by scientists and economists rather than political favors. In a single morning, with a landmark 6-to-3 decision, the Supreme Court erased over 90 years of established legal doctrine. President Trump immediately hailed the decision as a monumental victory, calling it the largest expansion of presidential power in over a century. He is correct about the scale of the change. The ruling legally grants the President the power to fire the head of any independent agency at any time for any reason. To understand how a foundational power of the United States government was dismantled overnight, we have to look at the legal theory that made it possible. The test case began in March 2025. The President abruptly fired Rebecca Slaughter, the last remaining Democratic member of the Federal Trade Commission. Since 1935, the standard for removing someone from these commissions was strict. You had to prove neglect of duty or malfeasance. But Trump argued he could fire her because her presence was inconsistent with his administration's priorities. This defense relies on the unitary executive theory, a framework conservative strategists have built since the 1980s. The core argument: as head of the executive branch, the President holds absolute authority over everything within it. No other branch can limit his control. By neutralizing Congress's ability to shield these agencies, this theory bypasses the legislative process. It takes national regulatory power and concentrates it into the hands of one person.

title: Day 1 Highlights | 2026 Bahrain Pre-Season Test 1
transcription: F1 is back for the first official test session of the season. All 11 teams and 22 drivers are present for 6 days of running across 2 weeks at the Bahrain International Circuit. McLaren entered the 2026 season as reigning back-to-back Constructors' Champions, and it was Oscar Piastri in the car for the morning of Day 1. The Aussie, who had battled for last season's Drivers' Championship until the very final round, was on the pace from the off in Bahrain. Despite McLaren running just over half the number of laps of Mercedes in Barcelona, the Woking-based outfit were raring to go in Bahrain. Piastri, second fastest in the morning session, just 2/10 of a second behind Max Verstappen. The Australian gave Turn 10 a wide berth following Aston Martin's Lance Stroll, but completed 54 laps before the lunch break. 2025 World Champion Lando Norris took over for the afternoon session, topping the Day 1 times with a 1:34.669. The Brit added a further 58 laps to McLaren's total, ensuring they ended the day with well over 100 tours of the circuit. George Russell was the only driver other than the title protagonists to win a Grand Prix in 2025, the Brit victorious on two occasions at Canada and Singapore. And the Silver Arrows were in fine form throughout shakedown, logging 500 laps in Barcelona, more than any other team. On to Bahrain, and Mercedes were again getting the laps in. Russell ran the morning session, completing 56 laps, before teammate Kimi Antonelli took over for the afternoon. The Brit did have a little trouble at the off-camber Turn 10, running wide on three separate occasions. Antonelli's running was delayed after Mercedes found an issue while changing setups, but the Italian was able to hit the track, completing 30 laps despite a wild snap at Turn 4. Team Principal Toto Wolff, offering his thoughts on Mercedes' progress so far: "I think everything goes according to the plan we have. You know, it isn't smooth sailing. We have complication on car balance, which are a little bit more articulated here than they were in Barcelona, obviously due to the hot conditions. And we've seen a very, very strong Verstappen this morning. So, you know, we have to get our act together, all of us, and then maybe by the end of the test we will understand more whether what we've done is good, and good enough." Max Verstappen described 2025 as his greatest-ever season, just 2 points away from a fifth world title, despite driving a car which, quote, "he hated at times". He's currently P2 in the drivers' championship, some 43 points behind Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli, but he was one place ahead of the Italian in second practice, P4 after the hour. transcription: Day two of testing in Bahrain. Eight further hours of running for teams and drivers to better understand their 2026 machines. Turn 10 was once again a talking point on the second day of running. The tricky off-camber corner caught out the majority of the runners on day one. And it was Sergio Pérez first to head off-piste after a big lockup in his Red Bull. The Mexican also brought out the day's first red flag, his team quickly fixing the issue, allowing him to return to the action soon after. But it was Alex Albon who locked up, not once, not twice, not thrice, but four times into the troublesome turn 10. The Thai driver also had a mishap at turn one on two occasions before setting the fifth fastest time of the morning. Two of the most experienced drivers weren't immune to a mishap either, both Fernando Alonso and Nico Hülkenberg locking up and running off at the 10th turn. Despite this, the German was optimistic with the progress made in Bahrain so far. I think good step forward in terms of performance, in terms of reliability and just, you know, being able to get laps in, to get kilometers on the car. We've made some some big steps forward there, you know, between Barcelona and here. Then, you know, Bahrain is a very, very different circuit to Barcelona, you know, much more stop-and-go, low-speed dominated. It's a very hard, you know, and unforgiving track that really exposes a lot of weaknesses usually, you know, and historically from from any car because the rough tarmac, kind of low grip, very windy, hot track temp, so, you know, it's a there isn't many other, you know, tracks that or where you find the harder conditions. So it's a it's a true good test. Teammate Gabriel Bortoleto would take over for the afternoon, the Brazilian struggling for purchase as he tested the limits of his 2026 challenger. It's uh it's like teaching a baby how to walk and and talk, and um yeah, we need to do this uh as quick as possible and uh in a good way as well. Charles Leclerc started the day for Ferrari, having set over 130 laps alongside Lewis Hamilton on Wednesday. The Monégasque driver claimed seven podiums last season but was unable to add to his eight Formula One race victories. A positive week in Spain...

transcription: Some, some people call me a survival expert. Well, as a survival expert, I want to clear up a common misconception. Survival is not something we just do in the woods. It's something each and every one of us has to do every single day. And whether you're building a fire, gutting a moose, or drafting a motion, we're just trying to survive as best we can with the resources we have. So, I would like to help give you some advice to survive whatever is coming next. And while I do not know what your future holds, I can tell you that the world is changing at a terrifying and fascinating pace. You know, so, here I am, I'm 47 years old, I'm not properly old yet, and, I've seen some crazy stuff. I remember watching the Berlin Wall come down live on television as a child. I remember hearing about the internet for the first time, and I thought it was a fake. I thought, I didn't understand that. I was an adult the first time I ever saw an email. I was married when 9/11 happened. And the year before I went to law school, this thing called YouTube was invented. I was practicing for 3 years before I ever got my first social media account. I've seen 7 US wars, 6 recessions, and I've survived one global pandemic so far. I'm only 47. I don't know what the next 40 years holds for you. But, I doubt any of us are going to get through it without seeing terrible and amazing things. We don't know what these changes are going to be, but we do know they're coming. You need to be ready to grab the opportunities that are going to come in this changing world. And, you need to be ready to survive the storms. And, the best survival advice I can give you is very pragmatic. I would say, save some money. It's pretty simple, but it's not. The best, the most important things are often simple, but hard to do.

title: YouTuber ‘Reckless Ben’ BREAKS SILENCE amid legal battle over missing Legos | Jesse Weber Live
transcription: Tonight, Reckless Ben is here. Yeah, in just a minute, the YouTube star is going to talk with us exclusively about his big legal win in the mystery of the missing LEGO. Yep, a judge just granted him the right to talk again. This is a big development. I got to give you a background though, a quick look at how this whole LEGO legal drama unfolded, okay? It all started when an Oregon family entrusted a franchise of a chain called Bricks & Minifigs to sell their reportedly $200,000 Star Wars LEGO set on consignment. But, the franchise was apparently sold, and the LEGO owners say they never got their LEGO, they never got paid. Now, the family sued the franchise claiming their agreement was breached, that Bricks & Minifigs stole the LEGO collection, and that is when Reckless Ben got on the case. He allegedly traveled to Utah where the franchise executive lives, reportedly started documenting attempts to make contact at his property, posted videos, all going viral. The executive apparently called police, led to Ben getting arrested twice, and as we reported, Bricks & Minifigs also filed a lawsuit against Ben. And, that brings us to this week. Ben is facing a total of four criminal charges. They're all misdemeanors. Provo, Utah, he's charged with disorderly conduct, also reportedly commercial obstruction for allegedly going to the Bricks & Minifigs corporate headquarters. Ben tells us he was there to ask for the LEGOs back. Over in American Fork, Utah, he's charged with stalking and residential picketing for allegedly going to the franchise owner, Josh Johnson's house. Now, Reckless Ben just scored a big legal win. This is when a Utah federal court, this judge lifted the ban that had been on him, posting videos related to Bricks & Minifigs. This was a TRO. However, the revised order still prohibits Ben from coming within 100 meters of any Bricks & Minifigs stores or offices, prevents him from making any threats. Now, we've reached out to Bricks & Minifigs for a statement today, but we haven't heard back. The company has maintained it does not have the LEGO, and in a statement to local media, they said that this issue in its civil case against Ben, real name, Ben Schneider, is going to be addressed through private mediation. It hopes to resolve everything in the coming weeks. But for now, Ben says he got his freedom back, his freedom of speech back. He's already made a new, a new YouTube video. Here's an exclusive sneak peek.

title: How to protect your investments from an AI bubble | The Economist
transcription: Why is investor confidence in AI now wobbling? In recent weeks, we've seen big companies announce that they're going to spend absolutely jaw-dropping amounts of money investing in AI. And whereas previously, investors were cheering those announcements, actually lately, we've seen the stock market wobble in response. It seems like they're getting a bit worried about whether they're going to get returns on all of this money that companies are spending on this new technology. So what exactly is it that's making the stock markets jittery? Well, it's not just that investors are worried about the amounts that companies are spending, although those amounts are vast. It's kind of this feeling that we've been here before. So there are lots of times throughout history where you've had a new technology emerge and it looks like it's going to transform the world. So take railways or canals or electricity or the internet. And in all of those cases, the new technology actually did transform the world. But in the early stages, when it was just coming out, investors got overexcited. They ended up bidding up companies' share prices out of all proportion with their underlying profits. Um, and they also ended up picking the wrong firms, you know, not buying the companies that would actually benefit from this. And then even when the new technology was really successful, a lot of investors lost an enormous amount of money. And there's kind of this worry that something similar is happening again, that AI might be this transformative technology, but share prices have been bid up out of all proportion with underlying profits. So we're at a very nervous moment. What is it then that investors can do to avoid getting stuck? This is something of a puzzle because you might think the obvious answer is, "Okay, shares are too pricey, so I'm going to sell my shares." Professional investors often don't have that as an option. For example, if I manage a stock fund and I tell clients, "invest in my fund and I'm going to invest in stocks," I can't just suddenly sell them and sit on a pile of cash. I, I might actually not be allowed to, even if I am, my clients are going to ring me up and say, "What are you doing? This isn't what I'm paying you for."

title: OPT In Highlights: 2026 ICAN Women's Leadership Conference
transcription: Positive leadership is not a luxury for calm times. It is a discipline for uncertain ones. It's not a soft skill, but a strategic imperative. Today, leaders are here to learn about the power of positivity and the power that positivity can have on both our personal and professional lives. I CAN is positive. I CAN is powerful. I CAN is a way to opt into the hope that we all need for the world. Because a lot of us think about having a vision for our lives, but that vision just doesn't materialize out of nothing. We have to create it. So a great vision plan gives you clear direction. It's going to help you to define your goals, it's going to increase your motivation. Motivation, folks, doesn't come from just effort. It comes from having that meaning. One of my favorite things about I CAN is just its pure mission to help develop individuals within our communities, women primarily, but also to just reinforce that we are important and making sure that we are invested in those individuals. Because at some point we are taught and we believe that to be in charge means to have the answers, and that might get you promoted one day, but it will make you less valuable every day. The only way that we overcome blind spots is that we operate in a frame of curiosity. I think women leadership conferences like this makes us pause and really be able to get up on the balcony and be strategic about wow, I'm doing all this work, but what am I doing to take care of myself? What am I doing to mentor or support other women in my life? It's an intentional way to pause and really, really connect. And we find that optimism is a fuel for nearly every aspect of our lives. You're more likely to survive a cancer diagnosis if you're optimistic, your children will do better in school, it runs the whole gamut. And when we broadcast this kind of mindset to other people, it changes them for the better as well. Technology is a tool that we can use to enhance our humanity. To not get too caught up, like I CAN, in the latest release from Claude or some technology or this is going to be the thing that fixes my team that we use, don't ever forget, the most important competitive advantage each and every one of you has is your humanity.

title: CVPR 2026 : CrowdGen
transcription: Let's talk about this paper titled Generative Adversarial Perturbation with Cross-Paradigm Transferability on Localized Crowd Counting. We have seen evasion attacks on all kinds of vision tasks, classification, face recognition to name a few, but crowd models are relatively less explored. They are more complex than the classification task, but they inherit the same weakness that other deep vision models suffer. And most importantly, they are widely deployed in real life scenarios such as public safety, retail analytics and so on. So an undercounting attack could be a safety risk. As we can see a clean example on the right, while passed by a model it outputs 428 people and their locations. However, if small adversarial perturbation is added, it slashes this prediction by over 40% and we get 285 people. So, the previous studies on crowd models are mostly patch-based attacks and they are limited to only density map-based models. So naturally, the question emerges is that can adversarial perturbations transfer across heterogeneous localized crowd counting paradigms such as density map and point regression models? So, to accomplish this attack, we design a perturbation generator that takes clean image as input and outputs the perturbation noise, and this noise is added to the clean image to produce the adversarial image. For black-box transferability, we design a loss function keeping the transferability, imperceptibility and effectiveness goal in mind. Our hypothesis is that even though these models vary by outputs, they share similar backbone architecture such as VGG, ResNet and same weights. So, we our, we hypothesis that this drives the transferability. On the other hand, the crowd scenes are low-frequency dominated, so we suppress the high-frequency and magnitude of the noise for, for subtle perturbation. And lastly, the effectiveness between two paradigms of models come from model-specific loss. So, density map models do the density suppression, and point regression-based models perform logit suppression. Together, this combined loss govern the training. So, this is a sample instance of adversarial examples, where adversarial perturbations are added to the clean images for various lighting conditions.

She introduces her team's methodology, which involves a perturbation generator designed with a loss function that balances transferability, imperceptibility, and effectiveness. The speaker details how the shared backbone architectures of different models facilitate transferability, how they suppress high-frequency noise to maintain subtlety, and how model-specific losses (density and logit suppression) are combined to govern training. She concludes by showing sample adversarial examples under various lighting conditions.
