title: VeriSHAP 5min Summary Presentation
transcription: Hi there, I'm David, and in the next few minutes, I present a short summary of our paper VerifySHAP, or VerySHAP for short, on computing provable bounds for the exact Shapley values of neural networks. SHAP is a popular feature importance technique that can help us explain deep neural networks. The goal is, for example, to find out what influence an input feature, such as the arrow in this image, has on the prediction a neural network makes. SHAP provides such importance scores by computing what is called the Shapley value of each input feature. So, for example, for this arrow feature, we look at a combination of the other features, once with the arrow present, here in yellow, and once with the arrow absent, here in pink. We then use a value function V to mask out the missing features and evaluate the network on that new input with the masked-out features. We then subtract the network output we get when the arrow is absent from the output we get when the arrow is present to compute what is called the contribution delta of this arrow feature. However, SHAP does not only look at one such combination of input features, but looks at all of the combinations of the other input features that we can have. This means that computing Shapley values requires enumerating an exponential number of these feature combinations that are also called coalitions. Because this clearly does not scale very well, previous work has investigated different statistical estimators that only sample a certain number of coalitions. While this is a lot more scalable, these techniques don't necessarily tell us how far off they are with an individual estimate, which can be problematic in sensitive applications. Additionally, for empirically evaluating these SHAP estimators, we need to know the ground-truth exact Shapley values. For these reasons, we introduce VerySHAP, a new algorithm for computing the exact Shapley values of neural networks faster on higher-dimensional feature spaces, and computing guaranteed lower and upper bounds on Shapley values using ideas from neural network verification. The key idea from neural network verification that we leverage is bound propagation. Bound propagation allows us to propagate an entire set of input features, such as this entire coalition space, through the contribution function. And then we obtain a guaranteed lower bound and a guaranteed upper bound on the contribution. We can then plug these bounds into the SHAP equation, and obtain a guaranteed lower bound and a guaranteed upper bound on the Shapley value itself.

title: Short Introduction of NeighborMAE (CVPR 2026)
transcription: Hello everyone, I'm Liangcong from KU Leuven. I'm glad to present our work, Neighbor MAE: Exploiting Spatial Dependencies between Neighboring Earth Observation Images in Masked Autoencoder Pre-training. The main idea of this work is simple. In Earth observation, images are not isolated samples. They are observations of the continuous Earth's surface. So instead of training masked autoencoder on each image independently, we ask whether neighboring images can provide useful spatial context for masked autoencoder pre-training. Masked image modeling has become a popular self-supervised learning strategy for Earth observation. The model masks parts of an image and learns to reconstruct the missing region. However, most existing MIM methods reconstruct a single image tile independently. This is a simplification of Earth observation data because satellite and aerial images are naturally spatially connected. Neighboring images often share useful information, such as terrain structure, land use, continuity, roads, buildings, and infrastructure patterns. At the same time, neighboring views may also differ in acquisition time, viewpoints, or sensor conditions. This means neighboring images provide varied signals, shared spatial context, and natural variations. Therefore, we ask: can neighboring images provide useful context for masked image modeling? To answer this question, we propose Neighbor MAE, which extends MAE from single image reconstruction to joint reconstruction of neighboring Earth observation images. The method has five main components. First, neighbor sampling: we use geospatial metadata to sample neighboring Earth observation images based on the intersection over union of the spatial footprints.

title: Dr. Mani Menon Receives the 2026 AUA Ramon Guiteras Award
transcription: The final award of the evening is the Ramon Guiteras Award, our highest honor, recognizing outstanding contribution to both the art and science of urology. For pioneering contributions in robotics resulting in a paradigm shift to the surgical treatment of prostate cancer, Dr. Mani Menon. President Palmer, President-elect Reed, past and future presidents, fellow awardees, and guests. Thank you. Shira Ruben, my official AUA handler, tells me that the Guiteras Award has been given since 1970, but that only three people in its history have swept all three AUA awards: the Gold Cystoscope, the Hugh Hampton Young, and the Guiteras. Pat Walsh, who hired me as his first resident and regretted it ever since, Darracott Vaughan, who hired me as his first faculty member and withdrew the offer after a disastrous interview, and Bill Catalona, my chief resident, who for 50 years has been telling me how wrong I am. Now we're four. That is humbling company. Shira also says that the only reason that I can say this with a straight face is that until 1975, the Gold Cystoscope Award was given to the best golfer in the AUA, which would have ruled out all four of us, except maybe Bill. Before I go further, I have been nominated four times for the Guiteras Award. The North Central Section, where I did the bulk of my work on robotic surgery, nominated me three times. The New York Section, my new home, made it stick. Lane Palmer and Steve Kaplan saw it through.

title: Ultrasound-CLIP(CVPR 2026)
transcription: Hello, everyone. I'm Jiayin Jin from Hangzhou City University. Today, I'm excited to present our CVPR 2024 paper, UltrasoundCLIP: Semantic-Aware Contrastive Pre-training for Ultrasound Image-Text Understanding. Ultrasound is one of the most widely used imaging modalities in clinical practice. However, ultrasound vision-language learning remains under-explored because of heterogeneous diagnostic attributes and weak image-text alignment. To address this problem, we propose a semantic-aware ultrasound vision-language framework, together with a large-scale ultrasound image-text dataset. Unlike natural images, ultrasound images are highly challenging for vision-language learning. First, ultrasound diagnosis involves heterogeneous diagnostic attributes. For the same lesion, radiologists may describe multiple diagnostic attributes, such as echogenicity, margins, internal characteristics, and calcification. Second, ultrasound images from different organs often look visually similar, even though they correspond to completely different anatomical structures and diagnostic semantics. Because ultrasound image-text pairs often exhibit weak semantic alignment, directly applying conventional CLIP-style contrastive learning is insufficient for ultrasound understanding. This motivates the need for semantic-aware ultrasound representation learning. To address these challenges, we first construct US365K, the first large-scale dedicated ultrasound image-text dataset. The dataset contains over 364,000 image-text pairs collected from more than 11,000 clinical cases, spanning diverse organs and pathological findings. More importantly, we introduce UDT, which stands for Unified Ultrasound Diagnostic Taxonomy. UDT standardizes both anatomical hierarchy and ultrasound diagnostic attributes, providing structured semantic knowledge for ultrasound understanding. This taxonomy serves as the semantic foundation of our framework.

She introduces herself and enthusiastically presents her team's paper for CVPR 2026, titled "Ultrasound CLIP: Semantic-Aware Contrastive Pre-Training for Ultrasound Image-Text Understanding." Her speech is articulate and well-paced, outlining the challenges of ultrasound image-text learning and presenting their dataset "US365K" and "UDT" taxonomy. title: Introduction to the Optim.AI™ test
transcription: Opti-My can be captured, the workflow of Opti-My can be captured in a four step process. So, basically we first start off with sample collection where we isolate live cancer cells from different tumor types such as biopsy resections, ascites or pleural fluids and blood or bone marrow aspirates. So, we then perform an ex vivo sensitivity test on the isolated cancer cells by treating them with 12 drugs in a mix of combinations based on proprietary design. So, we then measure the cell viability and use it for Opti-My analysis which then generates a final test report that ranks the top single, two, three and four drug combinations including any relevant clinical trial references. So, the main parameter that we are using is normalized cell viability or NCV score. This NCV score quantifies cell killing from zero to one after measuring the amount of viable cells left after drug treatment. So, NCV score of zero indicates that all cancer cells are killed, highlighting increased sensitivity to the treatment and vice versa if the NCV score is closer to one. Basically, I think as long as we can get a sample of the tumor tissue, we can test all cancer types. Yes. So, I think in our experience in our lab is more than 20 plus cancer types including cancer of unknown primary and some even very rare cancers we have also processed them before. Right now, for our Opti-My test we do short-term culture of the tumor cells. So, for hematological cancers we seed and within 24 hours we will do drug treatment. So, there is no real opportunity for the cells to have to grow or whether or not for them to die off too much. So, for solid cancers, it's a bit longer.

title: S9, Ep 12- What’s Coming For Rheumatology: Why Conferences Like EULAR Matter for Patients
transcription: Be inspired, supported, and empowered. This is the Global Healthy Living Foundation Podcast Network. Welcome to the Health Advocates, a podcast that breaks down major health news of the week to help you make sense of what's happening in the healthcare world. I'm Steven Newmark, Chief Policy Officer at the Global Healthy Living Foundation. And this week, I'm recording from London, where I'm attending one of the world's largest rheumatology conferences, EULAR, the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology. Now, if you're not in medicine or research, you might hear the word conference and picture doctors sitting through endless PowerPoint presentations and drinking too much coffee. And yes, there is definitely some of that going on here. But conferences like EULAR are actually incredibly important for patients because this is where new science gets unveiled, researchers and clinicians exchange ideas, pharmaceutical companies present emerging therapies, and patient voices increasingly shape the future of care. And for organizations like GHLF, these meetings are not just about networking, they are about making sure the patient perspective is present in rooms where important healthcare decisions and innovations are taking shape. So today, I want to pull back the curtain a little bit and explain what actually happens at conferences like EULAR, why they matter for patients, and some of the major themes already emerging this year, including artificial intelligence and the growing excitement around CAR T and cell therapies for autoimmune diseases. Let's start with the basics. One of the most important things that happens at EULAR is education. Thousands of rheumatologists from around the world gather to hear the latest research and clinical updates. And medicine changes very quickly, as we all know. New drugs emerge, new safety information develops, researchers discover new ways to diagnose and treat disease. For practicing doctors, conferences are often one of the fastest ways to stay current, and this matters directly to patients because the doctor sitting in front of you next month may change how they approach treatment based on something they learned this week at EULAR. That can mean earlier diagnoses, better disease management, more individualized treatment approaches,

title: [CVPR 2026] MoECLIP: Patch-Specialized Experts for Zero-shot Anomaly Detection
transcription: Zero-shot anomaly detection, which aims to detect anomalies in unseen categories, has recently attracted significant attention. In this work, we propose MOE-CLIP: Patch-Specialized Experts for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection. To perform zero-shot anomaly detection, existing studies primarily use pre-trained CLIP models and apply adapter fine-tuning methods to adapt them to the anomaly detection task. However, conventional approaches process all patches in a monolithic, patch-agnostic manner, without considering the unique characteristics of each patch, such as background patches or anomalous patches. To address this, we propose MOE-CLIP, a mixture-of-experts-based CLIP adaptation method that dynamically selects the most suitable expert for each patch. However, simply applying a mixture-of-experts framework leads to a functional redundancy problem among experts, where multiple experts learn highly similar representations instead of diverse knowledge. Therefore, we further propose FOFS and ETF loss, which encourage each expert to learn distinct and complementary knowledge. Here is the framework of our proposed MOE-CLIP. First, the mixture of LoRA experts module is inserted into the vision encoder layers, enabling dynamic expert selection and adaptation according to the characteristics of each image patch. The approach for achieving expert specialization, FOFS, is a technique applied at the input stage that enforces role separation among experts through the LoRA A matrices. Specifically, it decomposes the input feature space into multiple orthogonal subspaces, forcing each expert to observe only its own unique information without physical overlap with other experts.

transcription: My name is Katie Linden, and I'm the CEO at Exercise and Sports Science Australia, or ESSA. We represent over 10,000 members, including the allied health profession of exercise physiology. And I'm here today at our national conference, Activate, where we have over 800 clinicians from around the country here today to discuss research, emerging practice, and innovative models of care. My name is Jackson Howie, I'm a PhD candidate from the Centre for Heart Rhythm Disorders at the Adelaide University. I presented some of our work in pacemaker patients. It was a simple clinical question looking at the relationship between pacemaker-detected physical activity and objective exercise tolerance. I tried to tailor this to the exercise physiologists here at this meeting. It's a good opportunity for me to disseminate and share some of our research among exercise physiology colleagues. I've met some colleagues, early, early career stages all the way up to some more senior colleagues. This is a perfect opportunity to share some of our work with the broader exercise physiology community. Many of the members I've been speaking with over the last few days have echoed a very strong sentiment that we're hearing across our 10,000-strong membership, and that is the frontline challenges that businesses are facing in providing care to an increasing demand of the community for health service access. When the GST legislation was first introduced, exercise physiology was an emerging discipline. Soon afterwards, we were added to the Medicare Benefits Schedule, and we are recognized as an essential health service. But unfortunately, through a mix of timing and a legacy issue, we are still not exempt from GST, which is creating an incredible barrier to access to exercise prescription and programming for Australians. Since the GST was first introduced and exercise physiology was recognized in Medicare, our profession has grown exponentially. We now have over 9,400 accredited exercise physiologists working across Australia helping communities every day. Most people don't know this, and when they find out, they are genuinely shocked. But if you are someone with a health condition, then you have to pay an extra tax to do one of the best things you can do to manage that condition. You don't have to pay this tax to see your podiatrist, your physio, your optometrist, or your dentist, and you don't have to pay this tax for your medication. But if...

title: Dr. Dutton Address to the Senate Standing Committee on Agriculture and Forestry
transcription:
Dr. Dutton, you now have the floor.
Good morning. I'm an associate professor at Dalhousie University in department called Community Health and Epidemiology. I'm also a member of a research group called PROOF, with members across Canada and the US, who have a goal of identifying policy options to reduce household food insecurity in Canada. I want to open by pointing out that household food insecurity is a specific scientific concept. It sounds like it should be the opposite of food of food security, but it isn't. Household food insecurity is the inadequate or insecure access to food due to financial constraints at the household level. Food security has been used to refer to everything from our ability to produce enough food domestically to feed our population, food supply chain, access to food banks. Food security therefore is a term inclusive of many problems that have to do with food and people sometimes conflate action on anything related to food with solutions to household food insecurity, which is not correct. This inappropriate combination of household food insecurity with issues grouped under the banner of food security complicates the language for people in government trying to grapple with the problem of household food insecurity. So some find it helpful to think about food insecurity as part of consumption poverty uh and so is related to challenges attributable to general affordability, cost of living, labor market outcome inequality, housing, like we like we just heard. Statistics Canada measures household food insecurity using a specific questionnaire that's been agreed upon by researchers to accurately measure household material circumstances. Uh that means efforts to decrease that measure will improve the lives of Canadians by improving their health and decreasing healthcare command for uh healthcare demand, excuse me. For reference, about one in four people in Canada are in food insecure households. I know this standing committee has heard from government employees from AAFC and ESDC, ESDC and others uh who have also emphasized that food insecurity is tied to income and I heard it all morning, so that's great. This is consistent with decades of research on food insecurity. Uh PHAC recently published reviews on what impacts food insecurity in Canada and came to the same conclusion. Food insecurity is improved by actions that decrease financial hardship. Those reviews identified that giving households food through in-kind mechanisms does not make much of an impact on food insecurity. The idea that giving a household food does not impact food insecurity is a major sticking point for many people, because it sounds unintuitive.

title: Ramayana Trailer REVIEW | Deeksha Sharma
transcription: इतने सारे लीक्स में रामायण का ट्रेलर देखने के बाद अब ऐसा क्या ही बाकी बचा है जो मैं आपको नया बता दूंगी? सच बोलूं, बहुत कुछ। इतना ज्यादा हाइप भी नहीं करना चाहिए था ना क्योंकि रियल ट्रेलर में कुछ वर्ल्ड क्लास है तो थोड़ा बहुत चीजों में 50-50 फील आ रहा है। तो चलो शुरुआत उसी सवाल से कर लेते हैं जिससे हर कोई बचना चाहता है। सुबह 4:00 बजे ट्रेलर कौन डालता है? नहीं-नहीं, यह वाला नहीं, इससे भी बड़ा जरूरी दूसरा सवाल। भगवान राम के बिना रामायण कैसी और राम के लिए रणबीर कपूर का ही सिलेक्शन क्यों? क्या वाकई में मजा आ रहा है रणबीर को ऐस भगवान राम के रोल में देखकर? देखो यह बात किसी से छुपी नहीं है जब से ट्रेलर के क्लिप्स वायरल होना शुरू हुए थे और अब फाइनली ऑफिशियल वीडियो भी आ गया है, हर किसी ने यश को ऐस रावण टोटली एक्सेप्ट कर लिया है। नो इफ, नो बट, किसी दूसरे एक्टर का नाम तक नहीं लिया जा रहा है जो इस फिल्म में रावण बन सकता था या फिर यश से ज्यादा बेटर तरीके से एग्रेशन, गुस्सा, घमंड, इन सारे एक्सप्रेशन को डिस्प्ले कर सकता था। सबसे बेस्ट डिसीजन था ट्रेलर को यश के सीन के साथ शुरू करना। देखते ही अलग एनर्जी सी फील होने लगती है। उनके डायलॉग्स उनके चेहरे को पूरी तरह मैच कर रहे हैं। यश और रावण मेड फॉर ईच अदर हैं। चाहे आप इस बात को कितना भी कंट्रोवर्शियल क्यों ना समझो लेकिन हां, इस ट्रेलर के बाद काफी लोग ऐसे होंगे जो रावण की वजह से रामायण देखने जाएंगे। लेकिन इस तरीके का कॉन्फिडेंस लोगों को रणबीर के ऊपर फील नहीं हो रहा है, फिर चाहे वो 144p वाला वीडियो हो या फिर 4K एचडी का ट्रेलर। दिक्कत वीडियो क्वालिटी की नहीं है, एक्टर से एक्सपेक्टेशंस की है। ऑनेस्टली ट्रेलर में रणबीर के सीन्स ऑन-ऑफ टाइप के हैं। जब वो ब्लाइंड फोल्ड वाला सीक्वेंस आया, इतनी खुशी हुई ना अंदर से। यह है वो इंडियन सिनेमा विजन जिसके आगे अंग्रेज भी अपनी नजरें नीची कर लेंगे। लेकिन जैसे ही ट्रेलर में आंखों से वो पट्टी हटी, रणबीर पे भरोसा थोड़ा डगमगा सा जाता है। वो भगवान से धीरे-धीरे इंसान जैसे लगना शुरू हो जाते हैं। नोटिस किया, ट्रेलर में जो पास वाले शॉट्स हैं, वो काफी डाले गए हैं जिनका परपज था गॉड वाइब्स लेकर आना, पब्लिक का सर रिस्पेक्ट में झुकाना। बट ईमानदारी से बोलूंगी एक बात, मैंने सोशल मीडिया पे कुछ फैन मेड पोस्टर्स, एआई जनरेटेड इमेजेस देखी हैं जो रणबीर को भगवान राम के रूप में कई ज्यादा डिवाइन तरीके से प्रेजेंट करती हैं। मैं क्या बोलना चाह रही हूं वो शायद आप सौरभ राज जैन को स्क्रीन पे देखकर जो महसूस करते हो, उसे रामायण में रणबीर से कंपेयर करके अच्छे से समझ जाओगे। देखो जैसे शूर्पणखा का रोल है, उसमें रकुल प्रीत का अचानक आना आपकी एक्सपेक्टेशंस को क्रॉस कर जाता है। प्रेजेंटेशन जितना सोचा था उससे भी ज्यादा बेटर निकला। यही सेम बात अरुण गोविल के लिए भी कही जा सकती है। बट वो सेम फार्मूला रणबीर के केस में उतना फिट नहीं बैठ रहा है, उसका उल्टा हो रहा है फिलहाल। याद रखना इस शब्द पे खास जोर दिया है मैंने, फिलहाल। क्योंकि ऐसा भी नहीं है कि ट्रेलर देखकर आप रणबीर से अंधा हेट करने लग जाओ, सीधा उनकी कास्टिंग पे सवाल खड़े करने लग जाओ, या फिर इतना अंधा भी नहीं होना है कि एक्सपेक्टेशंस को मार ही डालो, जो है, जैसा है उसपे सवाल भी ना पूछा जाए। यह दोनों ही कैटेगरी के काम जो कर रहे हैं या तो उनकी आत्मा बिक गई है या फिर बैंक बैलेंस। फैन वॉर्स होते रहेंगे, पेड पीआर भी चलता रहेगा। वैसे भी उन लोगों से क्या एक्सपेक्ट कर सकते हो आप जो भगवान इंद्र के ऐरावत के बारे में कुछ नहीं जानते हैं और भगवान हनुमान को मंकी गॉड कहकर बुलाते हैं। लेकिन इस सब के बीच में रणबीर के पास तगड़ा मौका है टैलेंट के दम पर हेटर्स को अपना फैन बनाने का जिसमें नितेश तिवारी की बहुत ज्यादा हेल्प चाहिए होगी। यह भगवान परशुराम वाला सीन तो बोनस की तरह आ गया ना। कितने लोगों ने पहले

और हमारी मुलाकात बार-बार होगी। सबसे पहले अब मैं यहाँ खुल के कह सकता हूँ कि रावण का जो लुक अभी आपने ट्रेलर में देखा या लॉर्ड परशुराम का जो ग्लिम्प्स आपने अभी ट्रेलर में देखा या इवन कुंभकरण, वो हमने क्रिएटर इवेंट में मुंबई में देखा था नमित मल्होत्रा जी के घर। आई मीन इसके अलावा भी बहुत कुछ देखा था, ऐरावत वाली लड़ाई और कुछ एक कैरेक्टर्स। तो वही कुछ एक सेम कैरेक्टर्स इसमें भी दिखाए गए हैं एंड आई मस्ट से कि इस 4 मिनट के ट्रेलर में रावण के कैरेक्टर में यश बस कमाल ही करते नज़र आ रहे हैं। सी, आई एम नॉट ग्लोरिफाइंग रावण, बट आई एम टॉकिंग अबाउट यश की परफॉर्मेंस। एंड पूरा ट्रेलर देखने के बाद आई कैन प्राउडली से कि जितनी भी कास्टिंग की गई है वो एकदम ऑन पॉइंट लग रही है। अब देखो कोई बोलेगा कि रावण का कैरेक्टर इतना मस्त एक्शन वगैरह करते हुए दिखाया है, अग्रेशन में दिखाया है और रणबीर एज़ श्री राम को एकदम ठंडा सा दिखा दिया। भाई, वी आर नाउ हैबिचुअल टू सी मेनस्ट्रीम एक्टर्स इन टॉक्सिक मेल पर्सनालिटी। कबीर सिंह में शाहिद का अग्रेशन देख लो आप, रणबीर कपूर को एनिमल में पसंद किया गया था क्योंकि वो अग्रेशन से भरा हुआ था, यश को केजीएफ में पसंद किया गया था क्योंकि अगेन अल्फा मेल मस्क्युलिनिटी, मार्को में उन्नी मुकुंदन को, द बॉयज़ में होमलैंडर को, सेम विद पुष्पा, सेम विद अदर ग्रे शेड्स एंड एंटी-हीरो टाइप कैरेक्टर्स क्योंकि वो अग्रेशन एंड मार-धाड़ एंड टॉक्सिसिटी से भरे हुए थे एंड आजकल लोगों को वही पसंद भी आता है भाई। यहाँ रणबीर राम हैं भाई, वो जैसे थे वैसा ही प्रेजेंट किया गया है शांत मर्यादा वाले। एंड आई डोंट हैव एनी डाउट कि रणबीर एज़ श्री राम वैसा ही अपना कैरेक्टर को प्ले करेंगे जैसी रिक्वायरमेंट श्री राम की परफॉर्मेंस के लिए सूट करेगी। यश तो एब्सोल्यूट जेम लग ही रहे हैं। ही इज़ लाइक जैसे रामानंद सागर के रावण के बाद अगर कोई रावण सूट हुआ है तो वो यश ही हैं। इवन ईच एंड एवरी कैरेक्टर इज़ सूटेड फॉर देयर रोल। तो मैं कास्टिंग एंड उनके परफॉर्मेंस को लेकर कोई नेगेटिव पॉइंट ज़बरदस्ती नहीं रखना चाहूँगा। लेकिन जहाँ हम सबको पता है अबाउट रामायण, वहाँ हम इस फ़िल्म में बस प्रेजेंटेशन के लिए उत्साहित हैं एंड डैम, द प्रेजेंटेशन! रावण का वो पहला शॉट, वो एक लात से दरवाज़ा, आई मीन उतना बड़ा ह्यूज़ द्वार भव्य

title: Moondru Mudichu - Best Scenes 1 | 25 July  2026 | Tamil Serial | Sun TV
transcription: ஃபுல் மூன் சேல் காலை 9 மணியிலிருந்து இரவு 12 மணி வரை. ஜூலை 29 ஒரு நாள் மட்டும். ஏங்க கடைக்கா? கையில் பேக்கெல்லாம் பலமா இருக்கு. உனக்கு என்ன வேணும் இப்போ? நாங்க எங்க போய்ட்டு வந்தா உனக்கு என்ன? பின்னாடியே மோப்பம் பிடிச்சிட்டு வரதுக்கு பேரு மனுஷன் இல்ல. அதுக்கு வேற பேரு. என்னன்னு சொல்லவா? அதுவும் சரிதான். ஏன்னா நல்ல பெரிய இடமா எல்லாம் புடிச்சு முந்தானையில் முடிஞ்சு வச்சிருக்க. என் பங்காளி வீட்டுலதான் காசு, பணம், சொத்துன்னு எல்லாம் கொட்டிக் கெடக்க. அப்ப இதுவும் பேசுவ, இன்னமும் பேசுவ நீ. பேச மட்டும் செய்ய மாட்டேன். நீ ஓவரா பேசினா செயல்லயும் காட்டுவேன். அசிங்கப்படுறதுக்கு முன்னாடி வழியை விட்டுட்டு போயிரு. ஏம்மா ரோட்ல பார்த்து ஒரு நலம் விசாரிக்கிறது எல்லாம் ஒரு குத்தமா? நீ வேணும்னா அங்க நிக்கிற நாலு பேரை கூப்பிட்டு கேட்டு பாரு. இப்போ உனக்கு என்ன வேணும்? ஏய் உன்கிட்ட எனக்கு என்னடி வேணும்? என் நெஞ்சு அப்படியே கொதிக்குதுடி. அதுக்கான பலி தீக்குறதுக்குதான்டி இங்க வந்திருக்கேன். மரியாதையா பேசு. ஏய் உனக்கெல்லாம் என்னடி மரியாதை? நீ பாட்டுக்கு போலீஸ்ல என்ன பிடிச்சு குடுத்துட்டு மெட்ராஸ்க்கு ஓடி போய்ட்ட. உன்னை விட்ருவேன்னு நினைச்சியாடி நீனு? விடமாட்டேன்டி. ஏய் ஜெயில்ல இருந்து வந்ததுல இருந்து உன்னை தீர்த்துக்கட்டதான்டி வெயிட் பண்ணிக்கிட்டு இருக்கேன். இப்ப கூட நான் உன் கண் முன்னாடிதானே நிக்கிறேன்? உன்னால என்னடா பண்ண முடியும்? என்னது டா போட்டு பேசுறியாடி நீனு? ஏய் திமிருதான்டி உனக்கு. ஏய் நீ ஒன்னும் மெட்ராஸ்ல என் பங்காளி வீட்டுல ஒன்னும் பாதுகாப்பா இல்லடி. இப்ப என் கிராமத்துல என் முன்னாடி நின்னுகிட்டு இருக்க. அதை மறந்துட்டு பேசுறடி நீ. என்ன? மிரட்டுறியா? இது உனக்கு மட்டும் சொந்த ஊரு இல்ல. நானும் இதே ஊருதான். எனக்கும் நாலு பேர் இங்க வந்து நிக்கத்தான் செய்வாங்க. ஏய் உனக்கு நாலு பேர்னா எனக்கு 400 பேர் வருவான்டி. சரிடா. 400 பேரை வச்சு நீ என்னத்த கிழிப்ப? அதை சொல்லு. அம்புட்டு ஏத்தம்மாடி உனக்கு? என்னைக்கு இருந்தாலும் என்கிட்ட வசமா நீ சிக்குவன்னு பார்த்தேன்டி. ஆனா இம்புட்டு சீக்கிரம் நீ சிக்குவன்னு நான் எதிர்பார்க்கலடி. பார்த்துகிட்டே இருடி. நீ இங்க இருந்து போறதுக்குள்ளார உன் குடும்பத்துல ஒரு கொலை விழுவிலன்னா கேளுடி. இதுல என்னன்னா அது நீயா இல்ல என் சின்ன பங்காளியா இல்ல உன் தோட்டக்கார ஃபேமிலியானுதான்டி தெரியாம நிக்கிறேன். ஒரு கொலை கண்டிப்பா விழுமடி. அது மட்டும் கன்பார்ம்டி. டேய் நானும் சொல்றேன் எழுதி வச்சுக்க. என் மேலயோ என் குடும்பத்து ஆளுங்க மேலயோ நீ கையை வச்ச... அடுத்த நிமிஷம் என் புருஷன் உன் கை வேற கால் வேறையா பிச்சு திசைக்கு ஒன்னா வீசி எறிஞ்சிருவான். ஏய் அதையும் நான் பார்க்கிறேன்டி. வாடி பார்த்துக்கலாம். பார்ப்போம் பார்ப்போம். அடச்சீ வழியை விடு. அறுக்கத் தெரியாத கேனப் பயலுக்கு வாய் மட்டும் 50 மைலுக்கு நீளுமாம். ஆளப்பாரு. வாடி போலாம். வந்துட்டான்.

questions.answer: He mentions either the female speaker herself, his junior partner (chinna pangaali), or her gardener's family (thottakaaran family).

questions.answer: She warns that her husband will tear his arms and legs apart and throw them away in different directions.

questions.answer: She mocks him as a foolish guy who doesn't even know how to cut/fight but has a mouth that is 50 miles long (all talk and no action).

questions.question: Describe the overall tone and emotional delivery of the two main speakers in the dialogue.
questions.answer: The tone is highly hostile, dramatic, and tense. The male speaker exhibits intense anger, shouting, and mocking laughter, while the female speaker responds with defiance, anger, and sharp sarcasm.

title: 'It's sick!': Nicolle SLAMS Trump wanting to pay Jan. 6ers
transcription:
Let's discuss with the host of Deadline: White House on MS Now, and the Best People podcast, my friend Nicolle Wallace. Hi, Nicolle.
Hi. First of all, a belated congratulations on your wonderful new show. I'm so happy to be here on it with you. Um, you know, I watch those cabinet meetings, um, and I keep thinking that in Pyongyang, Kim Jong Un is the one throwing spaghetti against a wall. I mean, these are, for a president in such dire political straits, which he is, um, to have blocked out of his orbit, people who I find their politics loathsome, and their ethics non-existent, but their, their sort of understanding of MAGA politics were, were pretty great, people like Steve Bannon, um, people who are around Trump in the first term. I mean, this is not what the base wants to hear about. This is what about, you know, probably 3% of Trump's own voters want to hear about. The other, you know, 30% want to hear about the cost of groceries and the cost of gas, and this war that feels intractable in the Middle East, that Donald Trump specifically promised in 2015 and '16, he would never get the country involved in. title: Marco Rubio: We can't IGNORE the threat of Cuba
transcription: Secretary, great to have you back. Thank you so much. Glad to be back. It's been a while. Yeah. There's so much to talk about, but I want to start with Cuba. Um, this has been of particular interest to the State Department right now. You guys released a 100-page report on Cuba, calling it the capital of 21st-century communism, and this report talks about the fact that Cuba's goal, essentially, is to erase the United States from the earth. It also details a Cuban spy network that's been undermining American interests. How did we get to a place where Cuba has become so much of a threat, it feels like, again, to the United States? I think for those who have followed the issue of Cuba, this is not unfamiliar to us, but to the average American, you know, you see Cuba, small country, 90 miles off our shores, you know, 9 and a half million people population. What people forget that when it comes to things like espionage and influence operations, they actually are an influence and espionage superpower. If you look at the history of espionage in the United States, Cuba is the only country that consistently has implanted and embedded spies in our system without even paying them. We had an ambassador, a US ambassador who ended up being a Cuban spy and was recently convicted. We've had them penetrate the highest levels of the Defense Intelligence Agency. Ana Belen Montes was one of the single biggest intelligence failures on the part of the United States and one of the biggest penetrations we've ever had in our system. So, and then on the influence front, if you look all throughout Latin America, every communist, left-wing insurgency that's destabilized governments across the region, every single one of them over the last 40, 50 years has found its support, its help, in many cases its birth, from a Cuban influence operation. So, it was an important report just to highlight the role they play in our country, a very negative role. The report also links Cuban influence to the rise of Antifa, the riots that we saw in 2020, as well as the surge of radical activism that we've seen all over these college campuses. Um, to the average person, those things, I think, feel generally organic. But it turns out there are a lot of different powers, Cuba being one of them, that are influencing all of these things day to day. Absolutely. It's the same network of protesters around the country. There were the same people you saw in the streets burning things in 2020. They then flip it around and they become the pro-Hamas protesters. And they flip it around and within 48 hours of Maduro's arrest, have pre-printed signs outside the courthouse demanding his release.

title: PE Fund Journal Entry Bible | Private Equity Accounting Interview Guide
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Most candidates memorize PE journal entries and still fail the interview. Why? Because the interviewer is not testing debit and credit only. They are testing cash, NAV, investor capital and LP reporting. Take one private equity fund case: commitment $100 million, capital called $20 million, investment made $15 million, fund expense $1 million, management fee $2 million, fair value $18 million, exit $18 million, distribution to LPs $5 million. Here is the scoreboard. After every entry, ask: did cash move? Did NAV move? Capital activity or performance? What reaches LP reporting? First, capital call. The fund calls 20 million from LPs. Debit cash 20 million, credit investor capital 20 million. Cash increases, investor capital increases, but performance has not improved. This is capital activity, not income. Capital call brings cash, it does not create profit. Second, investment made. The fund invests 15 million into a portfolio company or SPV. Debit investment 15 million, credit cash 15 million. Cash goes down, investment asset goes up, but there is no immediate gain. Cash became investment, that is the trap. Investment made is not an expense and it does not automatically increase NAV. Third, fund expense. Assume 1 million of audit, legal or admin expense. Debit fund expense 1 million, credit expense payable or cash 1 million. This hits P&L, so NAV reduces. LP reporting shows fund level expense impact. The trap: fund expense is not capital activity. It reduces NAV because it hits P&L.

He presents a case study involving a fund with a $100 million commitment, walking through different scenarios such as capital calls, investments, and fund expenses. title: Journal Your Best Reality ✨ How to Manifest Your Dream Life Through Writing.
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Have you ever felt like you were just one step away from the life you actually want to live, but you just cannot seem to grab it? We have all been there. You have these big dreams and deep desires, but they feel like they are stuck in some alternate reality that you can only see from a distance. Well today, I want to share something with you that completely shifted everything for me. It is not magic and it is not just wishful thinking. It is the intentional practice of journaling to attract your best reality. I used to think journaling was just for recording what happened during my day like a diary, but once I realized it could be a tool for creation, my whole world changed. First, let us talk about why this actually works. When you put pen to paper, you are doing more than just writing words. You are focusing your energy, and giving your subconscious mind a clear roadmap. Most of the time our brains are cluttered with thousands of random thoughts, but journaling forces you to slow down and get specific. It is like sending a clear signal to the universe saying, 'this is exactly what I am ready for.' Your brain has a filtering system called the reticular activating system, and when you write down your desires, you are essentially telling that system what to look for in the real world. The first thing I always do before I start writing is get into a state of gratitude. You cannot manifest from a place of lack because the energy of wanting something often carries the heavy feeling of not having it. So, I start by listing three things I am genuinely thankful for right now. It could be as simple as a good cup of coffee, a supportive friend, or even just the fact that I have a quiet moment to myself. This shifts your vibration from 'I need' to 'I appreciate' which is the perfect foundation for attracting more. Now, let us get into the most powerful part of my routine, which is called scripting. Scripting is basically writing about your future as if it is happening right now, in the present tense. Instead of saying, 'I want to have my dream job,' you would write, 'I am so incredibly happy and fulfilled in my new career.' You have to get detailed. What does your office smell like? How does it feel when you see your name on that door? Who are you celebrating with at dinner tonight? The key is to involve all your senses. When you write these details, your brain starts to believe it is a memory rather than a distant hope. This bridge between your current reality and your desired one is where

title: Apple’s Journal App Helped Me Organize My Entire Life

transcription: Most of us have thoughts we don't want to keep floating around in our heads all day. Ideas, reminders, things we need to do tomorrow, things we're worried about, things we don't want to forget. For a long time, I tried keeping all that in paper journals. I actually loved them, I probably bought way too many of them over the years. But eventually, I ran into one problem: I didn't always have them with me when I needed them. And that's when something interesting started happening. Over the past few months, Apple's Journal app has quietly turned into something different for me. It's not just a journaling app anymore, it's basically become my digital notebook. The place where I organize my thoughts, capture ideas, and keep different parts of my life in one place. So, in this video, I want to show you how I set it up, how I organize my journals inside the app, and why it's slowly replacing paper notebooks for me. But I'm curious about something first. Has Apple's Journal app replaced your paper notebook yet? Or are there things still holding you back? Let me know in the comments. And if you enjoy calm tech videos about productivity and intentional living, hit that like button and subscribe. It really helps the channel. All right, let's get into it. I've always liked paper journals. There's something satisfying about finishing one and keeping it on a shelf. It feels like you actually own it. It's not locked away inside an app somewhere. And writing with a pen just feels natural. You can jot something down quickly, cross things out, draw arrows, sketch little ideas. Things that don't always feel as fluid when you're typing. In the past, I tried using digital journaling apps, but I usually ended up going back to paper. But paper journals eventually started becoming inconvenient for one simple reason: I didn't always have them with me. If I had an idea while I was out somewhere, on the train, traveling, or just away from home, I couldn't write it down unless the notebook happened to be nearby. Another issue was organization. At one point, I tried using a bullet journal system with calendars, indexes, and sections, but maintaining all that just started to feel like a chore. Searching for something I wrote weeks earlier could be frustrating unless everything was perfectly indexed, which I usually didn't keep up with. With the Journal app, that problem basically disappears. Everything is automatically dated, everything is searchable. And most importantly, it's always with me. I always have my phone nearby, and most of the time, my iPad is within reach, too. And once Apple brought the Journal app to the iPad with Apple Pencil support, it started giving me many of the same benefits that the paper journals had. I can still jot things down by hand, sketch quick ideas, or cross things out. But now, it lives everywhere I go. Over time, I started organizing the app into different journals. Right now, I have five journals, but three of them are the ones I use the most. I have separate places for different parts of my life, so I know where things belong. The first one is called Personal Log. This works like a traditional journal. I write about my life, things that are on my mind, things that make me happy, things that bothered me,

title: Moving Forward | My Anxiety Story (Part 7)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: What if understanding anxiety and panic attacks is not enough to beat it? For a long time, I believed that if I just learned enough about anxiety, if I became aware of its existence and its causes, it would eventually disappear. But knowledge alone didn't change much. The real change started only when I began taking action. Welcome back, or just welcome if this is your first time here. My name is Luka, and this is part seven of my anxiety story. In this video, I'll talk about the moment when I realized something important: it is not enough to simply learn a lot about our enemy, although that is certainly the first and essential step. To ultimately defeat it, or to overpower it to the point where there is no battle at all, we must create a solid plan and strategy, and then truly begin with active preparations. So, how do I stand on my own two feet again? How do I run freely without fear? All of us secretly hope that our problems will solve themselves, that someone will appear with a magic wand and make everything disappear. We just need to be patient, and it will happen. And yes, sometimes life really does work that way. Sometimes, someone unexpectedly helps you, sometimes a problem gets resolved by someone else. Sometimes, time slowly erases things. But the truth is, situations that get solved like that are actually very rare. When it comes to anxiety and panic attacks, you can be 100% sure of one thing: they will not disappear on their own. And if you do nothing, the situation will most likely only get worse. So, if we want to win the lottery, we first have to buy a ticket. That's when the first steps of self-help begin. And that's exactly what I did. My psychiatrist gave me advice and guidance on how to live with anxiety and panic attacks, how to slowly expose myself to the things that scared me, how to face those fears step by step. And I actually put many of those tips into practice. When my mind finally felt free enough to move forward, my real self-help journey began.

title: Exercise Burnout & Anxiety: My Recovery Story
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: What if your healthy exercise routine is secretly fueling burnout? Mine did, wrecking my nervous system, spiking anxiety, and turning sleep into a nightmare. I literally ran into my doom. A few tweaks to my routine, however, kept my cardio fitness soaring while calming my nervous system and restoring sleep. The changes I will share are backed by 40 years of scientific research proven to help runners and cyclists of all ages, and they're easy. Stick around, I'll reveal the symptoms I ignored and how I fixed them to reclaim my energy using the CAT, hockey stick, ego approach. Hello, all. I am Daniel, father of two, corporate and weekend warrior, and had a severe burnout last year. First, let's talk about the sneaky symptoms, all equally important, which indicated that I was on the verge of nervous system collapse, and I completely ignored because I thought I was invincible. Number one, changes in level of tiredness. Legs like lead, stiff even after rest. You start to also have post-run highs, crashing in the afternoons with headaches, or even directly after the run, not experiencing the euphoria you normally feel. This is hard to identify because you think, "This is just normal tiredness." Be alert of increases in duration and frequency. Any increase is a red flag. Number two, skyrocketing heart rate. My runs pushed me to max zones way too often. What was moderate became intense. Your body is basically screaming, "Slow down." Number three, sleep quality goes down. Exercise should help sleep, right? Nope, mine tanked. And this is essentially because too much exercise stimulates hormones to be elevated at the wrong times, leading to anxiety and body still on edge at night. For example, cortisol levels are elevated throughout the day and night. Number four, moody without workouts. Skip a run, felt off, guilty, irritable. Turns out it's hormone havoc from overdoing it, not just missing the endorphins.

title: The Anxiety Trick No One Talks About (True Student Story)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Have you ever caught yourself trapped in a loop of your own thoughts, lying awake at 2:00 a.m., replaying a conversation from years ago, convinced everyone secretly hates you? If you have, know this: you are not broken, you are not weak. Alex felt exactly what you're feeling right now. Alex was a first-year student. Good grades, tight friend group, a hard-earned scholarship, but underneath, his mind was a battlefield. Picture it: 6:00 a.m., Alex on the dorm floor, heart hammering like it might crack a rib. No fire, no danger, just a presentation due at nine. Here's what nobody tells you about panic: it doesn't need a reason, it just needs a nervous system running on empty. Alex missed that presentation. Then three more. Isolation crept in slowly, the way it always does. Skipped classes became skipped meals. Let that sink in. One of the sharpest minds in his program was disappearing, not from lack of ability, but from a mind stuck in survival mode. Stay with me, because the breakthrough in phase three is a tool most people ignore completely, and the quiet decision Alex made in the final month decides whether any of us can break free from our own mental traps today. One, naming the enemy. Alex thought something was medically wrong. Racing heart, shaking hands, walls closing in during lectures. The amygdala, the brain's alarm system, can't tell a tiger from a test. It floods the body with adrenaline and waits for you to run. Alex wasn't losing his mind; his mind was just aimed at the wrong target. The turning point? A counselor gave him one sentence: "Name it, don't become it." Instead of "I am anxious," he learned to say, "Anxiety is visiting." The fight wasn't in the classroom; it was between his ears. Two, rebuilding from the ground up. Naming it didn't erase it. Isolation is where anxiety thrives, and Alex knew it. So he built tiny, deliberate acts of discomfort: sitting in the library instead of his room, speaking one sentence in class, texting a friend back with shaking hands. This is behavioral activation.

title: Epstein Barr Virus- EBV  Reactivation Explained: Why You Feel Exhausted, Achy, and Inflamed
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Well hi, I'm Dr. Heikmeier and in today's video we're going to dive into a topic that I think is often overlooked in traditional medicine, conventional medicine, but I believe it plays a huge role in explaining why so many people suffer with chronic fatigue, brain fog and often autoimmune flare-ups. Today, I'm talking about the reactivation of Epstein-Barr. If you've ever been struggling with this relentless fatigue despite sleeping well, if your blood work comes back so called normal, but you're really feeling anything but, or if you've had mono in the past and never quite felt the same afterwards, today's video may provide a missing piece to what you've been searching for. Well, let's start with the basics of Epstein-Barr, EBV. This is part of the herpes family. You've probably heard this as mononucleosis or just simply mono or you may have heard this as just kissing disease. Most people are exposed to Epstein-Barr virus at some point in their life and by some estimates as much as 90% of people adults carry this. Now in many cases, the initial infection just passes and the virus becomes dormant in your body, especially in your B cells, which are again are part of your immune system. But here's the key, Epstein-Barr virus never fully leaves your body, it simply just goes into an inactive state. So, while Epstein-Barr virus can remain dormant really for years, certain stressors or triggers can cause it to wake up and then become reactive and when that happens, your immune system has to mount a response. This often looks and feels like chronic fatigue, autoimmune flare ups and some people muscle aches and joint pain and brain fog and sometimes even low-grade fever or even swollen lymph nodes. Unfortunately, most standard lab work does not check for Epstein-Barr virus or even reactivation unless specifically requested and many doctors, to be honest, don't even think about testing it for patients that present with persistent chronic fatigue or vague symptoms. So, let's take a closer look at some of these symptoms, right? You may be dealing with reactivated Epstein-Barr if you experience persistent or crushing fatigue that doesn't improve with rest, like I mentioned, a sore throat or swollen glands without necessarily infection, muscle or joint pain or brain fog and memory problems, maybe poor exercise tolerance, maybe changes in mood and energy

title: Why You Still Feel Like a Child Pretending to Be an Adult
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription:
You are sitting in a meeting, or maybe you're just paying your electricity bill. On the outside, you look like a fully functioning adult, but on the inside, you feel like a scared 12-year-old wearing oversized clothes, like you think, "it just feels like I was in my school," and you can't believe it. See, when a crisis happens, uh maybe a flat tire, a mistake at work, a medical issue, your first instinct is to look around the room for a real adult to come and fix it. And then, you get a terrifying uh realization, "I'm supposed to be the real adult, right?" Now you feel deeply embarrassed. Uh you look at your friends and coworkers and assume they all have life figured out, while you are just wondering how you got this old, because inside, you haven't aged a day over 12. In this video, we are going to talk about exactly why you are feeling like this and what the way out is.

Hi, I'm Gayatri Arvind, founder of Abasa Rehab and Wellness. We offer residential rehabilitation for people struggling with addiction, mental health disorders, eating disorders, and chronic conditions. Over the past six years, we have helped over thousands of people reclaim their lives through personalized care. Through this channel, we share practical wisdom to empower your mental health.

Clinical psychology says that your brain operates in different modes. Think of them as different versions of your personality that take over depending on your stress levels. For example, you have the demanding parent mode that constantly criticize you, the detached protector mode that numbs your feelings, the healthy adult mode that handles life rationally, and the vulnerable child mode. See, when you feel like a terrified kid pretending to be grown up, you are not imagining things. You have actually slipped into what we call the vulnerable child mode. Uh when you were growing up, if you didn't feel safe, or if your feelings were constantly ignored, your brain did something to protect you, right? It hits the pause button on your emotional growth. That part of your mind froze, and it got stuck at the exact age where you felt the most hurt or scared. So today, when your boss criticizes you, or when you face financial stress, you do not react with the brain of a capable 30-year-old. Your brain time travels, and that frozen, scared inner child grabs the steering wheel of your 30

title: Anxious About The New - Addiction Recovery Daily Reflection
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hello, and welcome to another Daily Reflections video. I'm Dr. Anastasia Hronis, clinical psychologist, author of the book, The Dopamine Brain, and I work in the field of addictions. And pretty frequently, I try to jump on here and provide you guys with a daily reflection in the context of addiction recovery. I'm currently coming to you from a hotel room in Hobart—not Hobart, in Tasmania, in Launceston, um, where I am doing some work over the next few days with the Royal Flying Doctors Service out here. Um, one of my hats and one of the roles that I have is to provide training to services, um, on the therapy of DBT, dialectical behavior therapy, which can be incredibly useful for people who are going through addiction recovery. But that is beside the point. Today, I have another daily reflection for you. Um, and this one is on the theme of anxiety. We haven't yet touched the theme of anxiety, but it is one that shows up quite commonly. If you're new here, I like to jump on and provide daily reflection videos. Yes, there's lots of daily reflection books out there that exist, um, for the purpose of helping people reflect on a particular theme each day in the context of addiction recovery. I like to write my own. And the reason for this is, I like to write them based on the themes that I'm hearing from the clients that I work with in the clinic who are going through the process of addiction recovery, um, but also based on the work of research that I do, as well, um, so based on what I'm hearing, what I'm thinking about, um, and the information that clients, um, who have experiences of addictions are telling me. I like to go on, way, think about those, um, marinate in those thoughts, and then write some daily reflections for you guys to think about and listen to. So, today's daily reflection is called, "Feeling anxious about the new." This is something I hear a lot of. So, I'm going to read it out, and then I'm going to share some thoughts with you. Change. Even good change can feel unsettling. When we leave behind what's familiar, substances, routines, or identities attached to the substances, we lose our old reference points. The new can sometimes feel too quiet, too predictable, too boring, or simply unknown. But that anxiety doesn't mean that you're doing something wrong. It actually means that you're growing. Recovery asks us to step into spaces that we haven't yet learned to trust. It takes time for that feeling of safety to catch up with the progress that you're making. The body and the mind need repetition to believe that the peace that you're experiencing won't just suddenly disappear. You don't have to rush into feelings of comfort. Just keep showing up for the life that you're building, even if your hands are shaking while you're doing it.

Anxiety is probably the most common thing that brings people into my office. Uh, it's actually anxiety disorders are the most common of all mental health disorders. So, this is like our bread and butter. I think of anxiety as being a close cousin of fear, right? Like fear is that sensation that you have when you are like staring down a threat, whether that's a rogue tiger or an enemy combatant or an oncoming vehicle, right? Fear is that in the moment, something is wrong, my life is in danger. Anxiety is, is that feeling, but it's future-oriented. So, it's sort of the anticipation that something bad could happen in the future, um, and it takes lots of different forms, and this is why there are so many different anxiety disorders. They all are distinguished by what the person is anxious about. And it doesn't necessarily, it doesn't necessarily mean that you're anticipating, uh, your life being threatened, but I mean, it, it could be an interview for a job or anything like that, right? Right. For, for somebody with social anxiety, it might be public speaking, you know, the fear of being evaluated or judged by someone else. title: How to Manage Anxiety and Depression Without Fighting Yourself | A Healing Story.
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Every morning, Daniel woke up tired. Not the kind of tired sleep fixes, but the heavy one, the kind that sat on his chest like a stone and whispered, 'What's the point?' Before his eyes even opened, his mind was already running. Bills, expectations, old conversations replaying themselves like punishment, future disasters that hadn't happened yet, but felt certain. Anxiety arrived first, loud and demanding. Depression followed quietly, like a shadow that refused to leave. For a long time, Daniel fought them both. He read articles with titles like 'Beat Anxiety in Seven Days' and 'How to Eliminate Depression Forever'. He forced smiles, forced productivity, forced prayer, forced gratitude. When none of it worked, he blamed himself. 'Other people are strong, why can't I just fix this?' One evening, after another day of pretending he was okay, Daniel sat alone on his bedroom floor. His phone buzzed with unanswered messages. The room felt too quiet, yet his mind was unbearably loud. That night, he didn't pray for healing, he prayed for permission. 'God,' he whispered, 'I don't know how to make this stop, but I'm tired of running.' Nothing dramatic happened, no sudden peace, no miracle, but something subtle shifted. The next day, Daniel decided to stop declaring war on his mind. Instead of saying, 'I must not feel anxious,' he tried something new. 'I am anxious, and I'm still here.' When the familiar tightness rose in his chest, he didn't immediately distract himself or criticize it. He sat down, placed a hand on his chest, breathed slowly, not to make the feeling disappear, but to stay with it. 'This is anxiety,' he told himself gently. 'It's uncomfortable, but it's not dangerous.' The feeling didn't vanish, but it softened just a little. Depression was harder. Depression didn't shout, it drained. It made simple things—showering, replying a text, standing up—feel like climbing a mountain with no summit. Some days, Daniel could do nothing but sit by the window and watch time pass. Instead of

title: I Drank Alcohol During Anxiety DPDR Recovery
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I drank caffeine the entire time that I was actually overcoming anxiety DPDR. I stopped caffeine, however, in the earlier stages, and believe it or not, it made me worse. Now, when I bring up the topic of caffeine, a lot of the times, people ask me about alcohol. And during my anxiety DPDR recovery, I did actually drink alcohol from time to time. And believe it or not, it was actually my family doctor who knew my whole situation, who knew that I was dealing with anxiety, depersonalization, derealization, and gave me the go-ahead if I wanted to drink caffeine, or if I wanted to drink alcohol, and even if I wanted to consume nicotine, he said it was fine, just to be aware that it might create sensations, and to be prepared to respond correctly. He understood the framework that I was trying to use in my recovery process, and he said that this aligned with it, just to be prepared in case symptoms should show up, to know that you will have to respond correctly. And at that point, I had already started drinking caffeine again as my normal routine, and told him it actually made me feel a bit better. I was just a bit skeptical and scared about having a drink of alcohol from time to time. And as far as nicotine goes, after I fell into the cycle, I've never consumed it since, not out of fear of the symptoms, but just for health purposes. And that's a huge distinction, because once you fully overcome anxiety DPDR, the symptoms have no bearing over your decisions whatsoever. However, when I did start drinking alcohol again from time to time, I noticed that it didn't calm me down the same way it really used to, and it didn't give me that euphoric feeling that it normally would, so I didn't really enjoy it the same way at first. When I did drink alcohol, I noticed I was a little bit more alert, and I was constantly still trying to focus on whether or not I felt the effects, and in turn, would analyze my symptoms a bit. But it just never seemed to give me that same relaxed, you know, euphoric feeling that it used to before falling into the cycle. But, I did still drink occasionally, because that's what normal me would be doing. And I tried my best to not focus on the sensations, and if sensations did come up because of it, then I would just redirect my attention the same way, and treat it like any other trigger. But, what I did do, was manage the amount of alcohol I would drink. Typically, back in the day, I could drink three to five drinks and have a great time and, you know, not feel the effects too much the next day. But, because I was aware that my nervous system was sensitized, I would only have one, two, and sometimes maybe three drinks at most, all while staying hydrated and drinking water or Gatorade alongside it. As I proceeded through recovery and gained confidence,

title: Dear Anyone Whose Anxiety Never Fully Goes Away...
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Dear anyone. You know that feeling when you wake up and for one second, just one, everything feels okay? And then it comes back. That quiet tightness in your chest. That feeling that something is wrong even when nothing actually is. You didn't even do anything. You just woke up and it was already waiting. If that's your life, not just bad days, not just stressful weeks, but this thing that just never fully leaves, stay with me because I don't think you're weak. I think you've been carrying something most people don't even know exists. Let me describe your day. Before you even check your phone, your body is already on alert. Not panic, not a breakdown. Just that background tightness that never fully turns off. You go through your day, you function, you talk to people, you laugh at the right moments, like a tab open in the background that you can never fully close. And the exhausting part? It's not the big moments. It's the small ones. The phone ringing unexpectedly, the slight change in someone's tone that sends your whole nervous system into high alert, and you think, "Why am I like this? Everyone else seems fine." Sound familiar? Here's what people around you don't get. They think anxiety is just worrying, just overthinking, just being a little nervous. They don't understand that for you, it's not occasional. It's waking up at 3:00 a.m. for no reason, heart already racing. It's replaying a conversation from three days ago and still finding new things to feel bad about. It's canceling plans not because you don't want to go, but because your body said no before your brain could argue. And when you try to explain this, they say, "Just breathe," or "Stop overthinking," as if you wouldn't choose calm if calm were that simple.

title: I FULLY Recovered from Anxiety DPDR Without Changing Much
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I suffered with anxiety DPDR for two years straight and honestly, I didn't change that much about me, if anything at all, really. I have a pretty bad sleep schedule, meaning I go to bed very late and I also wake up late. Didn't change that, not even once throughout my recovery. I like to drink caffeine, I drank caffeine throughout my entire recovery. I like to occasionally have alcohol, I drank alcohol during my recovery. I didn't have an extremely strict routine and ultimately, I really did not change anything about my core self or personality or the typical behaviors I would engage in. What I did change, I didn't drink extreme amounts of caffeine because before I fell into anxiety DPDR, I would drink like, and I'm saying insane amounts of caffeine, not just, you know, a few cups of coffee. I would pound pre-workout, like three scoops, which led to like, I think like 500 to 700 milligrams at a time before working out, not to mention the caffeine I'd have throughout the day. And I only stopped that because it was just generally unhealthy. Outside of that, I didn't change any actual things regarding my personality or regarding my behaviors at large. What I did change, however, is my understanding of anxiety, depersonalization, derealization, and nervous system sensitization. I suffered for two years because I didn't actually understand these concepts wholeheartedly. And a part of me kept wondering, "Maybe it's something worse," and that worry, in and of itself, kept it alive. Once I fully understood these concepts, and how they're intertwined, and how our nervous system operates, and the reason it produces these types of symptoms, I was able to change my relationship with the symptoms, which inevitably reduced the fear of the symptoms, which allowed me to let them exist alongside me while I lived life normally, still doing the, quote unquote, "crappy" things I would do in my behaviors. And despite my nervous system being incredibly sensitized for two years straight, and I mean like, terrible symptoms for two years straight, I actually recovered pretty quickly after I stopped caring about it. The hardest part is just reaching the point where you don't care. And truthfully, that just comes from going into the symptoms, and living life as normally as you possibly can, allowing them to come with you, labeling them as what they are, as just products of sensitization, and allowing them to take their time, take as much time as they need to. Not putting timelines on yourself, and not putting this extra stress on yourself, and just focus on responding properly to the symptoms, and not on the symptoms themselves. And I'm sure there'll be people that will say, "Oh, well, your case is different," or "maybe you didn't have it that bad." I had it for two years, and that was two years of constant 24/7 suffering, and I'm not exaggerating when I say, two years straight.

title: Why Your Future Therapy Clients Aren’t Searching for What You Think (SEO for Therapists)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: So most therapists and coaches I work with aren't struggling because they're bad at their work. They're usually struggling because the people who need them can't actually find them. And usually, it's not because they're bad at marketing or selling. It's because clients don't search for help the way we've been trained to talk about it. Before I dive in, just a little context, especially if you're new here. I work with therapists and coaches and heart-centered practitioners who want to be visible without becoming someone that they're not. Uh usually, people who care deeply about ethics and depth and how their words land and what they bring to their clients land, and who still want the right clients to find them. So a lot of what I share here sits at that intersection of psychology, lived experience, and a very practical question. How do we meet people where they actually are and not where we wish they were? And today's topic sits right in the middle of all of that. A potential client doesn't sit down and type: trauma-informed integrative psychotherapist specializing in nervous system regulation. As much as we might wish they would. So, what they actually type looks more like this: Why do I feel on edge all the time? I can't stop overthinking everything. Is something wrong with me or am I just exhausted? I feel fine, but also not fine at all. Those aren't neat keywords, you know, that hit on the spot of what we do. They're more emotional signals and half-formed thoughts like, like late night questions. We all know those. So, they are moments where someone is circling the idea of help without being ready to say the word therapy yet. So, most advice about SEO or visibility focuses on taking or talking about services you already offer, but that completely misses the moment before someone knows what they are actually looking for.

Throughout the recording, she discusses the challenges faced by therapists and coaches in connecting with clients, emphasizing that the issue isn't their skill level or marketing ability, but rather a disconnect in communication. She explains that clients do not search for services using clinical terms, but rather through emotional, raw queries reflecting their feelings of anxiety, confusion, or exhaustion. She shares her focus on helping heart-centered practitioners achieve visibility while maintaining their values, stressing the importance of understanding the client's search journey.

title: Fitness Isn’t Wrong, It’s Just Incomplete
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I wanted to share a few reflections around this post because I think some of the ideas can be a bit unfamiliar at first, specifically when trying to understand what we mean by these big ambiguous terms: movement, movement practice, or movement-oriented approach. I chose to start with fitness as a reference because it's the main cultural lens that many of us have inherited when thinking about the body or when thinking about physicality. One of the more important distinctions that I wanted to start with is that movement is not something that we can push or force back into fitness. It's actually the other way around: fitness ends up being nestled inside of movement. And this is something that I see regularly when I look out in the world and I see how movement is being represented. It's represented as movements, things that we do that are isolated in skill or meant to represent some particular outcome, yet it's not encapsulating this unique wholeness that movement is meant to offer. It doesn't mean that fitness is wrong when we think about this nestling or this being smaller than movement, it just means that it's incomplete. And like I said, fitness culture tends to narrow the conversation of the body towards isolated outcomes: strength, flexibility, aesthetics, performance, body comp, and so on. None of these are bad and they can all be valuable, but they don't represent the whole picture. And what we're calling the whole picture in this case is movement, this larger perspective, this larger ongoing study. Implicitly, the question fitness often asks is how can I improve the look or performance of the parts? What we're more interested in through a movement lens is how do these parts participate in the use of the whole? This shift in this way of viewing changes everything.
caption: An adult male speaks in a reflective and articulate tone, sharing thoughts on the conceptual differences between "fitness" and a "movement-oriented approach." The recording has high clarity with virtually no background interference, allowing his gentle, measured cadence to be heard clearly. He posits that movement is not something to be forced into fitness, but rather that fitness is nested within the broader concept of movement. He critiques how fitness culture often narrows the focus to isolated outcomes like strength, aesthetics, and flexibility, asking "how can I improve the look or performance of the parts?" In contrast, a movement lens invites a more holistic perspective, asking "how do these parts participate in the use of the whole?" He concludes that this shift in viewing the body and physicality changes everything.

title: Glimpse of the PC Space: JA JAYS EDITION
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hi, I'm Chelsea. Hi, I'm Gabby. Hi, my name is Kaylin. Hello, my name's Koey. Hi, I'm Sam. Hi, I'm Amelia. Hi, I'm Jen. Hi, I'm Katrina. Hi, I'm Luke. Hi, I'm Mar. What's up? My name is Aldwin. Hi, I'm Ari. Hi, I'm Danielle. Hi, my name is Hazel. Hello, my name is Caitlin. What's up, y'all? I'm John. And I'm a PC! If you could describe the PC Counseling space in one word, what would it be? And why? Is that a word? Useful. Open. Safe. Intentional. Authentic. Home. Impactful. I would describe it as community. This space has a way of bringing people together, inside and out. The space is very special because it brings a unique perspective, not only on your own life and your own experiences, but on other people as well, and how you want to change, and how you want to build your life moving forward from your situations and your prior experiences. And it's a really great space for reflection. I used to think to myself so much that nobody understands what I'm going through or nobody gets this emotion or feeling I'm getting. But when I entered this space and hearing all the experiences, even though like people haven't gone through the exact situations I've been through, it's that like shared emotion or that shared feeling, and that helped me realize that like, wow, I do have such a support system around me. How has the PC space helped you grow as a mentor towards your students? Just seeing the impact I have on them. All my students are very different, have different personalities, but I love that. Being a mentor isn't all about being perfect. At the end of the day, it's mostly about just being real and being someone that people can authentically look up to. Being someone that gives others a comfortable space to just be. What would you want to say to someone who's hesitant on joining the PC space? Like what Miles Morales says in, like, Into the Spider-Verse, you have to take a leap of faith. You really do. You can definitely go in with a lot of fear. But it's one of those spaces that you definitely grow into and you realize that you're not growing alone. Your presence alone is more than valued in the PC space. To apply as a PC, to get a PC, to come to open practicum, to befriend a PC, you just have to be open. Whether it's open to conversation, open to listening, open to learning, your perspective still matters even if you don't think it does. I, I was in the experience where I was really scared. I was not involved in KP anymore. I knew that it meant doing the commute like twice a week for me. But when you, when you take that first dip in and it's your choice of like if you're going to pull back or if you're going to fully go in, and I think the best choice you can do is just fully go in. What do you love most about the PC space? Oh, no! 100%

title: I Stopped Fearing Anxiety And This Happened
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Sunny days are overrated. That's what I just kept thinking about in this moment. Chasing sun was only a part of a program they gave us. And maybe that's where we get it wrong. Anxiety is not that bad. But, like all things, complexity seems to creep in. The human mind is quite complex. Deals with many things, calculates many decisions, and makes judgments every moment. It is said that mental pain is less dramatic than physical pain. Both are hard to carry, but mental pain seems to stay a little longer. This message hit harder when I landed in South Africa. I didn't really understand it, but at that point, when I reflect on it now as I edit this video, it really hit me. This was a place I always wondered about, place I imagined, place I only saw in pictures and videos, and then I actually was here. And all I can see is the small things that I've never seen before. Different air, different sky, different road in front of me. And you would think at a moment like this, it would be perfect. But then I felt it, that little tiny itch of anxiety. Not some big panic attack, no heavy breathing, just a feeling inside like something was still trying to get my attention. I started asking myself, why is this even here? I'm in the place I always wanted to see, across the ocean, took the longest plane ride of my life, and I'm standing inside something I used to only imagine. So why am I still feeling a little unsettled, uneasy? And maybe that's what anxiety does. It follows you into beautiful places, not always to ruin them. Maybe sometimes, and just sometimes, to ask you what you've been ignoring.

title: Why A Psalm for the Wild-Built Feels Like Therapy for the Soul.
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Becky Chambers' A Psalm for the Wild-Built is a thoughtful, calming story that blends hope, philosophy, and adventure into a deeply human journey. Here's a friendly, engaging audiobook summary style script designed for around 10 to 11 minutes of narration. In a world where people often feel exhausted, disconnected, and overwhelmed by the pressure to constantly do more, imagine a future where humanity actually chose a different path. A future where society stepped away from endless consumption and rebuilt itself around balance, sustainability, and peace. Now, imagine that, one day, after centuries of silence, a robot walks out of the wilderness and asks a simple but life-changing question. "What do people need?" That's the heart of A Psalm for the Wild-Built, a beautifully quiet yet powerful novella by Becky Chambers. This isn't a story packed with giant battles or dramatic twists. Instead, it's the kind of story that gently sits beside you and asks you to think about your own life, your purpose, and what truly makes you happy. And by the end, it leaves you feeling strangely comforted, like someone finally gave you permission to breathe. The story takes place on the moon of Panga where humans once lived alongside robots, but long ago, the robots gained self-awareness and decided they no longer wanted to serve humanity. Instead of fighting, the robots peacefully walked away into the wilderness and humans let them go. Over time, people adapted. Society became slower, greener, and more community focused. Technology still exists, but it no longer controls people's lives. The world Becky Chambers creates feels hopeful because it imagines humanity learning from its mistakes instead of repeating them forever. At the center of this story is a character named Sibling Dex, a tea monk. In this world, monks don't simply live in temples. They travel around offering tea and emotional support to anyone who needs comfort. Dex spends their days listening to people's worries, helping them process emotions, and giving them a brief moment of peace in a busy life. On the surface, it sounds meaningful and fulfilling, but despite helping everyone else, Dex feels restless inside. There's an emptiness they can't explain. A quiet voice keeps asking, "Is this really all there is?" That question becomes the emotional engine of the story.

title: The Psychology of the Self-Doubt Loop: Why Reassurance Never Works
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: In 2016, Casey Neistat ended the most-watched daily vlog on the internet at the exact moment it was still growing. 5 million subscribers, over a billion views, revenue climbing every month. He stopped anyway, telling his audience there was nothing left to say through the format. The metrics were screaming reassurance at him. He ignored them. Seth Godin has published something close to 8,000 blog posts. On his own site, he's written that focus groups and informal feedback are a trap. The people you ask are rarely the ones your work is actually for. He built one of the most cited marketing platforms alive by refusing to let outside opinion gate what got published. Jason Fried co-founded Basecamp on the same refusal. In Rework, he and David Heinemeier Hansson call waiting for perfect information a trap with no exit. Decisions don't get safer the longer you sit on them, they just pile up. Basecamp shipped early and often, without waiting for a chorus of yeses first. Three different fields, same move. All three stopped asking if it was okay and started reading the actual result instead. There's a name for what they refused to do. It comes out of three separate, unconnected corners of clinical research that landed on the same finding without meaning to. Paul Salkovskis' 1985 model of health anxiety, James Coyne's 1976 theory of depression, Adam Radomsky's research on what's called checking by proxy in OCD. Different disorders, different decades, same mechanism. Reassurance lowers anxiety immediately, then the anxiety comes back, often stronger, because the uncertainty underneath it was never actually resolved, just rented for a few hours. I call this the certainty debt loop. Every time you ask for reassurance instead of letting the uncertainty sit, you're not paying off the doubt
