title: Evidence in Nolan Wells case points to an accident, ex-FBI agent says
transcription:
Nolan Wells. He's the 18-year-old whose death during a 4th of July boat trip to a remote Mississippi island is igniting nationwide debate. Jennifer, I want to take a moment to hear what Stephen A. Smith said about this case on Cuomo just a few days ago.

Listen, you're a dad. I'm a dad. We send our children out, and first of all, regardless of what ethnicity, regardless of what color we're talking about here, we send our children out, and you're the only one that doesn't come home alive. I'll be damned if the Chris Cuomo that I know doesn't want answers and doesn't expect answers. You know me, and I'm going to push for answers. So for no one to have answers as to what happens is when the s- is when the suspicion elevates exponentially.

Seeing the video of Nolan is just so heartbreaking. He seems like such a happy kid. Now, the Daily Mail has identified a 19-year-old young woman who Nolan was last seen speaking to. Now, his friends said he chose to stay behind on Horn Island, but with that woman. But the woman's sister is claiming that's not true, he was ready to get back on the boat that he came on. Are all these differing, differing accounts and a lack of understanding concerning to you?

Well, I think two things can be true at once. It makes sense that he went off to see about a girl, as they say, and that they had conversation and that she decided to go back and be with friends. So, I think it's more of a timing issue rather than something that is untrue on either end. I think both can be true at the same.

Nolan's death is going to the Mississippi Grand Jury. The DA said something interesting, that the evidence will not be public until the Grand Jury reviews it first. The DA says this is to protect the integrity of the investigation, and that the Grand Jury will ultimately decide if someone will be charged. Jennifer, do you believe someone could be charged in his death? Is this just an accident gone terribly wrong?

Well, with what we know, in other words, review of all the surveillance information we have with actually getting to hear from one of the- one of the witnesses, one of his best friends that was there throughout the situation, listening to the calls that were made, the Coast Guard contact, as well as the rip tide situation in that area. When you add it all together, what we see publicly seems to be an accident. Having said that, of course there's going to be more information, 60 witnesses interviewed. I doubt if this, from what we know, will come back with a true bill.

All right. Hopefully, the families, both families, get some answers. Jennifer Coffindaffer, thank you. I'll see you soon.

Thank you for watching. Subscribe below and download our NewsNation app right now on your phone and you will get fact-based, unbiased news for all Americans.

title: Barron Trump’s emergency call to police
transcription: Just days before his father's second inauguration last January, President Trump's teenage son Barron placed an urgent call for help to police in London. Quote, "I'm calling from the US," Barron Trump told an operator at the UK's 999 emergency line. "I just got a call from a girl, you know, she's getting beat up," adding, "it's really an emergency." That call's transcript, released by prosecutors, now key evidence in the London trial of 22-year-old Russian national, Matvey Rumyantsev, accused of rape and assault, which he denies. The January attack allegedly witnessed in part by Trump, whose late-night video call to the victim was briefly answered by the defendant, whom Trump would describe in an email to prosecutors as a quote "shirtless man with darkish hair," according to British media covering the trial. The victim reportedly praising Trump in testimony Wednesday, quote, "He helped save my life. That call was like a sign from God at that moment." Barron Trump, the only son of the President and First Lady Melania Trump, keeps a low public profile, with no public speeches and few appearances. His father crediting the teen for his help finding ways to reach young voters. "He knew the youth vote..." On the night of the incident, the operator pressed Trump for details about the victim and how he knew her. Quote, "I don't think those details matter. She's getting beat up," Trump replies, adding, "I met her on social media." British media reporting that the defendant testified today that he told the victim in the fall of 2024 that he was quote "upset" about her talking to Barron Trump. Both the White House and the First Lady's office declined to comment on this case. Tom? Garrett, thank you. When we return at six, we thank you for watching, and remember, stay updated on breaking news and top stories on the NBC News app or watch live on our YouTube channel.

title: JonBenét Ramsey's Dad Responds to Claim She's in Epstein Files | E! News
transcription: John Ramsey is setting the record straight about a new rumor involving his daughter JonBenét Ramsey and Jeffrey Epstein. After a TikTok video recently circulated claiming the child beauty queen is in the Epstein files and that the millionaire convicted sex offender had a relationship with her, JonBenét's father is speaking out. Telling TMZ January 27, "Absolutely no truth to it. I haven't seen this but with AI, anything is possible. I figured one of these days I would be accused of being an Epstein pal. Hasn't happened yet. Internet people can be very cruel." The viral video also alleges that Epstein's co-conspirator, Ghislaine Maxwell, who was found guilty on several charges, including sex trafficking of a minor, was at JonBenét's sixth birthday party. Another claim, John denies. E! News has reached out to John for comment, but hasn't yet heard back. These conspiracy theories come 30 years after JonBenét was found sexually assaulted, beaten, and strangled in the basement of her family's Boulder, Colorado home the day after Christmas. Following her death, authorities initially suspected parents John and Patsy Ramsey, however, they were never prosecuted. Patsy later died in 2006, and the case of JonBenét's mysterious murder remains unsolved.

title: Conference Highlight: Dr. Jennifer Mullan  |   Keynote Speaker of the LMHANJ 2026 Annual Conference
transcription: The first thing I want to say is that this is not my keynote. Just kidding. This keynote is because of you, you know, your work, what you do already in the world. There is probably nothing that I'm going to come here and say that you haven't already felt in your bones, that you haven't taught, that you haven't done in your sessions in some way shape or form, that you haven't even felt like you needed to hide from certain supervisors, clinics, partial care units, nonprofits, dot, dot, dot, dot. Allow yourself to take a breath or two or three, paying attention to any air that's stuck anywhere, if your shoulders are hunched. I would be remiss if I did not talk about my favorite thing in the whole entire world: rage. She's so sexy, you know? You can please close your eyes or look down and receive a little bit of this goodness. I invite you to think of the people before you and the ways that we held grief and joy and love and celebration. And so, my work here today is to bring home even further, a little bit more of what ancestral medicine might mean in our work, what that can look like, and why more than ever, people are thirsty and hungry to talk about what has happened so we can honor it, so we can give it a good, loving death, so we can grieve for all the loss that we've been experiencing, and we can allow ourselves some rage. Are you with me? Hello, I'm Dr. Jennifer Mullan. I am the founder of Decolonizing Therapy, and the author of Decolonizing Therapy. And why I decided to come and speak here is because this is a place where culture meets the ancestral, meets community, meets clinical practice. I wouldn't be anywhere else.

Following this, a soulful and atmospheric chant begins, prompting the audience to reflect on their ancestors and the ways they held grief, joy, love, and celebration. She speaks about "ancestral medicine" and the collective need to grieve, honor the past, and allow space for rage. The audio concludes with her introducing herself as Dr. Jennifer Mullen, founder and author of "Decolonizing Therapy," explaining that she chose to speak at the event because it is a space where culture, ancestry, community, and clinical practice meet. Throughout the recording, a blend of rhythmic, uplifting music and spiritual chanting supports her spoken words, creating a powerful and immersive atmosphere.

title: “Every talk was thought provoking” | Therapists' highlights from EMDR conference 2026
transcription: I've really enjoyed Carson's talk about OCD because I think a lot of what he described is is something that I see a lot in clinical practice and some of the challenges of working with people with OCD is is yeah it's very familiar and really helpful. Lots of new ideas, definitely. I feel like every talk has been kind of very thought-provoking and I've left each of them thinking, "Oh God, I really want to go and read more about that and learn more about it." So there's been lots that I thought I could integrate into my practice. The fact that, um, instead of having lots of speakers, there is just two per session, which means you can go into so much more depth in the topic that is covered and not just little tasters. I particularly enjoyed Silva Neves' yesterday, um, talking about sexuality in a really accepting way and really informative, and encouraging people to, uh, be open about what they don't know and really has made me think about my practice, how I ask questions about sexuality. We've had a lot of really diverse group of speakers. Um, I've enjoyed the balance between research and applied practice. Um, I've enjoyed the opportunity to meet other people, and that's why I come in person because I just think that being able to have those conversations, being able to go to a talk and then afterwards, discuss it with colleagues, that's just amazing. I've loved coming to these conferences and just networking, you always meet new people, always take some cards away with me. It's just brilliant, really. I think it's just a a really good opportunity to meet other sort of EMDR practitioners and and exchange ideas, hear about research, I think there's been some really good research that has been done. Oh my god, I've just come out of the Filippo talk on, um, it was actually a research one, and I was a bit like, "Oh really?" but it was so clinically relevant, really exciting, it talks about the benefits of EMDR for psychosis, just the highlight of the conference for me, totally brilliant.

title: Spoken-Word Quiet Kind Of Heavy
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription:
Lingering memories follow him
like shadows along the wall
The echoes of a screaming past
refusing to fall
Chaos
crashing through his chest
lightning strikes in his lungs, thunder roars in his thoughts and
grey skies left standing there alone and
torn
untamed storm
His mind on endless repeat
every ache silent, looping, every wound carved deeper
heavier
every piece of his soul it chose to take
moment by moment, it consumes a little more
torment after torment
and in the quiet
he whispers
am I something I can't restore?
He begins to feel unfamiliar
a stranger in his own skin
where safety is a memory and fear is moving near
filling every corner of his own mind, every breath, every thought, every space
until even peace feels like
a forgotten place
And still, he searches for calm in the night
finding refuge in fractured light
from the demons that dance
just beyond his sight
His healing moves slow
but it moves
through roads that twist
through paths that bruise
a journey that tests the strength of his soul
yet step by step
he regains control
head held high, eyes sharp awake
though exhaustion whispers
he's still there
because something inside him refuses to break
refuses to bend, refuses to fade
He won't
he can't
a silent vow
through the dark he'll devour
to reclaim his light
from his own shadowed hour

title: Sustainability Strategy Masterclass: Industry Best Practices
transcription: Reinventing the wheel doesn't add value or drive change, whether that's to sustainability strategy or to a carbon footprint. So I always recommend taking a bit of time before you begin designing your sustainability strategy to look at what else is out there. Um, most organizations can benefit from looking at the UN sustainable development goals and the greenhouse gas protocol, and this will give you ideas of potential topics for your pillars, for your focus areas. It's also really important to look at what regulation that your organization either needs to comply with today or is likely to have to comply with tomorrow, because what you don't want is a central sustainability strategy and then an add-on, "this is how we will comply with EUDR", for example. You want a single sustainability strategy that shows, "these are what's important to us, this is how we're going to move the needle, oh, and whilst we do this, this is how we're going to comply with all of the regulation". And then equally, it's always a good idea to look at what your competitors are doing, um, because if you're working in the same industry, you're likely to be facing the same challenges and whilst each organization is unique and I would never expect two sustainability strategies to be the same, it can just be a really good starting point to help you start thinking thematically about where you want to be looking. So, just on that note, these are the sustainable development goals and these are really broad themes that, I, I find it a really useful exercise with any organization to sit down with the sustainability manager or the health and safety and environment manager or the finance officer, whoever it is who's been tasked with coming up with the sustainability strategy and going through these SDGs and saying, "which really apply to your business, how is your business contributing towards climate action, quality education?" and normally two or three will come out that are incredibly relevant to the business and that can be kind of used as the foundation for how that business should think about sustainability.

title: How to Bullet Journal in 2026 (Every New Technique)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: There's a quiet rebellion happening against the algorithm life, a return to the physical world. Australia just passed a law against young people accessing social media, no-phone cafes are popping up in big cities around the world, and traditional gyms are slowly losing ground to wellness centers focused on health and community. These all address a need that can only be met in the physical world: connection. Nowhere is this need for connection more necessary than with yourself. What are you thinking, feeling, doing about your life? Hi, I'm Ryder Carroll, the creator of the Bullet Journal Method, and today, I want to show you why a paper notebook just might be the most radical productivity tool you can use this year. I'll also include specific ways that the Bullet Journal Method has evolved to help us navigate an increasingly busy, digital, and disconnected world. Let's dive in. Bullet Journal is not a notebook or a type of paper. It's a personal operating system that helps you write a better life. We use notebooks as our preferred platform to run that operating system because it helps us go offline and think with less distractions. That said, you can Bullet Journal in any app you would like. So how does this operating system actually work? Here are the four main steps. Record: This is about creating a record of your life using one-sentence journal entries to capture your notes, actions, moods, and events. Each is paired with a symbol to visually categorize them, hence, Bullet Journal. Reflect: This is about regularly reading your record. As the saying goes, "You don't learn from experience, you learn by reflecting on experience." We do this through practicing daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly reflection rituals. These help us become more aware of patterns in our thinking, feeling, and doing that are impacting our lives. Refine: This is about applying any insights we gain from reflection. It's about cutting what isn't working and cultivating what is, which brings us to the last step. Respond: Respond is the most critical step. It's the step that takes us out of our notebooks into the world by taking intentional action based on all the previous steps.
caption:
In this audio clip, a calm, articulate male speaker, identifying himself as Ryder Carroll, the creator of the Bullet Journal method, delivers a structured presentation. His voice is clear, with a deliberate, engaging pace, set against a backdrop of soft, ambient electronic music with a gentle, relaxing beat. At one point, a subtle sound of keyboard typing is heard as a transition. 

He speaks about a growing movement back to the physical world, driven by a need for genuine connection, particularly with oneself. He positions the paper notebook as a radical tool for productivity and self-awareness in a digital age. He clarifies that the Bullet Journal is not just a notebook but a personal operating system, and goes on to explain its four main steps: 'Record' (using brief entries with symbols), 'Reflect' (regularly reviewing entries), 'Refine' (acting on insights), and 'Respond' (taking intentional action in the physical world).

title: I Found My Old Journal...I Didn't Recognize Myself.
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I found an old journal recently. I don't date my entries, I've never been good at that, but I can tell when it was because of the entries around it. But, I can tell that this one is an older one, it's from before my mother passed away. This is hard. I don't know how to be seen. I keep thinking I will open up my mouth and something will come out that makes sense of me, but it never does. I look at other people and it seems so easy for them. They just exist and people respond to them like they matter. I feel like I'm always just on the edge of everything. I want to be heard. I want to express myself. I want to be someone who has something inside of them that's worth noticing. But I don't think there is. Sometimes I think it would just be easier if I just wasn't here. Just... if I disappeared, I wouldn't have to keep failing as a person. This was before my mother died.
caption: In this audio clip, a male speaker is heard reading from an old journal entry, his voice heavy with emotion and trembling as he struggles to speak through tears. The speaker is crying openly, his words interrupted by deep sniffling, shuddering breaths, and soft whimpers. He reads a poignant passage about feeling invisible, unable to express himself, and feeling like an outsider in a world where others seem to exist effortlessly. The reading reaches a deeply somber note as he reads about his past thoughts of wishing he could disappear to avoid "failing as a person." He prefaces and concludes the reading by noting that this entry was written before his mother passed away, adding a layer of grief to the already painful memory. The recording is clear, capturing the raw, intimate nature of his emotional distress with no background noise.

title: Staying | The Cost of Choosing Loyalty Over Safety
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: The hardest battles are often fought in silence. Behind polite smiles, behind tired eyes, behind voices that still say, "I'm fine." Some people carry storms so quietly that even the people closest to them never fully see the rain. And sometimes, the mind becomes heavy for so long that exhaustion starts feeling normal. Thoughts repeat themselves, doubts grow louder. The world slowly loses color and people begin believing they are far less important than they truly are. Pain has a way of shrinking perspective. It whispers things that sound permanent during temporary seasons. It tells tired hearts that nothing will change, that peace belongs to other people, that healing was never meant for them. And slowly, the weight of those thoughts begins to feel real. But thoughts are not always truth. Some people are not trying to leave life behind, they are simply trying to escape the heaviness of carrying everything alone. The pressure, the expectations, the loneliness hidden beneath functioning lives. And sometimes, the people who seem strongest are simply the ones who learned how to suffer quietly. Not because they are weak, but because they became used to surviving silently. One day at a time, sometimes one hour at a time, and occasionally, one breath at a time, there is no shame in surviving slowly. None of us truly know how deeply we are woven into the lives of others. Sometimes, we minimize our importance because pain has made us forget how much of our presence...

transcription: Yeah. Look. You ever feel the storm coming before the first drop of rain even hits? It's a specific kind of terror. When you look around your room and you realize it's happening again. You're watching your own mind slide into the dark, and you can't find the brakes. I can feel it in my chest. Listen. I can feel the exact moment the chemistry starts to shift. The heavy gravity pulling me down, beginning to drift away from the people I love, away from the things that I enjoy. My phone rings and the sound of a simple notification just starts to annoy me. I haven't left my bed in two days, the sheets feel like a prison cell. I'm looking at the clutter in my room, it's just a physical reflection of my mind. Motivation is dead, the creative spark is a ghost. The things that used to bring me joy are the exact things I'm avoiding the most. It starts with a heavy sigh, then it moves to a blank stare, then suddenly you're sitting at the edge of the bed, completely unaware of the time passing by. An hour feels like a second or two. And you're desperately trying to remember the last time you felt like yourself. I'm pulling away from my friends, I'm making up excuses to hide. I'm just tired, I'm busy, I'm good. But the truth is, I am lying. I see the shadows stretching out, and I can hear the train coming down the track. Oh, I can feel it in my bones. I'm headed for the dark again. I'm losing all my focus, I don't know where the light has been. I see the walls closing in, I feel the weight on my chest. I'm trying to fight the shadow, but my spirit can't arrest. Is anybody out there watching themselves start to slip? Losing your footing, losing your mind, losing your grip. I'm screaming at the mirror, trying to make the monster stop. But I'm standing on the edge, and I am terrified

title: Inside Robinhood's Original Pitch Deck: Why Investors Said Yes
transcription: In 2013, two Stanford math graduates named Vladimir Tenev and Baiju Bhatt attempted to pitch a radical concept: zero commission stock trading managed entirely through a mobile phone. At this point, they had been entrepreneurs for the better part of five years. They had built several pieces of financial software for high frequency firms, but they had very little tangible success to show for that time. When they tried to raise money for Robinhood, they ran a brutal gauntlet. They were rejected 70 times, then 90 times. Eventually, 110 investors told them no. The feedback was consistent: professional investors didn't believe people would manage their finances on a smartphone. They looked at the founders' math backgrounds and dismissed them as being incapable of building a product for regular consumers. Many founders react to this kind of rejection by treating their pitch deck like a sales brochure. They try to hide their lack of traction behind flashy design elements or unrealistic multi-billion dollar projections. Robinhood took a different path. They realized that before a deck can sell a product, it has to prove the founders are worthy of trusting. Vlad and Baiju began a process of ruthless subtraction. Instead of adding slides to answer every objection, they cut the presentation down to its absolute essentials. They removed the industry jargon and the dense maps of the financial ecosystem. They focused the entire narrative on one universal problem: the high cost and unnecessary friction of the traditional brokerage model. They avoided the trap of pitching a vague, massive market. Instead, their narrative shrinks the opportunity down to a single, sharp data point. They targeted an underserved generation of millennials wanting to invest, but frustrated by $10 commission fees. This narrow focus made it difficult for investors to dismiss the idea with broad generalizations. By proving they understood one user group better than anyone else, they signaled a level of competence that forced investors to take them seriously. But the digital slides are only half the battle. Eventually, that trust has to be validated by the founders in the room. This reached a breaking point during a meeting with Tim Draper...
caption: In this high-quality audio clip, a woman delivers a clear, professional narration detailing the origin story of Robinhood. Her voice is articulate and engaging, set against a subtle, modern electronic background track. She recounts how, in 2013, Stanford math graduates Vlad Tenev and Baiju Bhatt pitched their concept for a zero-commission stock trading mobile app. Despite having years of experience building financial software, they faced immense difficulty securing funding, suffering 110 rejections from investors who doubted everyday consumers would manage finances on smartphones. Instead of inflating their pitch with complex projections, the founders simplified their presentation, eliminating jargon and focusing on a single, compelling issue: the frustration of millennials facing high commission fees. This strategic simplification ultimately established their credibility and won over investors.

transcription: You know, first of all, we are doing this for her, okay? Because neither one of us wants to get divorced. And second ofly, I know you're the big marriage expert. Oh, I'm sorry, I forgot. Your wife is dead. This might be the most perfect episode of Arrested Development. Not because of any single joke, but how each joke is constructed and told. Where most sitcoms rely entirely on funny dialogue and quips between characters, this show builds comedy through editing, music, narration, and structure. Stacking jokes so each moment works on multiple levels at once. I once saw a tweet that said, "The comedy of Arrested Development folds in on itself so much, we no longer process it as funny, but as beautiful." And no episode proves that more than Season 2, Episode 3, Amigos. Here's some money, go see a Star War. An episode that reaches comedic heights I am constantly in awe of. Amigos opens with a simple exchange between Michael and his brother Gob. On the surface, it's just funny dialogue, but the script is quietly planting seeds. In fact, the callback is probably what Arrested Development is most famous for. The number of times it can put a different spin on the same punch line is kind of ridiculous. Her? Her? Her? Her? Her? transcription: It was a really great way to start the Wednesday morning in Leeds. I think the importance of events like today is making sure that you've got a diverse range of opinions. There's lots of different issues in the planning in the planning system and when we can come together collectively and discuss these issues there's more opportunities for solutions. I'm really passionate about showing the industry that there is a different way to engage and when you do, when you engage the people that are in need of housing, we can speed up delivery, we can give stakeholders more confidence to approve schemes that should be approved and essentially help get the homes that we need delivered. My role is to make sure that actually they're hearing from the people that are in need of new homes, so they got confidence to say yes and they're they're hearing from the wide range of views in their community, not just with kind of self-serving 1%. I found it a really engaging panel discussion. And I think that's demonstrates one of the things that I really like about this event and coming to UKREiiF is that you come here to listen, to learn. As a, an industry, we have to change, we have to adapt. That sometimes takes time to explore like different models of developments. Me personally, in terms of what I do, I had to look at redesigning schemes, you know, to respond to the Building Safety Act. We're seeing like a a trend towards single family housing and away from apartments, which I'm very positive about. It's amazing to be in Leeds at the center of UKREiiF um in an office that is absolutely fantastic, one of you know, one of many we have right across the country, and putting us at the center of, you know, re- of a regional network. You know, we're here to provide that advice, we're in Leeds, not just for UKREiiF, we're here all of the time to provide an absolute A1 service to our clients who want to be in Leeds.

title: Does Civic AI Mean? | Ron Ivey (Noēsis Collaborative) | Civic AI Conference 2026
transcription: With the question that we've been wrestling with today about how should AI care for communities and who gets to decide, I think one of the challenges I have is the it's kind of very fundamental uh kind of premise of that question, whether AI can care. From what I understand and from, you know, talking to and working with uh the developers of these systems, there's there's a real debate whether AI actually cares, where whether it actually has the capacity for empathy, uh whether it has the capacity for moral consideration of others, attentiveness to others, and and really understanding others' uh feelings and perceptions. We already heard this morning about how, you know, the systems themselves cannot distinguish between these issues of of parental sacrifice, which I'm a parent, I'm having to sacrifice every day in terms of my relationships, and child sacrifice. So, just that fundamental understanding of relationship of relational language uh these systems don't understand. So, can an AI care? I don't think so, but could an AI system be designed to support care, to support human relationships? Well, we had already have some great examples from today's conference uh of both in the context of democracy, the use of of AI as a tool to support uh participation uh and engagement and real understanding and legitimacy of bills that are being passed related to synthetic media. That's exciting. Uh we have the application of AI to support uh care and relationship in the healthcare context, in terms of what's happening related to to some of the patients and and getting data that their caregivers can can improve the care. That's exciting as well. And then, in terms of who gets to decide, I think it goes back to this fundamental question of how these systems are built and the power that's that's driving them. Do we have the right kind of cultural framework, uh ethical framework, and the right kind of policy framework to decentralize uh power and decentralize the way these markets are concentrated right now? Until we do that, until we fundamentally deal with the market concentration, the wealth concentration, the power concentration, we'll have challenges on a broader scale in terms of really implementing AI systems that support both those intimate, close relationships and then as the relationships expand into these larger uh contexts of solidarity and trust. Now, that being said, we do have an opportunity, even in the midst of the dominant systems, to to create an alternative ecosystem. To think about funders and investors and inventors and and researchers and policy uh uh experts and local activists and community uh groups. I, you know, seeing inspiring things at the local level where communities are taking control and building their own models, and that's exciting. So, even if we have a dominant system that's can continue to move forward in one direction, there might be a pathway, and I'm hopeful there is a pathway, for alternative systems. It's just about encouraging those and and supporting them and and finding the right kind of resources and uh connecting the dots between those that are doing incredible things in different communities around the world.

title: Broken Bone Healing Process | How Plaster Helps in Fracture? | Bone Fractures | Dr. Binocs Show
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: What are you timing, little kitty? Figuring out how quickly this plaster cast helps my broken bone heal. Ah, then let's find out how does plaster help heal fractured bones? Zoom in! You might think that a plaster cast heals a broken bone. Surprisingly, that's not the case. Plaster doesn't repair the bone itself. Instead, it provides the support and stability your body needs to heal the fracture naturally. In fact, the healing process begins the moment the bone breaks. Firstly, a blood clot forms around the fracture, helping stabilize the fracture site and causing swelling. Meanwhile, specialized white blood cells, including macrophages, remove damaged tissue and prepare the area for repair. Before applying a plaster cast, doctors examine the injury and use x-rays to assess the position of the fractured bone. If the broken pieces are out of alignment, the patient may first be given pain medication or sedation to improve comfort. The doctor then carefully moves the bone fragments back into their proper position in a procedure called a reduction. Once the bone is correctly aligned, the injured limb is wrapped in a protective layer and covered with wet plaster bandages. These bandages can be molded to fit the body shape and gradually harden

title: Hokum - Movie Review
transcription: Caveat, the on-screen video game adaptation that's not—it's not a video game adaptation. Does feel like it at a point though. Let me explain. So Caveat is written and directed by Damian McCarthy, stars Jonathan French. He comes to this house in the middle of nowhere. Long story short, he ends up trapped on an island in a house and he has to get out. Also, it may very well be haunted by a ghost, there is that. Now, that's the flyby version for this movie. We've all heard the hype, you know, people are like, "This is unsettling!" "This will have you at the edge of your seat!" Okay, let's calm down. The movie has creepy moments, sure, but what I liked about this film is it's not cut and dry. It has layers, nuance, depth of character. You take Jonathan French's character. In the setup of this film, I was like, "Well, he's kind of a piece of shit. I hope whatever is haunting that house torments the hell out of him." "Oh, man, I guess everyone has their story." Right? Ha, you know, it's kind of cool that the movie made me do that, made me flip so easily. Not easily, I don't flip easily. The film made it seem easy. Writing, folks, execution, you know, that was when the film really hooked me. And this movie looks solid. It's all about the unsettling imagery, usually in facial expressions. More than a few faces, whether it be little figures, and the film concentrates on them and has that depth of field, or unsettling-ass faces with those Marty Feldman eyes that come on a TV, you're like, "Please stop." The film's effective in that respect, which pleased me because in the buildup, I was like, "Okay, seen a couple jump scares, you're just, you're going to go that route here?" But the film's not built on that, and, okay, fine. I feel bad for people going into this film hearing the creepy hype, you know, hearing the horror movie hype, and I feel like they're going to get let down. Kind of reminds me of Crimson Peak. This movie's nothing like Crimson Peak, but when Crimson Peak came out, it looked like a Gothic horror film, and really it was a Gothic romance, it was just mismarketed that way. Same with the movie Mother!, which looked creepy as hell from the trailer, that's not really the movie. This film, I feel, runs the risk of that same audience letdown because the movie itself is not what it's marketed as. Horror film? It does have horror-ish elements, but it's really about a guy trapped in a house on an island, so he needs to find a way out, also he needs to come face to face and process his own personal demons. And yes, there's possibly a ghost involved. But at a point, this is where the video game reference from the intro of this video comes in, I was like, "This is Resident Evil with no zombies."

title: Doctor on How Screen Time Hurts Kids' Cognitive Development
transcription: Thank you guys. My name is, uh, Dr. Jared Cooney Horvath. I'm a former teacher turned cognitive neuroscientist who focuses on human learning, and I do not receive funding, nor have I ever, from Big Tech. Um, so a sad fact our generation has to face is this: our kids are less cognitively capable than we were at their age. Um, since we've been standardizing and measuring cognitive development since the late 1800s, every generation has outperformed their parents. And that's exactly what we want. We want sharper kids. And the reason for this, largely, has been school. Each generation spends more time in school. We use school to develop our cognition. Congratulations, you see your correlation. Until Gen Z. Gen Z is the first generation in modern history to underperform us on basically every cognitive measure we have, from basic attention to memory to literacy to numeracy to executive functioning to even general IQ, even though they go to more school than we did. So why? What happened? What happened around 2010 that decoupled schooling from cognitive development? It can't be school. School basically looks the same. It can't be biology. This hasn't had enough of time to change. The answer appears to be the tools we are using within schools to drive that learning. Across 80 countries, as Jean was just saying, if you look at the data, once countries adopt digital technology widely in schools, performance goes down significantly. To the point where kids who use computers about five hours per day in school for learning purposes will score over two-thirds of a standard deviation less than kids who rarely or never touch tech at school, and that's across 80 countries. Bring it home to the US. Let's go to the US. We have our NAEP. That's our big data. Take any state, and here's, here's a fun experiment you can try. Take any state NAEP data. Compare that to when that state adopted one-to-one technology widely, and watch what happens. The NAEP data will plateau and then start to drop. Now, as Jean said, of course, this is all correlative. What we really want is causative. To get causation, what you need is academic research and you need mechanisms, explanations for why we're seeing what we're seeing. Luckily, we have academic research stretching back to 1962 that shows the exact same story for 60 years. When tech enters education, learning goes down. In fact, one of the biggest, um, ed psychologists right now, Dylan Wiliam out of the UK, recently said, "EdTech is a revolution that's been coming for 60 years, and we're going to have to wait another 60 because it ain't doing anything." Now

transcription: This decision to launch this operation was based on a cumulative effect of various direct threats that Iran posed to the United States of America, and the President's feeling based on fact that Iran does pose an imminent and direct threat. Secretary Rice, thanks for being here. You know, we have these polls out about Iran, national security threat. You know, most people who answer these polls, it's 61% yes, 38% no. What's your thoughts about where we are right now and where we may be headed? Well, the most important thing, Brett, and thank you for having me, but the most important thing is to recognize that Iran has been at war with us for at least 41 years, all the way from 1979. People may forget they took our embassy hostage 440... 444 days. They were responsible for the killings of 300-plus marines in Lebanon in the early 1980s. And if you ask people about Iraq, what was the source of many of our casualties in Iraq, you'll get estimates as high as 75 or 80% of them were due to Iranian-made roadside bombs. And so they've been at war with us a long time. They also have developed the military capability to have reach outside of the boundaries of Iran, including Hezbollah and Hamas, which they both arm and equip and continue to arm and equip even after the events of the summer. So, to say that this regime was not a threat, I think is simply not... it's ahistorical. They have been a threat for a long time.

title: This Michael Jackson Biopic Feels Off...
transcription: It's been a while since my last video. I had two weeks to give myself just a little break and it's good to be back. What's on the schedule? Oh, f- goddammit. I'll tell you the truth, I've been dreading the Michael video for weeks. I didn't know how I was going to feel about it, but I knew whatever I did say would be met with capital O opinions. Michael Jackson is just that kind of figure. He means a lot to a lot of people and people weren't being normal about this movie well before it even came out. Appropriately so, he's not a normal guy and naturally, this is not a normal movie. Michael, if you're unaware, is the long-awaited Michael Jackson biopic starring his nephew, Jaafar Jackson, which recaps the first half of Michael Jackson's career focusing mainly on his relationship with his father, Joe Jackson, played by Colman Domingo. The film has been on the radar since 2019 and after numerous setbacks, reshoots, and a lot of tinkering, it's here and you can feel all of that interference on the screen. Much of these complications stem from the fact that the script originally focused on the sexual abuse allegations towards Jackson, so much so that the film supposedly opened with that part of his life and looped back around to focusing on the scandal for the third act. But after an attorney for the Jackson Estate discovered a clause in one of the accusers' settlements with Jackson, barring the depiction or mention of him in any movie, things changed. This and some other factors ultimately pushed the film back an entire year, leading to 22 days of reshoots that occurred as recently as last June. And the result is a movie about a flawless protagonist, a really talented guy who, after overcoming some seemingly minor hurdles, became the most famous person on the planet thanks to writing some of the best songs of all time. Michael was, like any musical biopic about a beloved artist, always going to work on me just a little bit. These movies are carried on the backs of some of the best music ever written, they coat themselves in it. title: "No Country Matches India's Energy": Sam Altman's Viral Speech at AI Summit 2026 | News18
transcription:
**Shereen Bhan**: I'm Shereen Bhan and we've got probably one of the biggest headliners here at the India AI Impact Summit, OpenAI's Sam Altman. Sam, great to have you join us on CNBC-TV18. It's wonderful to see you here back in India. You were sharing the stage with the Prime Minister just a few moments ago talking about how important India is, but how significant is India for OpenAI specifically? It is your second-largest market today.

**Sam Altman**: It is our second-largest market and the energy here, that people are, what people are building with the technology is just amazing to watch. We have more than 100 million weekly active users of ChatGPT. This is the fastest-growing market for Codex. And it's, it's amazing to see the energy here. **Shereen Bhan**: Sam, can you give me a sense of what we can expect now from OpenAI for India? How much can you customize OpenAI and ChatGPT for India? What should we expect?

**Shereen Bhan**: Is that something you are going to double down on?

**Sam Altman**: Totally. Everything changed since you left. Skeletor. Skeletor took my family and he destroyed our world. It's all my fault. I know how it feels to fail. Take this sword. And when you fall, that's your chance to stand tall. I have the power! The very Earth shall quake and shudder. This is my home. I'm going to fight for it. But I can't do it without you. Somebody wants to brawl. I need every man, woman, or... whatever that is. You may have the power, but you're too scared to use it. Trust me, I know how to use it. You tell everyone that you're from another planet. It just makes you sound a little, very crazy.

title: 'What are we doing here?': Fmr. fed judge slams Trump admin naming 'worst of the worst' judges

He's name-checking them on social media over their immigration-related rulings the Trump administration disagrees with at a time when threats against judges are escalating. And that phrase, "the worst of the worst," you've probably heard it before because Percival is borrowing that from the department's description of undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes. Joining us, former Chief Judge for the US Middle District of Pennsylvania, appointed by President George W. Bush, John Jones, III. He's currently the president of Dickinson College. Judge, uh, Jones, thank you so much for joining us. Just your reaction, first off, to this DHS, this, this administration official posting judges' names.

And, uh, he's also showing, uh, the, the, a picture of, uh, my, my good friend, uh, Esther Salas, uh, who's a judge, as you know, in New Jersey who lost her only child, her son, uh, shot by an assailant a couple of years ago. This is really, my view, uh, beyond the pale. And I guess Mr. Percival missed the hearing a couple weeks ago, uh, with, uh, Justices Kagan and Coney Barrett, uh, who, as you just said, indicated that the threat level is higher than it has ever been, uh, for judges and for justices. And James Percival, I should say, is the General Counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, and it's stunning that someone who is in that position is doing this. Every "I'm sorry" came with more resistance.

but I found my voice.

I was broken by abuse,
but I'm not destroyed.

Thought if I was better, it wouldn't hurt.

But healing showed me what I couldn't see.

The pain you gave had nothing to do with me, no.

I'm unlearning all the lies you told.

Rebuilding a heart that was left in the cold.

Piece by piece, I'm choosing me.

Learning what safe love is supposed to be.

You tried to break me down to feel in control.

title: Dax – “My Silence Was Crying for Help” (2026 Lyrics Video)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: The loudest cry ever made, was the one nobody heard. Stopped asking for help, and everybody thought I was healing. And everybody thought I was healing. I became the friend everybody leaned upon. The one who stayed steady when everything went wrong. Always saying, "I'm good" with a practiced smile. Even though I've been breaking for a long, long while. I mastered the art of hiding in plain sight. Laughing in daylight, unraveling at night. Every "I'm okay" felt heavier to say. Because the truth kept begging me, not to look away. I answered every message, returned every call, but nobody noticed I was disappearing through it all. Not because they didn't care, maybe because I became too good at pretending I wasn't hurting. How do you explain a wound nobody can see? How do you ask for rescue, when you've convinced everyone you're free? My silence was crying for help. Every quiet moment said my name. I smiled so nobody would worry, while carrying invisible pain. My silence was crying for help, but nobody knew what to hear. Sometimes the strongest disguise is looking like you're doing fine. The hardest conversations that ever left my chest, I rehearsed them a thousand times, then buried every sense. I wasn't afraid of being judged, I was afraid of becoming a burden, so I carried everything myself until my own heart began to feel too heavy to lift. People celebrated the version of me they could see, nobody met the exhausted soul trying to survive behind closed doors. There were nights I stared at the ceiling not asking for answers, just hoping.

What did Donald Trump know, and when did he know it, about Jeffrey Epstein's child sex trafficking? From that reporting, quote, "In July 2006, just as Jeffrey Epstein's criminal sex charge became public, Donald Trump called then Palm Beach Police Chief Michael Reiter to tell him that Epstein's activities with teenage girls were well-known in both New York and Palm Beach." Reiter recalled his conversation with Trump in a 2019 interview with the FBI. More from the reporting, quote, "Thank goodness you're stopping him, everyone has known he's been doing this," Trump told Reiter. Reiter told FBI agents that Donald Trump revealed that Epstein's associate Ghislaine Maxwell was Epstein's, quote, "operative," and that Donald Trump said, quote, "She is evil," and to focus on her, according to the reporting. Trump told Reiter that, quote, "He was around Epstein once when teenagers were present, and Trump got the hell out of there," the report said. Donald Trump also told Reiter that he threw Epstein out of his Mar-a-Lago club. A Justice Department official tells us that, quote, "We are not aware of any corroborating evidence that the president contacted law enforcement 20 years ago." Well, this squares with something the White House has said in the past, it does not square with what Trump has said himself about the past. This is from 2019, the days after Jeffrey Epstein's arrest. Did you have any suspicions that he was molesting young women? Underaged women. No, I had no idea. I had no idea. I haven't spoken to him in many, many years. title: Break The Cycle | A Song About Generational Healing, Hope & Family Restoration | Renee Solace
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hum. We learned to whisper when our hearts wanted to cry. We learned to smile while something inside of us died around this table. There were stories never told. Generations carrying burdens that were never theirs to hold. We inherited silence. We inherited fear. We inherited wounds. No one knew were still here. But healing begins the moment someone says, enough. Break the cycle. Let love speak louder than the pain. Break the silence. We don't have to live this way. What was handed to us doesn't have to stay today. Healing has a new beginning today. The hurt stops with me. Break the cycle. Oh. Maybe grandma never knew how to say, I'm sorry. Maybe daddy learned that tears made him weak. Maybe mama carried more than anyone could see. Maybe everybody was surviving but nobody was free. We became experts

transcription: The world is changing faster than ever before. The challenges are growing, but so are the opportunities to find solutions together. The German-American Trade and Tech Dialogue is a high-level transatlantic platform dedicated to strengthening cooperation between Germany, Europe, and the United States. For decades, our partnership, trade, and dialogue have shaped the world. We must make room for new priorities, address emerging challenges, correct long-standing imbalances, and set clear expectations for a sustainable relationship that can carry us through the next 80 years of partnership and beyond that. In three online workshops and one conference, the Aspen Institute Germany brings together leading voices from politics, business, science, and civil society, discussing topics like AI, innovation, tariffs, and the future of transatlantic relations. And the relationship between Germany and the United States, this is far more than a unique historical friendship. It's a strategic alliance rooted in shared values in democracy, the rule of law, free trade, and the conviction that innovation drives progress. Today, over 1.5 million people work transatlantically. 1/5 of all European exports cross the Atlantic heading toward the future. Mutual transatlantic investments that build trust. Join us at the German-American Trade and Tech Dialogue to bridge divides, strengthen cooperation, and shape a transatlantic future built on shared values and a vision of unity.

title: DevOpsDays Zürich 2026 Recap
transcription: It was my first time attending the DevOps Days here in Zurich, and I really enjoyed the different perspectives people bring in from cultural backgrounds. The one main thing I'm looking forward to at the DevOps Days is talking with people about specific topics, either you bring your own or they bring some in. This year we have the theme bubbles, so it's a really bubbly DevOps Days that we have. My favorite format are the open spaces, because there you can bring in your topics. I attended an open space about how to bring more women in tech, and the way the whole thing was introduced, the rules, it really made, made it easy to be there and contribute. Yeah. I love about the DevOps Days the community. There's so many nice and friendly people, it's always a good groove, it's really, really nice. My favorite moment was being very welcomed by the community, and I'm really looking forward to the next year. Next year, 2027 is our 10-year anniversary, and it will be great, many surprises. Stay tuned!

title: Just do the right thing. The rest doesn’t matter.#Selflessness#PersonalGrowth#selfimprovement
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: On action and duty. Great ideas from the book Meditations by Marcus Aurelius. Just do the right thing, the rest doesn't matter. That quote is basically saying focus on what you can control, and let go of what you can't. Here's what that breaks down to. 1. Just do the right thing. This is the part you can control. It's about your own choices, your own actions, and your own character. Is it kind? Is it honest? Is it helpful? Does it align with who you want to be? Your job is to figure out the right, decent, ethical thing to do in a situation and then do it. That's your duty. 2. The rest doesn't matter. This is the part you can't control, so don't let it paralyze you or stop you from doing your duty. What other people think of you for doing it, whether you'll get credit or even be thanked, whether it will be successful or work out perfectly, how hard or scary it feels. The outcome, sometimes, you can only control your effort, not the final result. Think of it like this. You see someone drop their wallet. The right thing is to pick it up and give it back to them. So you do it. The rest, that doesn't matter. Whether they are suspicious of you, whether they say a heartfelt thank you or just grunt, or whether you're late to your next appointment because you stopped. You did your part. The rest was out of your hands. In a nutshell, pour your energy into being a person of good action. Don't waste your energy worrying about the noise, the results, or the opinions that follow. Your peace comes from knowing you did what you should, not from how the world reacts. It's a call for integrity over image, for courage over comfort, and for focusing on your own behavior in a world you can't control.

transcription: आशीष, आपसे शुरुआत करते हैं। इंडेक्स स्टॉक पहले BEL। क्या एक्सपेक्ट करें? स्टेडी नंबर्स यहां पर देखने को मिल सकते हैं। अच्छा BEL में ख़ास बात ये होती है कि मैं ब्रोकरेज हाउस की रिपोर्ट्स पढ़ रहा था कि क्वार्टरली बेसिस पर हर बार क्योंकि प्रोडक्ट मिक्स अलग-अलग होता है तो हर बार मार्जिन एक जैसे या फिर हर बार मार्जिन में ग्रोथ आप एक्सपेक्ट करके नहीं चल सकते। ख़ास बात होती है कि आर्डर बुक कैसी है, एग्जीक्यूशन कैसा देखने को मिला और टॉपलाइन कैसी है। ये BEL के केस में बड़ा इंपॉर्टेंट होता है। तो सबसे पहले आप देखें तो टॉपलाइन काफी हेल्दी है, कारण ये कि आर्डर इनफ्लो बहुत अच्छा रहा है। पूरे FY24 में देखें या क्वार्टर 4 में, तक़रीबन 14% की बढ़त यहां पर एक्सपेक्टेड है। 10,371 करोड़ का अनुमान मार्केट लगाकर चल रहा है। अगर आप आपरेशनल फ्रंट पर देखें तो स्टेडी क्वार्टर है, हालांकि कोई गिरावट नहीं है, बढ़त भी नहीं है, 2% के आसपास के चेंज आपको देखने को मिलेंगे। और मार्जिन जैसा कि मैंने बताया कि प्रोडक्ट मिक्स के ऊपर बहुत ज्यादा डिपेंड करता है तो जो 30.6% का एबिटा मार्जिन पिछले साल थे, अब इस बार 27.4 देखने को मिल सकते हैं और मुनाफे का आंकड़ा भी बिल्कुल फ्लैट है, कोई बढ़त नहीं है, सिर्फ 3% की ग्रोथ यहां पर देखने को मिलेगी। लेकिन बड़ा इंपॉर्टेंट होता है कि एग्जीक्यूशन कैसा है। तो इस क्वार्टर के दौरान एग्जीक्यूशन क्योंकि वैसे भी इनकी तरफ से जो अपडेट आया था क्वार्टर 4 का, उसमें पता चल रहा था कि एग्जीक्यूशन बढ़िया देखने को मिला है और आर्डर इनफ्लो की बात करें तो 11,200 करोड़ के आसपास यानी पिछले साल के मुकाबले 30% ज्यादा है। एक्सपोर्ट की रेवेन्यू, एक्सपोर्ट के ऑर्डर्स ये लगातार बढ़ रहे हैं, पिछले साल के मुकाबले एक्सपोर्ट की रेवेन्यू 34% बढ़ सकती है और ख़ास तौर पर इनका एग्जीक्यूशन इनके की-प्रोडक्ट्स में कैसा है, इसका मार्केट पर ज्यादा फोकस रहेगा। नंबर्स के लिहाज से आप एटलीस्ट स्टेडी नंबर्स एक्सपेक्ट करके चल सकते हैं। स्टेडी नंबर्स फ्रॉम BEL। ये आशीष ने अगर आप देखें, एक्सपेक्टेशन जाहिर की, पूर्वानुमान में।

title: TCS Q4 Results 2026 : Tata की कंपनी ने रचा इतिहास, शेयर पर दिखेगा सीधा असर! | BIZ Tak
transcription: नमस्कार, आप देख रहे हैं बिस्तख और मैं हूं आपके साथ चिराग ठाकुर। देश की दिग्गज आईटी कंपनी टाटा कंसल्टेंसी सर्विसेज यानी कि टीसीएस ने गुरुवार को अपने चौथे तिमाही के नतीजे जारी किए, जिसमें कंपनी का प्रदर्शन मजबूत रहा। कंपनी का कंसोलिडेटेड नेट प्रॉफिट सालाना आधार पर 12% बढ़कर ₹13,718 करोड़ पहुंच गया। पिछले साल इसी तिमाही में यह ₹12,224 करोड़ था। कंपनी ने ₹31 प्रति शेयर का फाइनल डिविडेंड घोषित किया है। इससे निवेशकों को सीधा फायदा मिलेगा। टीसीएस का ऑपरेशन से रेवेन्यू 10% बढ़कर ₹70,698 करोड़ हो गया है। कंपनी को यह फायदा ऐसे समय में हुआ है जब आईटी सेक्टर आर्टिफिशियल इंटेलिजेंस में नए-नए बदलाव के कारण उतार-चढ़ाव भरे दौर से गुजर रहा है। इस कारण कंपनी के शेयरों में हाल में बड़ी गिरावट आई थी। टीसीएस ने इस तिमाही में 12 अरब डॉलर की कुल डील वैल्यू यानी कि टीसीबी हासिल की है। जिसमें तीन बड़ी मेगा डील शामिल है। कंपनी की विकास दर में आर्टिफिशियल इंटेलिजेंस की भूमिका सबसे अहम रही है। कंपनी की सीओओ आरती सुब्रमण्यम के अनुसार FY26 एआई अपनाने के मामले में एक निर्णायक साल रहा। चौथी तिमाही में कंपनी का सालाना एआई रेवेन्यू 2.3 अरब डॉलर के पार निकल गया है। टीसीएस ने अपने हाइपरवोल्ड निवेश के जरिए ओपनएआई, एएमडी और एबीबी जैसी दिग्गज कंपनियों के साथ रणनीतिक हाथ मिलाया है। कंपनी ने इंटरप्राइज ट्रांसफॉर्मेशन, डिजिटल इंजीनियरिंग और क्लाउड मॉर्डनाइजेशन जैसे क्षेत्रों में मजबूत डील्स हासिल किया है। कंपनी ने माना की वैश्विक आर्थिक चुनौतियां बनी हुई हैं लेकिन ग्राहकों का टेक्नोलॉजी निवेश पर भरोसा मजबूत है। नतीजों के ऐलान से पहले बीएसई पर टीसीएस का शेयर 1.09% की तेजी के साथ ₹2587.75 पर बंद हुआ। एक्सपर्ट का मानना है कि शानदार मार्जिन और एआई क्षेत्र में कंपनी की बढ़ती पकड़ आने वाले समय में स्टॉक को और मजबूती दे सकती है। इसके अलावा, टीसीएस ने 1 अप्रैल से सभी ग्रेड के कर्मचारियों के लिए सालाना सैलरी बढ़ोतरी लागू करने का ऐलान किया है। हालांकि, इस बार कितनी बढ़ोतरी होगी इसका खुलासा नहीं किया गया है। खास बात यह है कि कंपनी एक तरफ सैलरी बढ़ा रही है तो दूसरी तरफ कुल कर्मचारियों की संख्या में सालाना आधार पर कमी भी देखने को मिली है। हालांकि, इस बार सबसे बड़ा सवाल यही है कि सैलरी में कितनी बढ़ोतरी होगी। कंपनी ने अभी तक हाइक का परसेंट स्पष्ट नहीं किया है। पिछले साल FY25 में टीसीएस ने सैलरी हाइक में करीब 5 महीने की देरी की थी और सितंबर 2025 से इसे लागू किया गया था। उस समय औसतन 4.5% से 7% तक की बढ़ोतरी दी गई थी। जबकि बेहतर प्रदर्शन करने वाले कर्मचारियों को डबल डिजिट हाइक मिला था। आप टीसीएस के नतीजों के बारे में क्या सोचते हैं, कमेंट करके हमें जरूर बताएं और बने रहे बिस्तख के साथ।

title: Afroman speaks after winning civil lawsuit
transcription:
A jury has sided with the rapper Afroman in the civil lawsuit filed against him by Adams County deputies. WCPO 9 News reporter Jay Shakoor is live outside the courthouse tonight. This verdict, Jay, was read right about 30 minutes ago, and you spoke to Afroman as he was leaving. What's his reaction?

That's right, Afroman had a very emotional reaction, the jury, as you mentioned, siding with the rapper Afroman, whose real name is Joseph Foreman, in this case. Here's video from inside the courtroom as this case went on. During closing arguments, the attorney representing the deputies in this case claimed Afroman intentionally lied about and defamed the deputies in his songs, but Afroman's attorney maintained throughout this trial, it is his right to say what he wants to say. This goes back to 2022 when Afroman's home was raided following search warrants related to possession and trafficking in drugs and kidnapping. Though he was never charged, the attorneys for the deputies suing say Afroman used security video from the raid on his home and put it in a music video using deputies' likenesses without permission. Again, this jury in Adams County finding he did not defame those deputies. Here is Afroman speaking directly after that verdict.

I didn't win. America won. America still has freedom of speech. It's still for the people, by the people.

Afroman becoming emotional there as he says this fight was bigger than him. It was about free speech and what he describes as corruption in this sheriff's department. I spoke to one supporter who came all the way from Dallas. I have more on that and more reaction from the rapper tonight at 11:00. In Adams County, Jay Shakoor, WCPO 9 News.

title: South Asian Conference on Extreme Loadings 2026
transcription: Extreme loads, unpredictable, dynamic and often devastating. From earthquakes and blasts to high winds, impacts and fire, structures are constantly challenged beyond conventional design limits. Designing for such extremes demands advanced analysis, innovative materials, and resilient engineering solutions. To address these challenges, leading experts come together at South Asian Conference on Extreme Loadings 2026. The conference is organized by the IAPS Sri Lanka Chapter in collaboration with UNIGAP and GAP HQ, bringing together global experts, researchers and industry professionals to share cutting-edge insights in protective structures and extreme loading design. Selected high-quality papers will be published by Springer Nature. Be part of SCEL 2026, contribute, collaborate, and lead the future of resilient design. We look forward to your submission at South Asian Conference on Extreme Loadings 2026.

transcription: एक तो ये बाली की जो डिस्कनेक्टिंग फ्लाइट थी यार, SpiceJet... किया है अपनी सुरक्षा में ट्रैवल? आपको पता है आजकल, आजकल पायलट इसको चालू कैसे कर रहा है? मैं चढ़ी हूँ उस फ्लाइट में पहली बार मेरे साथ ऐसा हुआ है कि मेरे अराउंड पांच बुड्ढे बैठे हैं, ठीक है, फार्टिंग नॉनस्टॉप। बिना पासपोर्ट के जर्मनी गई हूँ मैं क्योंकि जो गैस चैम्बर बना दिया था, पायलट अनाउंसमेंट कर रहा है, "Currently we are facing some turbulence from the inside of the aircraft. अरे, राजेश जी, रुक जाइए।" एयर होस्टेस इन बुड्ढों को इंस्ट्रक्शंस दे रही है कि "ये इमरजेंसी एग्जिट है, इसको खुला ही रखेंगे।" वो सेफ्टी के लिए सीट बेल्ट लगा रहे हैं... कह रही है, "आप हमारी सेफ्टी के लिए मत लगाइए। सर, उसपे और प्रेशर मत डालिए।" पता है, इन बुड्ढों ने एकदम फार्टिंग का रिले रेस बना लिया था। एक का ख़तम हो रहा था, दूसरा बोलता है, "I'll take it from here." मैं आपको कैसे समझाऊँ, गाइज़, इस फ्लाइट में अगर अल-कायदा भी होता, वो भी अपने हाथ खड़े कर लेता यार और फिर नाक पे डालता। वो भी अपने सुपरवाइजर को कॉल कर रहा है, "हाईजैक करने आये थे, हॉस्टेज बनके रह गए हैं। सौ-दो सौ ज़्यादा ले ले, लैंड करा दे भाई, जान..." पता है, आप देखोगे, आपके अराउंड जब भी बुड्ढे बैठे हैं ना, तो आपको कभी कोई ज़रुरत ही नहीं पड़ेगी उनसे कुछ पूछने की। वो खुद ही अपना चिट्ठा आपको बताने लगते हैं। ऐसे कह रहे हैं, "बेटा, हम तो एयर फोर्स में काम किया करते थे।" अंकल, आप एयर फोर्स हैं। काम तो आप ज़बरदस्त कर रहे हो यार। अचानक से एक अंकल की तबियत बहुत ख़राब हो गई पीछे। ऐसा लग रहा है उनको हार्ट अटैक जैसा कुछ आ रहा है। तो पायलट कह रही है, "Any doctors? Any doctors, please come help." Next thing we heard, guys, was the absolutely worst thing we could have heard.

title: HOW OUR INDIAN EDUCATION SYSTEM FAILED US | StandUp Comedy by Rahul Dua | 2026
transcription: मैं तो CBSE में पढ़ा हूँ right तो CBSE में 6th class में algebra हमारा introduce हुआ है तो हमारी class teacher maths पढाती थी वह अपना लगी हुई है। बच्चों से लेकर teacher तक किसी को X नहीं मिल रहा है। अपना लगी हुई है। तो मुझे समझ नहीं आ रहा है मेरे को ऐसा लग रहा है कि जब X मिल जाएगा बता देगी यह। तो मैं अपना अपने दोस्त से बात करनी शुरू, मैंने अब मैं बात करनी शुरू करी ही है, मैंने तो hello का 'है' बोला, 'है'। मेरे यहाँ आकर चौक बजा चौक। रविंद्र जडेजा ने मुझे खड़ा किया। मुझे मुझे मुझे मैडम ने खड़ा किया। मुझे खड़ा करके कहती, कहती, 'बात क्यों कर रहे हो?' मैने कहा 'बात क्यों कर रहे हो' का क्या मतलब है? बात इसलिए कर रहे हैं क्योंकि man is a social animal. बिना बात किए उससे रहा नहीं जाता, societal construct है यह। यह अभी तो पढ़ाया मैडम moral science में। मैम however obviously in absolutely no mood for any sort of explanation, मैडम ने मुझे 5 मिनट पूरी class के सामने अच्छे से झाड़ा है जो है। और 5 मिनट डांटने के बाद मुझसे कह रही, 'You have wasted 5 minutes. There are 60 students in the class. You have in total wasted 300 minutes.' मैने कहा 'मैम, मैम, time has been wasted in parallel. Not in series. मैम, you have disturbed 60 students. I was at max going to disturb one. That too for 5 seconds only. ओए टिफिन बचा है? नहीं बचा, ओहो that's it.' तो मैम, maths भी ख़राब है, logic भी ख़राब है आपका। और moral science के तो हाल हम देख ही लिए हैं। Zero civic sense. I believe that the Indian schooling system is horrible. या तो गलत पढ़ा रहे हैं या unnecessary पढ़ा रहे हैं। English हमें गलत पढ़ाई हुई। अंग्रेजी मुहावरे आधे अधूरे पढ़ा के छोड़ रखे हैं। I recently got to know that 'Jack of all master of none' is an incomplete proverb.

title: Ayushman card kaise banaye | how to apply Ayushman card online | ayushman bharat kyc kaise kare
transcription: তো বন্ধুরা তোমরা কিন্তু আগের ভিডিওতে অনেকেই কমেন্ট করেছ যে দাদা, যে আয়ুষ্মান ভারত নতুন কার্ডের জন্য কিভাবে আপনারা অনলাইন আবেদন করবেন, সেটা নিয়ে ভিডিও বানাও। তো সেজন্য আজকের ভিডিওতে আমরা দেখে দেব যে আয়ুষ্মান ভারত নতুন কার্ডের জন্য কিভাবে আপনি অনলাইন আবেদন করবেন, নিউ এনরোলমেন্ট কিভাবে করবেন তার স্টেপ বাই স্টেপ প্রসেস দেখে দেব, যাদের কিন্তু ৭০ প্লাস বয়স তারা অনলাইন আবেদন টা কিভাবে করবেন এবং আয়ুষ্মান ভারত নতুন কার্ড কিভাবে পাবেন, সেটা আপনাদের স্টেপ বাই স্টেপ দেখিয়ে দিচ্ছি এবং যাদের ৭০ প্লাস নিচে এবং যাদের আর কে এস ওয়ান টু রেশন কার্ড রয়েছে, তারা নতুন কার্ডের জন্য কিভাবে আবেদন করবেন বা কিভাবে কার্ডটি পাবেন সেটাও কিন্তু এই ভিডিওতে আমাদের স্টেপ বাই স্টেপ জানিয়ে দিচ্ছি। সেজন্য ভিডিওটা প্রথম থেকে শেষ পর্যন্ত অবশ্যই দেখবেন মনযোগ সহকারে এবং আমাদের চ্যানেলে প্রথমবার ভিজিট করে থাকলে, আমাদের চ্যানেলটিকে সাবস্ক্রাইব করে রাখুন এবং পাশে থাকা বেল আইকনটিকে অবশ্যই প্রেস করে রাখুন। তো চলুন আজকের ভিডিওটা শুরু করা যাক। তো সর্বপ্রথম কিন্তু আপনি আয়ুষ্মান ভারত যে অফিশিয়াল ওয়েবসাইট এখানে চলে আসবেন। প্রথম আপনাদের দেখিয়ে দিই যাদের ৭০ প্লাস বয়স তারা নতুন কার্ড কিভাবে অনলাইন আবেদন করবেন সেটা দেখিয়ে দিই। তারপরে যাদের কিন্তু ৭০ বছরের নিচে এবং যাদের আর কে এস ওয়ান টু রেশন কার্ড রয়েছে তারা নতুন কার্ডের জন্য কিভাবে আবেদন করবেন সেটা আপনাদের জানিয়ে দেব। দেখতে পাচ্ছেন লেখা রয়েছে যে আয়ুষ্মান ভারত নতুন কার্ডের জন্য অ্যাপ্লিকেশন সিনিয়র সিটিজেন যাদের ৭০ প্লাস বয়স এখানে ক্লিক হেয়ার টু এনরোল এই অপশনে ক্লিক করবেন। এবার এই অপশনে ক্লিক করে দেওয়ার সঙ্গে সঙ্গে তার নেক্সট পেজ কিন্তু আপনার সামনে ওপেন হয়ে যাবে। এর পর আপনি কি করবেন? এখানে আধার নাম্বার বসিয়ে ক্যাপচা বসিয়ে আপনি সার্চ বাটনে ক্লিক করবেন। এবার যদি এরকম শো হয় যে নো রেকর্ড ফাউন্ড ক্লিক হেয়ার ফ্রেশ এনরোলমেন্ট এই ক্লিক হেয়ার অপশনে ক্লিক করবেন। ক্লিক হেয়ার অপশনে ক্লিক করে দেওয়ার সঙ্গে সঙ্গে তারপরে ইকেওয়াইসি পেজ কিন্তু ওপেন হয়ে যাবে। হয়ে যাওয়ার পর তারপরে আধার নাম্বার দেওয়া আছে এবার ভেরিফাই অপশনে ক্লিক করবেন, ঠিক আছে? ভেরিফাই অপশনে ক্লিক করে দেওয়ার সঙ্গে সঙ্গে তারপরে কনসেন্ট ঠিক চিহ্ন মারবেন। ঠিক চিহ্ন মেরে দেওয়ার পর এলাউ অপশনে ক্লিক করবেন। এবার এলাউ অপশনে ক্লিক করে দেওয়ার সঙ্গে সঙ্গে তারপরে সেই ব্যক্তির যে আধার কার্ডের সঙ্গে যেই মোবাইল নাম্বার লিঙ্ক রয়েছে, সেই মোবাইল নাম্বারে ওটিপি যাবে। এবার সেই ওটিপি টা সঠিক ভাবে এখানে বসিয়ে নেবেন। ওটিপি টা সঠিক ভাবে বসিয়ে নেওয়ার পর তারপরে এইভাবে লোডিং হবে। লোডিং হয়ে যাওয়ার পর এরকম পেজ কিন্তু ওপেন হয়ে যাবে। দেখতে পাচ্ছেন এলিজিবল ইকেওয়াইসি সাকসেসফুল। এবার এখানে বলা হয়েছে যে আর ইউ বেনিফিসারী অফ... এখানে দেখতে পাচ্ছেন কতগুলি অপশন দেওয়া রয়েছে। এবার আপনি কোন অপশন সিলেক্ট করবেন? দেখুন যেহেতু নতুন করছেন সেজন্য আপনি কি করবেন সবার শেষের যে অপশনটা, নান অফ...

And, well, the other significance here is that this is the first time that the 6-3 conservative court has ruled against President Trump in one of these major cases that have gone before the court since he returned to power in January. This is, uh, Pamela, a major slap at the President of the United States who has made a major effort over these many, many months to impose all of these tariffs. And just to look at some of the background I have here, over these many months, the, uh, administration has collected $150 billion, billion dollars in these tariffs. So what happens to that money? Um, so yeah, I'm going to take you with, with me as much as I can. I hope I'll be able to film in hospital. Obviously, I won't be able to film in the theater, um, but yeah, I'll see you there. Well, it's just before the procedure. I've had six people visit me so far. I've had someone take my menu, I've had a physiotherapist in here, I've had a nurse in here. Who else we had? The surgeon, two nurses, yeah, the anesthetist, and the anesthetist. So, it's uh, been a busy old time, it's barely stopped, but I just wanted to do a quick update. So, uh, next update, see you on the other side. So, that's it, I'm out the other side. They've given me fentanyl, they've given me morphine. My knee feels like it's been hit with a sledgehammer, but it's not a sharp pain, it's a dull pain, and I'm, I'm not going to lie to you, a little bit out of it. But it's done, it was a success. I think less than an hour ago, I was, was in it. Um, keen to get the PhysioLab thing on as quickly as possible. But yeah, it's not, it's not that bad. I guess the drugs are doing their job. So, yeah, I'll do another update in a little bit and see how I'm getting on, but at the moment, I just think, I think I'm just going to have a nice little sleep now. Yeah. And uh, that's starting to fade off now, so I'm going to have a little bit of dinner in a minute. But, interestingly, they've already put the PhysioLab on me and that cold compression feels absolutely glorious, probably the fentanyl as well at this stage. But so far, so good.

title: I Found My Grandfather's Old Journal, and What I Read Shocked Me!
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: We live our days as if we have an endless supply of tomorrows. But every spring here in Japan, the cherry blossoms remind us of a truth we often try to ignore. A beautiful life isn't one that lasts forever. It is one that blooms fully before the wind takes it away. Every spring, the entire country stops to watch the sakura open. People gather under the trees, lay out blankets, and share food, tea, and be happy together. It's a tradition called Hanami. But if you've never experienced this exact thing in your life, you might not realize what makes the sakura so deeply connected to how we experience life. They only bloom for about 10 to 14 days, sometimes even less. A single strong wind or an early heavy rain can take them all away in one night. And that is exactly why they are so beautiful. If cherry blossoms stayed on the trees forever, nobody would stop to look at them. Since everyone sitting under those trees knows that this moment will not last, they pay attention. They just sit there and soak it in, feeling a deep stillness, aware that the petals are already falling. When I was younger, I used to live as if time was unlimited. I would waste entire days doing things I didn't care about. I would stay in situations that made me unhappy, telling myself I'd change things later. I felt this constant pressure to do everything faster and achieve more, while consistently postponing the things I truly wanted to do. This truth about time really hit me when my grandfather, Daiki, passed away. It happened so quickly that one season, he was sitting with me in his garden, pouring tea and telling me stories. And the next season, his chair was empty, like a petal falling from a branch. After he passed, I was going through his things and found an old journal entry he had written during his last spring. I carry his words with me every single day. He wrote, "Hiroto, the real tragedy of life is how many of our years we waste. The sakura never worries about tomorrow's wind."

Speaking with a slow, deliberate pace and a slight accent, he draws a parallel between human existence and the brief, beautiful blooming of cherry blossoms (sakura) in Japan, explaining how their short-lived nature is what makes them so deeply appreciated during the Hanami tradition. The speaker transition into a personal reflection, recalling how he once wasted time until the sudden passing of his grandfather, Daiki, made him realize how quickly life can change. He closes with a touching quote from his grandfather's journal, reminding the listener not to waste their years and to live fully in the present.

title: Learning How to Learn | The Feynman Technique Explained | Study Method -1

transcription: I think one of the biggest lies students are taught is that spending more time with a book means more learning. Because honestly, most of us have experienced this in our life. You sit with a chapter for hours, you underline important lines, you reread the same paragraph again and again, and by the end of the day, it feels like you studied, but then, someone ask then someone ask you to explain this topic in simple words, and suddenly, your brain goes blank. I used to study like this all the time. I thought if I kept rereading my notes enough times, eventually, everything would stay in my head, but most of the information dissipated after a few days, and the frustrating part was that I genuinely worked hard. And then I came across something called the Feynman technique. It's name it is named after Richard Feynman, a Nobel Prize-winning physicist who was known not just for being intelligent, but for explaining extremely complex ideas in a way almost anyone could understand, and he had this simple core idea that if you can't explain something simply, you don't really understand it yet, and that line stayed with me for long time, because most of us studied in a very passive way. We read, we highlight, we memorize definitions, but we rarely stop and ask ourselves, "Can I actually explain this clearly?" And that's where the Feynman technique becomes powerful. The method i- the method itself is surprisingly simple. First, you choose a topic. It could be anything, a biology chapter, a math concept, a grammar rule,

Whether you're an avid journaler or looking to start this beneficial habit, Joplin can help you organize your entries in a way that makes them easy to manage and review. Let's start by setting up your journal notebook. To begin, you'll need to open Joplin desktop. Once you have the application up and running, take a look at the left sidebar. You'll find a button labeled "New notebook." Go ahead and click on that. A prompt will appear asking you to enter a name for your new notebook. In this case, you should name it simply "Journal." Naming your notebook distinctly helps maintain clarity and keeps everything organized as your digital journal grows. Now that you have your journal notebook created, you can start thinking about how to organize your entries effectively. A well-structured journal system can provide insights and make reference easier over time. One effective way to structure your journal notebook is to create subnotebooks for different aspects of your journaling practice. To do this, look at the file above your journal notebook. There, you will see an option to create a "new subnotebook." For starters, you might want to create a subnotebook titled "Daily entries." This section will be where you jot down your thoughts and reflections every day. It's a space for freeform writing, capturing everything from daily events to personal reflections. Next, consider adding a subnotebook for "Weekly reviews." This section is great for reflecting on the week that just passed. It offers a valuable opportunity to see how your thoughts and experiences have evolved over the past seven days, and help set intentions for the following week. Finally, there's the "Monthly reviews" subnotebook. Monthly reviews are vital for looking at the bigger picture. They allow you to track longer-term goals and assess progress over time. Reflecting monthly provides a macro perspective of your life, habits, and achievements. When you envision this structure in Joplin, it might look like a tree, with "Journal" as the trunk, "Daily entries," "Weekly reviews," and "Monthly reviews" act as the branches extending from it, providing a clear pathway for your thoughts to spread. By organizing your journal in this manner, you create a harmonious and systematic approach that enhances your journaling practice. This customized structure caters to different aspects of life reflection, and makes it simpler for you to navigate through your thoughts and feelings. Once everything is set up, you can start using Joplin to capture your life's details, review your growth, and make journaling an enriching experience.

title: The Smile Nobody Questioned (New Spoken Words 2026)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: I got really good at smiling. So good, that nobody noticed the war happening behind my eyes. I laughed loud, showed up, answered messages with "I'm good". Even cracked jokes while my chest felt like it was carrying a thousand pounds of silence. And the scary part is, after a while, even I started believing the performance. See, depression doesn't always look like darkness. Sometimes it looks like being tired all the time for reasons sleep can't fix. Sometimes it looks like staring at the ceiling at 3:00 a.m. replaying every mistake like your mind signed a contract with regret. Sometimes it sounds like, "You're not enough! You're falling behind! Everybody else figured life out except you!" And you begin to drown in thoughts nobody else can hear. That's the thing about invisible pain. People only notice broken bones, not broken spirits. So you learn survival tricks. You become the therapist friend who secretly needs saving. You become the strong one because strong people aren't allowed to collapse. You disappear into music, into work, into scrolling endlessly at night, hoping distraction feels something like peace. But silence, silence is dangerous. Because when you sit alone long enough, you meet every version of yourself you tried to outrun. The insecure child, the abandoned heart, the exhausted soul. And one day, I realized I wasn't just fighting depression. I was fighting the version of me that believed I had to earn love by suffering quietly. I thought healing meant never hurting again. But healing is actually waking up and choosing to stay, even when your mind tells you to disappear. Healing is messy. It's crying in parked cars, it's canceling plans to breathe, it's admitting, "I'm not okay." before your breaking point introduces you to the ground.
