His delivery is slow and deliberate, filled with raw emotion, shifting from whispered, somber tones to intense, passionate outbursts. The speech is set against a dramatic, cinematic background score featuring melancholic piano chords and swelling orchestral strings that rise and fall in harmony with the speaker's emotional state. He speaks of the facade of smiling to hide a 'war happening behind my eyes,' the exhaustion of invisible pain, and the dangerous nature of silence. The climax of the piece is both intense and hopeful, as the music swells and the speaker passionately declares that healing is not about never hurting again, but rather a messy, daily choice to stay and admit to not being okay.

title: Gen AI in Libraries Conference Poster on AI Tools for Literature Reviews: A Rubric for Evaluation
transcription: Our poster presentation documents the creation of a rubric by a group of librarians at American University to evaluate which AI tools, if any, made sense for us to subscribe to and promote. We ended up creating this rubric ourselves because we couldn't find an already extant tool that fit our needs, and we thought detailing our process might be helpful to other institutions currently considering the adoption of AI tools. Our university librarian asked our department to pilot an AI research tool. This group then decided to review AI tools focused on the literature review process. Literature review tools were selected for a few reasons. One, they're discipline agnostic. We're a social science heavy institution, which tends to be pretty interdisciplinary. Two, faculty, students, and staff all do literature reviews. And three, there are a number of AI tools with literature reviews built specifically in mind. In order to determine how we would evaluate these tools, we met as a group and discussed what we would want a rubric to measure. We reviewed some of the literature related to this, there wasn't much, and determined the questions by consensus. We then created a survey in Qualtrics. We divided up the list evenly between group members, with some claiming tools in which they were particularly interested or had experience with. Then, each member analyzed three to four tools and recorded the results in Qualtrics. Ithaka, the nonprofit behind JSTOR, has created the Ithaka Generative AI Product Tracker that lists generative AI tools that can be used for postsecondary teaching, learning, or research activities. The tracker includes roughly 150 AI tools and counting, many of which support key stages of the research lifecycle, including discovery, understanding, and creation. We went through the entire list and identified 18 AI tools that could help in the literature review process in subject areas within the curriculum at AU. We then developed a shared evaluation framework based on eight criteria. They include, one, access model, whether the tool is free or subscription-based...

title: How to think like a lawyer | Zero-L from Harvard Law School
transcription: Imagine I asked you, what do you learn in law school? Well, you've decided to take this course, so maybe you're more informed than the average person. So instead imagine I asked your college roommate or your parents, assuming they're not lawyers. The image that may come to mind of law school is sun-deprived, bespectacled law students surrounded by large numbers of dusty books, reading intently so they can memorize a bunch of law cases. And don't get me wrong, we do make students read a lot from books, and there's some memorization involved. But that image of someone learning the law by just memorizing things that are already out there is not at all what law school is really about. If it were, law school would be much less fun, and also much less useful. The law is always changing. So if you just learned a number of dry rules, much of what you learned might be outdated by your fifth year in practice. The chief value of legal education is not to know stuff, but to know what stuff to look for, where to find it, how to interpret what you find, what to think when some stuff says one thing, and other stuff says another. And how to use what you find to give legal advice. Let me put this very tangibly for you. If you call up a lawyer on anything other than a very simple question, and without pausing, she quickly gives you a straightforward answer, you should fire her. She's not doing a very good job for you. She's just not thinking like a lawyer. That's a phrase you'll hear a lot in law school, and while we might over-use it a bit, it does capture something important. Law is mostly about questions, choices, and analysis, about thinking and not so much about simple answers. That is the main thing we try to teach you in law school. Yes, we want to teach you a good amount of content about the law. To use an example from a course I teach, civil procedure, we want you to know what claims without subject matter jurisdiction can get jurisdiction by way of being joined to other claims through 28 U.S.C. 1367. If that sounds a bit intimidating at first, that's very normal, it is. But by the end of 1L fall, that knowledge will be at the tip of your brain, or at least somewhere in there.

title: How to Stop Panic Attacks: 5 Tools for Anxiety Recovery (My Story as a Single Mum)
category: Mental Health Vlogs & Personal Video Diaries
transcription: Hi. Today I want to tell you about the day I realized something was very wrong. For months, my daughter had been waiting to go to a big Disney show in Rome, and she was so excited. Really counting down the hours and the days. But when the moment came, as we were getting ready to leave, my body just stopped. I started to feel like I was going to faint, I was sweating, I felt sick to my stomach, and honestly, I thought I had a virus because I didn't even know what a panic attack was yet. I just knew that I didn't have the energy to drive for an hour, find parking, find dinner, deal with the crowds, deal with the loud music, and then drive us both back home. So, eventually my dad ended up taking her to the show so she wouldn't miss it, thank God. But I still remember sitting at home and feeling so much guilt. I felt like a failure because I couldn't be there for her. I felt sad that my dad had to do it on my behalf when he had work the next morning. And if you have ever felt that mom guilt because your anxiety is stopping you from being the parent you want to be, please listen to me. You're not a bad mother. You're just a person whose nervous system is overwhelmed and there is a way back. When I was at my lowest point as a single mother, I had to find ways to heal that were simple, fast, and free because I couldn't afford to pay for therapy. And these are the five things that saved me at the very beginning. First of all, I stopped fighting the panic. I learned that when a panic attack starts, if I fight it, if I resist it, it just stays longer. So I started saying to my body, "Okay, I feel you. You can go through." And I just imagined this kind of wave of electricity going through me. And when I stopped resisting, the attacks started coming less often. Second, Bach Flower Rescue Remedy. This was my safety net. I kept it in my bag everywhere I went. At grocery store, train, social situations. And it helped me feel like I had an escape because the moment I could feel a panic attack arising, I knew I could rely on the remedy to stop it then and there. Third, I had to remove the triggers. So I had to stop putting things in my body that made my heart race

title: Disconnected Management Systems Are Undermining Strategy Execution
transcription: Here we're focusing on strategy and performance, right? And when we talk about strategy and performance, there is a series of corporate processes that are part of this big umbrella that we call strategy and performance corporate processes. So we have governance, we have succession management, we have project management, audits, balanced scorecards, ISOs, certifications, innovation management, KPIs, OKRs, budgets and so much more, right? I'm not going to go through all of these. The idea is there is a number of practices or processes or management models that have, that interact with each other and we call corporate management. And each one of these can have a software to support that practice, right? So you can have a software for OKRs, for example, another software for your BIs or your dashboards or your balanced scorecard, another software for your Scrum projects or task management and so on. So for each of these practices, we have a whole ecosystem of softwares to support that practice, right? And what we've been seeing in organizations is that as you adopt an app or a software for each of these practices, they stop interacting with themselves. This should be practices that are make sense independently, but they're also part of a management system, and they should interact with each other. But when you have apps or softwares for each of these, they stop talking to each other. They start acting as silos of information, right? And this is the reality that we see in most organizations. If we take a look at this chart, this chart is the number of app SaaS apps, on average, for each organization, right? So the average number of SaaS apps. And we see that in 2015, we had only 8 SaaS apps, on average, for an organization. And this jumped to 80 in 2020 in just 5 years, then to 130 in 2022. This is the phenomenon that we call SaaS sprawl or app sprawl, right? It was the proliferation of SaaS applications in organizations, and it just boomed, right? From, in 7 years, from 8 to 130. And all of these specialized apps came about and companies adopted them, and for each activity, each management practice, you had an app for that or you have an app for that. But this created big problems in the organizations, right? Managing SaaS is a new problem for IT. So there are so many providers, that managing it all is a huge problem. And integrating it all is a huge problem. So if you have 8 SaaS applications, and you buy the 9th, okay, you're going to integrate, you know, this new SaaS application with 8 others to connect the information. But if you have 130 apps, and you buy the 131st, how are you going to connect all this? It's- it's impossible, right? So this has become a big pain in, especially in larger corporations.
caption: In this clear and professional audio clip, a male speaker with a noticeable accent, likely Portuguese or Brazilian, delivers an informative talk on corporate strategy, performance management, and the challenges of modern software ecosystems. He begins by outlining various corporate processes like governance, project management, OKRs, and KPIs, noting that each typically has its own supporting software. The speaker then highlights the problem of 'information silos' that occur when these individual apps fail to communicate with each other. To illustrate the scale of this issue, he presents statistics showing the dramatic increase in the average number of SaaS applications used by organizations—growing from just eight in 2015 to 130 in 2022—a phenomenon he terms 'SaaS sprawl' or 'app sprawl.' He concludes by explaining how this proliferation creates significant management and integration hurdles for IT departments, particularly within larger corporations. The speaker's delivery is measured and educational, making the complex topic easy to follow.

title: FP1 Highlights | 2026 Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix
transcription: A brand new race at a very familiar circuit. First practice ahead of the inaugural Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix. George Russell has been disappointed by recent results. A combination of bad luck, poor planning, and a teammate in white-hot form have left him 68 points back in the driver standings, now in third place behind Lewis Hamilton. But he found something in FP1 in Barcelona, topping the tables with a lap time of 1 minute 16.363. Ferrari have brought a slew of upgrades to Spain, including a new front wing and endplate, a redesigned floor, reshaped sidepods, and amendments to the diffuser. Added to the changes already brought in Miami, the Scuderia will be hoping these new bits will bring them much closer to Mercedes. Charles Leclerc got a little sideways at turn 10, trying out unfamiliar aerodynamics. Incidentally, the last Ferrari winner at the circuit was Fernando Alonso in 2013. The two-time champ is one of the two Spaniards contesting the weekend, the other being Carlos Sainz, who failed to finish in Monaco last time out after being tagged twice during the late restart. His first session at one of his two home races this season didn't start too well either. The Williams driver, unable to get going in the pitlane. His FW46 pushed back into the garage for a fix. Once out on track, Sainz caused some consternation for Liam Lawson. "Why, what are these guys doing? Just middle of the track?" "Classic, mate." There was a new look, too, to the VCARBs, Racing Bulls opting for a football-inspired livery and teamwear this weekend as the Copa América gets underway across the pond. Max Verstappen wasn't happy at the outset. "Yeah, I don't know what to make of it, Travis." "Yeah, copy." "Like, one corner I have understeer, then oversteer, everything is... horrendous." The Alpines were looking pretty decent, Esteban Ocon with some tidy laps for a fine P10 at the flag. And there was great news for teammate Pierre Gasly before the session. He's had his P3 from Monaco reinstated after Alpine's right to review his penalties was upheld. He had an issue, though, late on. "Uh, something is broken, guys. I think I need to box." "I can't... turn 4, it's... Yeah, think it's, something with suspension." The Frenchman's repromotion in Monte Carlo dropped Oscar Piastri down to fifth in the final standings. He was the standout McLaren driver in the Principality and put an excellent stint in here in FP1. His best lap just two tenths off the lead and good enough...

title: Ransom Note Clues Revealed | Jesse Weber Live
transcription:
6 months ago tonight. This is after 84-year-old Nancy Guthrie disappeared from her Tucson-area home. The Pima, the Pima County Sheriff's Office has finally released the alleged ransom notes that were supposedly sent by these alleged kidnappers. Now, as you may know, these notes have been the source of more than a little controversy in the months since Today Show host Savannah Guthrie's mother vanished, mostly because we still don't know if they're real. And though the cops still won't verify their authenticity, because of something that I'm going to get into in just a little bit, it is important to read them in full. So here we go. The first alleged note that was apparently sent on February 2nd says this, "Hello, Savannah. We have your mother, Nancy. She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom and once payment is received, she will be released unharmed. We will be holding her for a maximum of 7 days. You will need to send Bitcoin in the amount of $4 million USD, United States Dollars, before 5:00 p.m. on Thursday the 5th. If payment is not received, the ransom will be increased to $6 million USD, which will need to be paid by 5:00 p.m. on Monday the 9th. Once payment is received to the Bitcoin address below, she will be released within 12 hours of deposit to a safe drop-off location back in Tucson. If payment is not received by the last deadline on Monday the 9th at 5:00 p.m., she will be killed. Your mother is aware of this, and her life is in your hands. It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible. You will not be able to contact me from here on out. There will be no negotiation. Do not play games. Law enforcement will not be able to help you. She had a white smartwatch on the floor of the foot of her bed, and the white floodlight in back yard was destroyed."

Then you have the second alleged note. Very different, very different tone. This was apparently sent on February 6th, so 3 days before the deadline from that first note. It says, "Guthrie family, we did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition. We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention. She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart-related. She is buried in nature now. Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this, and hope you can find peace. We are truly sorry."

Now, despite the fact that the Sheriff's Office couldn't authenticate the notes, they are now asking for the public's help in finding whoever wrote them. Said in a press release, quote, "These communications reveal distinctive patterns of word choice, syntax, and phraseology that reflect the writer's unique linguistic style. We believe these distinctive linguistic characteristics may be recognizable to someone who knows or has interacted with the note's writer."
